**Reflection.** This is the sūrah's most complete portrait of what faith looks like under a death sentence, and its center is a grammatical observation: the sorcerers' petition is not for rescue but for patience in what is coming. They had asked God, or perhaps their own art, for a wage that morning; by the afternoon they are asking for the strength to die without recanting. **[Saʿdī]**'s phrase — that the indefinite "patience" points to something great because the trial costs the self — measures the distance between their first request and their last: the same men who bargained for nearness to Pharaoh now ask only to be taken home as submitters [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. And the tradition's verdict on them — sorcerers at the day's beginning, martyrs at its end — makes the verse's last word the truest they ever used of themselves, for *muslim* is not a label they inherited but the state in which they asked to be found [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran].

## 7:127

*"And the notables of Pharaoh's people said, 'Will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?' He said, 'We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are over them dominant.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the council's pressure on the king: the assembly of the men of Pharaoh's people said to Pharaoh, "Will you leave Moses and his people of the Children of Israel" — that is, will you let them be — "to work corruption in the land," that is, to corrupt your servants and slaves against you in your land of Egypt, "and to abandon you and your gods" — to abandon your service and the worship of you and of your gods. And he sets out two interpretations of the phrase. On the first, the clause "and abandon you" is not conjoined to "to work corruption" but stands in the accusative on the pattern of *ṣarf*, the sense being: will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption in the land, when he has already abandoned you, and your worship, and the worship of your gods? On the second, it is conjoined: will you leave them to corrupt in the land and to abandon you and your gods? Ṭabarī's preference is the first, because the reports came that way, and he finds clear evidence for it in Ubayy b. Kaʿb's codex: "and they have already abandoned you, that they should worship you and your gods." He also records that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī used to read the verb with the *wāw* attached to "will you leave" — "and he abandons you" [Ṭabarī]. On "your gods" he notes that the reciters of the cities read *ālihataka* with the *hamza* vowelled by *fatḥah* and prolonged, "your gods," and he records from Ibn ʿAbbās that Pharaoh had a cow which he worshipped. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid that they used to recite it *ilāhataka* with *kasrah* on the *alif*, meaning "and your worship" — that is, he abandons your worship, the sense being that Pharaoh was worshipped, not a worshipper. Ṭabarī's verdict is that the reading of the cities is the one not to be departed from, by the consensus of the authoritative reciters [Ṭabarī]. He then gathers the reports on Pharaoh's gods: al-Suddī from Ibn ʿAbbās, that his gods were cattle — when they saw a fine cow they were ordered to worship it, and that is why a calf and a cow were brought out for them; al-Ḥasan, that Pharaoh had a bead (*jumānah*) hung at his throat which he worshipped and prostrated to; and al-Ḥasan again, in two reports: it reached me that Pharaoh used to worship a god in secret; and he had a god he worshipped secretly. And on the reading *ilāhataka*: Ibn ʿAbbās, by ʿAmr b. Dīnār and Muḥammad b. ʿAmr b. al-Ḥasan, said that Pharaoh was worshipped but did not worship [Ṭabarī]. Then the answer of Pharaoh: "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are over them dominant" — the reading *nuqattilu* with intensification, or *naqtulu*, both carried; that is, the same policy he had inflicted on them at the time of Moses's birth, renewed [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the gloss on "to work corruption in the land": by creating division and scattering their unity; the grammar of "and abandons you" with its accusative as the answer to the question, the *wāw* standing in place of *fāʾ*; and the reports on Pharaoh's worship: al-Ḥasan said Pharaoh used to worship idols, so he both worshipped and was worshipped; Sulaymān al-Taymī said, it reached me that Pharaoh worshipped cattle — and he asked al-Ḥasan whether Pharaoh worshipped anything, and al-Ḥasan said: yes, he worshipped something he had placed round his neck. It is also said that "your gods" means your obedience, as in "they took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God" (9:31) — they did not worship them, but obeyed them, and so it became a likeness. Then he records the readings: Nuʿaym b. Maysarah read *wa-yadhruka* with the *rāʾ* vowelled, on the analysis "and he abandons you"; al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī read *wa-yadhraka* unvowelled, the *ḍammah* lightened; Anas b. Mālik read *wa-nadhraka* with a *nūn*, "and we abandon" — the notables informing of themselves that they would abandon his worship if he left Moses alive; and ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read *wa-ilāhataka*, "and your worship." Al-Anbārī's explanation of that reading: its followers held that Pharaoh, when he said "I am your lord most high" (79:24) and "I do not know any god for you other than me" (28:38), was denying that he had a lord or gods; so it was said to him, "and he abandons you and the people's worship of you" — the general reading being built on the fact that Pharaoh claimed lordship in his outward affairs while knowing himself to be a creature, the proof being his word at the approach of death, "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe" (10:90), not accepted from him after the door of repentance had shut; and that before this state he had a god he worshipped secretly, as al-Ḥasan and others said. Al-Zajjāj said: he had small idols which his people worshipped to draw near to him, and so they were attributed to him — hence his saying "I am your lord most high." Ismāʿīl b. Isḥāq said: Pharaoh's word "I am your lord most high" indicates that they worshipped something other than him [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the conspiracy: God mentions the plotting of Pharaoh and his people, their ill intentions and their hatred for Moses and his people. "The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said" to Pharaoh, "will you leave Moses and his people to spread mischief in the land," spreading unrest among your subjects and calling them to worship their Lord instead of you? And he makes the observation the verse invites: amazingly, these people were worried that Moses and his people would cause mischief! Rather, Pharaoh and his people are the mischief-makers, but they did not realize it [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the full psychology of the accusation: this, and Pharaoh and his notables and the generality who followed the notables, had grown arrogant against God's signs and denied them wrongfully and haughtily; they said to Pharaoh, inciting him against Moses and asserting that what he had brought was falsehood and corruption: "will you leave Moses and his people to corrupt in the land" — by calling to God and to noble character and good deeds, which are precisely the reformation of the earth, while what they themselves were upon was the corruption; but the wrongdoers do not care what they say. "And abandon you and your gods" — leave you and your gods, forbid [people] from you, and turn them from following you. Pharaoh answered, claiming he would leave the Children of Israel with Moses in a state in which they would not grow, and he and his people would be safe from their harm, as he supposed: "we will kill their sons and keep their women alive" — that is, we will keep them alive and not kill them; if we do that, we are safe from their numbers, and we can employ the rest and subject them to whatever work we wish — "and indeed we are over them dominant": no exit for them from our rule and no power. And that, says Saʿdī, is the limit of Pharaoh's tyranny, arrogance and harshness [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** reads the passage as evidence of the king's fear: he had been somewhat successful in keeping his ignorant people in their former ignorance through clever false statements, but they noted that all his fury was limited to the sorcerers only — he did not dare say a word against Moses and Aaron, his real opponents; and this is obvious from the statement of his people, "Do you leave Moses and his people alone to spread disorder in the land, even when he abandons you and your gods?" Pharaoh had no convincing answer to this question; he only said, "We shall slaughter their sons and let their women live, and we have full power over them." According to the commentators, he tried to satisfy his people by saying that by killing their males and leaving their women alive he would eliminate them within a period of time, the women being spared to serve his people as maidservants; in fact, he was so frightened by the miracle of Moses that even on this occasion, threatening to kill all the men of Israel, he could not utter a single word of threat against Moses and Aaron. He quotes Rūmī: *Whoever adopts taqwā and fears Allah is feared by all human beings and spirits.* And the phrase "even when he abandons you and your gods" makes it plain, he says, that Pharaoh himself used to worship other gods, even though he claimed to be the god of his people; the law of killing the males of the Israelites was now promulgated a second time, the first having been before the birth of Moses, and Pharaoh was witnessing the failure of the first in the huge crowd of Israelites present — when God intends to bring disgrace on a people, all they contrive leads to nothing but disaster [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** confirms the sequence: although Pharaoh killed the sorcerers, he allowed Moses to go free; his notables thus express concern that he would leave Moses and the Israelites to live and worship as they prefer, and to abandon the worship of Pharaoh and his gods for obedience to Moses and the worship of the One God (Ṭabarī). The commentators are unclear on the identity of Pharaoh's gods: some say he worshipped the sun or certain sacred cattle — hence the Israelites' inclination to make an idol in the form of a calf in 7:148 (Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī); still others assert that Pharaoh was himself worshipped but did not worship anything himself (Ṭabarī), or that the gods were idols Pharaoh had made and commanded people to worship as a way of worshipping him (al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī). The question might also be rendered, "Will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption upon the earth, when they have left you and your gods?" (Ṭabarī); see 40:26, where Pharaoh indicates he will kill Moses himself, fearing that Moses will alter their religion or cause corruption by leading people away from the worship of Pharaoh. On the threat: slaying their young sons and sparing their women is consistent with Pharaoh's means of collective punishment elsewhere (7:141; 2:49; 14:6; 28:4; 40:25); and although Pharaoh did not harm Moses, out of fear of his great power, he reportedly carried out his threat upon his Israelite followers, hoping to weaken Moses indirectly by terrifying his supporters (al-Rāzī). Finally: "dominant" translates *qāhirūn*, a plural of *qāhir*, which is a name or attribute of God in the Qurʾān (6:18, "He is Dominant over His servants"); that Pharaoh speaks of himself in terms used elsewhere in the Qurʾān for God alone suggests his claim of divinity and lordship for himself (26:29; 28:38; 79:24; 7:123) [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** carries it all briefly, with the note on the notables and on Pharaoh's secret presumption: then the council of Pharaoh's folk said to him, "Will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption in the land, by calling to disobedience against you, and to flout you and your gods?" — and Jalālayn explains the phrase: Pharaoh had fashioned small idols for them to worship and had said to them, "I am your lord and their lord," which is why he said, "I am your lord most high" (79:24). He said, "We shall slaughter" — read *nuqattilu* or *naqtulu* — "their new-born sons and spare their women, keeping them alive for us, as we did with them before; for surely we have irresistible power over them!" And so they did this to them, and the Children of Israel grieved [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Malāʾ* — the notables, the assembly whose opinion carries a community — is the sūrah's recurring term for the leadership of a people (7:60, 75, 88–90, 103, 109), and it is the notables who here demand the resumption of the terror [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Yudhruka* / *yadhraka* — leaves, abandons — is the verb whose readings Ṭabarī and Qurṭubī catalogue; the variant readings (the *wāw* of conjunction, the *nūn* of "we abandon," the *ilāhataka* of "your worship") show the ancient reciters exploring what precisely the notables accused the king of tolerating [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Qāhirūn* — dominant, overmastering — is the word that gives the verse its theological edge: it is used of God elsewhere in the Qurʾān (6:18, 6:61), and Pharaoh's appropriation of it is his claim of divinity in the grammar of the sūrah itself [Study Quran] [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** Three points the exegetes establish. First, the accusation of corruption is the standard political inversion: in **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s words, they were worried that Moses and his people would cause mischief, when it was they themselves who were the mischief-makers — and **[Saʿdī]** spells out the inversion exactly: what Moses called to — worship of God, noble character, good deeds — is the reformation of the earth, while what the accusers were upon is corruption [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī]. Second, the reports on Pharaoh's gods settle a doctrinal curiosity: the Qurʾān's record that the king both claimed divinity and practiced worship is coherent with 10:90, his confession at the point of drowning, which came after the door of repentance had closed [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. Third, **[Maʿārif]** draws the lesson of the king's restraint: his fury fell on the sorcerers and not on the prophets, and that timidity before the messengers is a sign of the terror that faith inspires in its enemies — his silence about Moses and Aaron is itself the evidence of his fear [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "Pharaoh said: Let me kill Moses and let him call upon his Lord; indeed I fear he will change your religion or cause corruption in the land" (40:26); "Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and letting their women live" (28:4; cf. 2:49; 14:6; 7:141); "And He is Dominant over His servants, and He is the Wise, the Aware" (6:18; cf. 6:61); "I am your lord, the most high" (79:24); "I do not know any god for you other than me" (28:38); "And they took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God" (9:31) [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** Three accusations are made against Moses in this single verse, and each is the reverse of the truth. Moses works corruption: he teaches people to worship God and to deal justly, and it is the state that kills children to preserve its labor supply. Moses abandons the king: he was in the king's own palace as an infant, and it is the king who will not release a people to worship. Moses's sign is sorcery and the sorcerers are his secret teachers: the court had gathered them itself, under its own eye, and the professionals among them were the first to say plainly that what they had seen was not their art [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī]. The verse's last clause — "and indeed we are over them dominant" — takes a divine attribute for a royal title, and the sūrah will not let the theft stand: within a generation the same word describes whoever holds the world at that moment, and the One who decides which of the two masters of Egypt will keep it [Study Quran].

## 7:128

*"Moses said to his people, 'Seek help from God and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it in inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the outcome belongs to the reverent.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse in its immediate moment: Moses said to his people of the Children of Israel, when Pharaoh said to the notables of his people, "We will kill the sons of the Children of Israel and spare their women": "Seek help from God" against Pharaoh and his people in what comes upon you of your affairs; "and be patient" under what has touched you of hardships in yourselves and your children from Pharaoh. And he records the number of those who had followed Moses: Ibn ʿAbbās said that when the sorcerers believed, six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel followed Moses [Ṭabarī]. Then the promise: "the earth belongs to God; He gives it in inheritance to whom He wills of His servants" — the earth is God's, and if you are patient under what has befallen you and your children from Pharaoh, and count it for God, and remain steadfast in rectitude, it may be that God will give you the land of Pharaoh and his people as an inheritance, destroying them and making you successors in it, for God gives His earth in inheritance to whom He wills of His servants; "and the outcome belongs to the reverent" — the praiseworthy end belongs to the one who fears God and watches Him, avoiding His disobedience and performing His obligations [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** unfolds the counsel as spiritual strategy: Moses said to his people, advising them — in a state in which they could do nothing and resist nothing — with divine resistance and lordly aid: "seek help from God," that is, rely on Him to bring what benefits you and repel what harms you, and trust God that He will complete your affair; "and be patient," that is, keep to patience under what befalls you, awaiting relief. "The earth belongs to God" — it is not Pharaoh's or his people's, that they should dispose of it as masters; "He gives it in inheritance to whom He wills of His servants," rotating it among people according to His will and wisdom — but the outcome is for the reverent, for though they may be tested for a period by God's trial and wisdom, victory is theirs, and the praiseworthy sequel is theirs over their people. And he draws the rule: this is the servant's function — when he has power, to employ the available means to ward off harm from others; and when he is powerless, to be patient, seek God's help, and await relief [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the verse as counsel in extremis: when his people are facing the terrible punishment of Pharaoh described in the previous verse, Moses advises them to seek help from God (see 1:5) and to have patience, in the same manner that the Qurʾān enjoins believers to seek help in patience and prayer as a general spiritual attitude (2:45, 153), for God is with the patient (8:46). He encourages them by reminding them that the land — meaning Pharaoh's domain (al-Rāzī) — belongs to God, and that He may cause others to inherit it after him; and indeed at 7:137 God bequeaths the eastern and western parts of the land that We blessed to the Israelites (cf. 28:5–6) as a reward for their patience. Moses further promises that the end belongs to the reverent, a general promise also made at 11:49 and 28:83; the end may refer to the reward of the reverent in the Hereafter, to the later worldly success of the Israelites in vanquishing their enemies (7:129) and settling in the land, or to both (al-Rāzī) [Study Quran]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the verse in his heading for the passage — Pharaoh's vow to kill the Children of Israel, their complaint to Moses, and God's promise of victory — and reads Moses's instruction as the answer to the despair his people had shown [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** treats the verse as a lesson in the technique of deliverance: after being defeated by Moses, Pharaoh enforced the law of killing the male children, and the Israelites were greatly alarmed by the punishment they had experienced before Moses came. Moses, mindful of this and out of his kindness, offered two wise solutions: the only way out of the trial was, firstly, to seek help from Allah, and secondly, to remain patient until things changed in their favor — and he promised them that they would inherit the whole land if they faithfully observed the two instructions. He then expounds the promise: all lands belong to Allah, and He lets whomsoever He wills inherit them, and decidedly the end result is for the God-fearing; so if they observe *taqwā* by acting on the two instructions, they shall ultimately rule the whole country. And he calls the pair the sovereign remedy that never fails against any difficulty: the first ingredient is seeking Allah's help, which is the essence of the remedy, for if the Creator of the universe comes to one's help, who is there to stop Him — and he quotes Rūmī's couplet on earth, air, water and fire being the servants of Allah, dead to us and alive to Him, adding that it is reported in a ḥadīth that when Allah wills to do something everything turns in favor of that purpose, so nothing is more powerful against an enemy than seeking Allah's help with full sincerity — mere words are not enough. The second ingredient is patience: the word *ṣabr* literally signifies keeping oneself under control against unfavorable happenings, and nothing significant is achieved without hardship; whoever prepares himself to face hardship is generally successful in most objectives, and he cites the ḥadīth: "No greater blessing has been given to anyone other than patience" (Abū Dāwūd) [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: Moses said to his people, "Seek help in God and be patient" under their persecution; "surely the earth is God's, and He bequeaths it — He gives it — to whom He will from among His servants; the praiseworthy sequel belongs to those who are wary of God" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Istāʿīnū* — seek help — is the tenth form of the root of *ʿawn*, aid, and the imperative's object is placed first in God alone: the first instruction is not resistance but reliance [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. *Yūrithuhā* — He gives it in inheritance — is the verb of succession, and it is the sūrah's keyword for the rise and fall of peoples: the towns of Noah, Hūd and Ṣāliḥ were inherited by later generations (cf. 7:100; 6:165), and the promise to Israel is expressed in the same vocabulary, so that the verse quietly instructs the Israelites that they will be tenants of the same Lord who dispossessed the nations before them [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran]. *Al-ʿāqibah* — the outcome, the sequel — is the end that follows a course of action; **[Ṭabarī]** glosses it as the praiseworthy end belonging to the God-fearing, and **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse's conditional logic as offering the sequel to those who meet the two conditions — reliance and patience [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** extracts from the verse a principle of action for the believer in any trial: when able, he uses the means available to remove harm; when powerless, he is patient, seeks God's help, and waits for relief — the verse is thus both a counsel to the enslaved and a rule for the whole of life [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** converts the two instructions into a formula whose first ingredient is sincerity of reliance and whose second is *ṣabr* in its literal sense of self-restraint under pressure, and supports the latter with the ḥadīth he cites [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** connects the counsel to the Qurʾān's general spiritual teaching, citing 2:45 and 2:153 with their pairing of patience and prayer, and 8:46's assurance that God is with the patient [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, God is with the patient" (2:153; cf. 2:45); "And We made the people who were considered weak to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts which We had blessed" (7:137; cf. 28:5); "Then, is it the outcome of the evil doers other than the Fire?" (cf. 30:10); "And the outcome will be for the righteous" (11:49; cf. 28:83); "And He is the One who has made you successors upon the earth" (6:165; 35:39) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse's three claims are each an answer to a fact the Israelites can see: the earth belongs to God although a man on the Nile thinks it is his; God gives it in inheritance to whom He wills although the Egyptians believe inheritance runs in dynasties; and the outcome belongs to the reverent although every visible arrangement at that moment says otherwise. Moses does not promise his people freedom next week; he gives them a method and a horizon. And the method is not the one the situation seems to demand — they are slaves, and he tells them to rely and endure rather than to organize — because the sūrah's theme for six stories has been that the deliverance of the weak is God's work and not the weak's project [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. The promise is fulfilled at 7:137, and it is fulfilled exactly as stated: the sea, the drowning and the inheritance of the land on the far side belong to God's disposal alone.

## 7:129

*"They said, 'We have been harmed before you came to us and after you came to us.' He said, 'Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, so He may see how you act.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the complaint and the answer: Moses's people said to Moses — when he had said to them, "seek help from God and be patient" — "We have been harmed" by the killing of our sons "before you came to us," that is, before you came to us with God's message, since Pharaoh used to kill their male children when the time of Moses overshadowed them, as he had explained earlier in the commentary; "and after you came to us," since when Pharaoh's sorcerers were overcome and he said to the notables of his people what he said, he wanted to renew the torture upon them by killing their sons and sparing their women. It is also said that Moses's people said this when they were afraid that Pharaoh would overtake them as they fled, with the two hosts coming in sight one another: "O Moses, we were harmed before you came — they used to slaughter our sons and spare our women — and after you came, today Pharaoh will overtake us and kill us." Mujāhid said: "before you came to us" means before God sent you, and after it. Al-Suddī narrates: when the two hosts saw one another, and the Children of Israel saw Pharaoh following them, they said, "Indeed, we are overtaken" (26:61), and said this [Ṭabarī]. Then the answer: "Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, so He may see how you act" — God's promise that He would destroy Pharaoh and make them successors in the earth, and it was fulfilled as He said [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** adds detail: the harm before was at the beginning of Moses's own life, by the killing of sons and the enslavement of women; the harm after is now renewed, meaning Pharaoh's threat; it was also said that the harm before consisted in their being conscripted for forced labor until midday and released for the rest of the day to earn for themselves, while the harm after consisted in their being made to work the whole day without food or drink (Juwaybir); and al-Ḥasan said the harm before and after was one and the same thing — the taking of the tribute. Then the answer: "perhaps your Lord" — and *ʿasā*, "perhaps," from God is obligatory, so the promise was renewed and confirmed for them; they were made heirs in Egypt in the time of David and Solomon, and they conquered the Holy House with Joshua b. Nūn. It is reported that they said this when Moses brought them out and Pharaoh pursued them, so that Pharaoh was behind them and the sea before them, and God fulfilled the threat by drowning Pharaoh and his people and saving them. And "so He may see how you act" — He will see the deeds by which recompense becomes due, because God does not recompense them for what He knows of them, but for what actually occurs from them [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the complaint as the weariness of a people under prolonged suffering — "they said" to Moses, vexed by the length of their stay in Pharaoh's punishment and harm: "we were harmed before you came to us," for they inflict on us evil punishment, slaughtering our sons and sparing our women, "and after you came to us" likewise — and Moses answering them with hope of relief and deliverance from their evil: "perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land," that is, establish you in it and give you its management, "so He may see how you act" — whether you are grateful or ungrateful. And this is a promise God fulfilled when the time He willed came [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** supplies the narrative logic: the Israelites respond that they were persecuted before Moses came to them — since the Qurʾān elsewhere indicates that the punishment of slaying sons was inflicted by Pharaoh upon the Israelites at the time of Moses's infancy (28:4–9) — and that they are now being persecuted in the same way again. Moses's display of power had raised their hopes of deliverance from Pharaoh's oppression, but when they heard Pharaoh announce the same brutal collective punishment he had inflicted earlier, they became despondent (al-Rāzī). Moses, seeking to strengthen their resolve (Ibn Kathīr), reminded them that God may yet destroy their enemies and make them vicegerents upon the earth after Pharaoh and his people. The successive vicegerency of different peoples is a recurring idea in this sūrah (6:165; 7:69); and if God grants them victory, it will be so that He may observe how they behave — whether or not they continue to worship the One God and obey His commands (al-Rāzī) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the complaint its plain sense — the Israelites, who seemed to have no conception of such matters, could not understand how patience alone could free them from Pharaoh's punishment and bring them success against him; they blamed Moses, saying they had been persecuted before he came to them as well as after, meaning, perhaps, that they had been looking for a prophet to deliver them from Pharaoh's oppression, but their fate remained unchanged even after he came — and then draws from the answer a lesson that extends well beyond the Israelites: the last phrase provides a wise observation that sovereignty or dominion is not in itself an aim or objective but a means to achieve the objective of making peace and justice prevail in the land. Sovereignty or dominion is a sacred trust bestowed by Allah for making good prevail over evil; the verse warns them that if they are given this trust they should not forget the ill fate of those before them. The direct addressees are the Israelites, but indirectly the verse warns all those entrusted with rule or dominion: sovereignty and power belong to Allah alone; He has made man His deputy on the earth; He designates with power and takes it away when He wills, as in "You give power to whom You please, and You strip off power from whom You please" (3:26) [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** keeps the complaint and the promise in one heading — the Children of Israel complain to Moses and God promises them victory — and the answer as Moses's strengthening of their resolve [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: they said, "We suffered harm before you came to us and since you have come to us." He said, "Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, that He may observe how you shall act in it" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Ūdhīnā* — we were harmed — is the passive of *ādhā*, to injure, and the verse preserves a people's complaint in their own words, not the narrator's: it is the language of fatigue, spoken to a prophet who had just told them to wait [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. *Yastakhlifakum* — He will make you successors, vicegerents — is the verb of *istikhlāf*, the appointment of one people in another's place, the sūrah's recurring pattern for the rises and falls of nations (7:69, 74; 6:165) [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. And *ʿasā* — "perhaps" — is, the commentators note, a word of hope in human speech and of certainty when God speaks: **[Qurṭubī]** states the rule plainly, that *ʿasā* from God is obligatory, and the promise was therefore a firm one [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn].

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** derives from the verse a principle of political ethics that the exegetes of the subcontinent state with some force: dominion is not an end in itself but a means to establishing peace and justice, and the clause "so He may see how you act" turns the grant of power into an examination — the Israelites must not repeat the fate of those before them, and the warning extends to every ruler [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]**'s note that God recompenses people for deeds that actually occur rather than for what He knows of them preserves the verse's moral seriousness: the grant of succession is precisely for the purpose of seeing how the successors behave [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. And **[Ṭabarī]** and **[al-Rāzī via Study Quran]** both read Moses's answer as the management of a demoralized people: the complaint is met not with rebuke but with an eschatologically framed promise, and the promise's condition is conduct [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And We made the people who were considered weak to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts which We had blessed" (7:137); "And We desired to bestow a favor upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them the leaders, and to make them the heirs" (28:5); "And He is the One who has made you successors upon the earth and has raised some of you above others in degrees, that He may test you through what He has given you" (6:165); "And [remember] when He made you successors after the people of Noah, and increased you in stature" (cf. 7:69, 74); "You give power to whom You please, and You strip off power from whom You please" (3:26); "And He made you heirs of their lands, their houses, and their wealth" (cf. 33:27) [Study Quran] [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse has the shape of so much religious life: a promise, and a complaint against the length of time it takes. The Israelites measure the promise by the day's news — the same decree of child-murder, now reissued — and Moses answers not with more detail but with the one clause that reframes their whole situation: the land will be given so that God may see how they act in it. That clause turns the future from a prize into an examination, and the sūrah returns to it at 7:137, where the inheritance is described as the reward of patience, and at 7:141, where the story reminds its hearers what the alternative had been. **[Maʿārif]**'s reading is the verse's longest shadow: every dominion is a borrowed dominion, and the question that follows every grant is the same — how did they act in the land they were given? [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī].

## 7:130

*"And We seized the people of Pharaoh with the years and a shortage of fruits, so that they might remember."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as the beginning of the account of how God dealt with the Egyptians between the coming of Moses and the final deliverance: God says, We tested the people of Pharaoh and his followers, in the error they were upon, "with the years" — with droughts year after year, and barrenness; and from it is said *asnata al-qawm* — the people were struck with drought; "and a shortage of fruits" — We tested them, along with the droughts, with the loss of their fruits and their crops except a little; "so that they might remember" — an admonition and a reminder to them, so that they might refrain from their error and flee to their Lord in repentance. He then gathers the glosses: Ibn Masʿūd said, "the years of hunger"; Mujāhid said, "the years" is the blight, and "the shortage of fruits" is less than that; and Rajāʾ b. Ḥaywah said, "the shortage of fruits" meant where the palm tree would bear only a single date [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the lexicon and the tradition: "with the years" means the droughts and barrenness of the land, well known in the language — one says *aṣābathum sanah*, a dearth befell them, meaning a year of drought. And he cites the prophetic supplication against Quraysh: "O Allah, make it for them years like the years of Joseph" — meaning famine. He then records the grammarians' discussion: some Arabs inflect the *nūn* of *al-sinīn*, and al-Farrāʾ recited the verse of poetry on the passage of the years which has taken from me, and al-Naḥḥās noted that Sībawayh recited it with the *nūn* vowelled; al-Farrāʾ reports that the Banū ʿĀmir say "I stayed with him *sanīnā*" with inflection, while the Banū Tamīm do not inflect and say "years passed him" without. *Sinīn* is the plural of *sanah*, and *sanah* here bears the sense of drought, not merely of a year — from it comes *asnata al-qawm*, "the people were struck by drought" — and he quotes the verse of ʿAbdallāh b. al-Zibaʿrā on the men of Mecca being drought-stricken and lean. Then: "so that they might remember" — that is, so that they might take admonition and their hearts might soften [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** expands the affliction: God punished the people of Pharaoh — He tested and tried them — "with years of drought," of famine due to little produce, "and lack of fruits," which is less severe, according to Mujāhid; and he cites Rajāʾ b. Ḥaywah's report that the date tree used to produce only one date [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** sets the verse among the plagues and in the sūrah's theology of adversity: cf. 7:133, where the other plagues sent against Pharaoh and his people are mentioned; that drought and a shortage of crops were visited upon them during the time of Moses's mission is consistent with other verses indicating that the adversity suffered by a people in connection with the coming of a prophet is meant to make them humble and cause them to hearken to God's message — 6:42, "We have indeed sent messengers unto communities before you, and We seized them with misfortune and hardship, that they might humble themselves," and the sūrah's own 7:94. The phrase "that haply they would be reminded" indicates that the famine and drought were meant as an admonition to Pharaoh and his people and to frighten them, so that they would repent and believe in God (Ṭabarī). Adversity in general may also have the effect of "softening the heart" (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī), although not in the case of Pharaoh, whose heart according to the Biblical account was increasingly hardened by the successive plagues (Exodus 9–11), and who here too remains unrepentant (see 7:133). Some commentators see this verse as proof that God does not compel people toward belief or disbelief, but rather arranges matters so as to encourage belief and then allows people to choose how they will react (al-Ṭabrisī); others cast doubt on this interpretation [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** puts the verse in the flow of the sūrah's account of the plagues and its law of nations: God says, explaining how He dealt with the people of Pharaoh in this last period — for it is His custom and practice with nations to seize them "with hardship and adversity, that haply they may humble themselves" (cf. 6:42) — "and We seized the people of Pharaoh with the years," that is, with ages of drought, "and a shortage of fruits, so that they might remember," that is, so that they might take admonition that what had befallen them was a reproof from God, that they might turn back from their unbelief. But it did not profit them and did not avail; rather they persisted in wrong and corruption [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: and verily We seized Pharaoh's folk with the years of drought and dearth of fruits, so that they might remember, that they might heed the admonition and become believers [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Al-sinīn* is the plural of *sanah*, and the commentators insist that here the word carries the sense of famine rather than of calendar years — *asnata al-qawm*, the people were stricken with dearth — so that the verse's first affliction is a sentence of years that will not feed anyone [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Naqṣ min al-thamarāt* — a shortage of fruits — names the second and lighter blow: not the loss of the harvest but its dwindling to almost nothing, the single date on a palm (Rajāʾ b. Ḥaywah) [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Yadhdhakkarūn* — they might remember — is the fifth form of *dhakara*, with the doubled *dhāl* of the recitation: not mere recall but taking admonition, letting the memory of God do its work; **[Qurṭubī]** glosses it as the softening of hearts, and **[Saʿdī]** as the turning back from unbelief that the affliction was meant to produce and did not [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** The verse states the purpose clause of divine affliction, and the commentators read it as the continuation of the principle stated at 7:94: hardship is sent not as simple vengeance but as a summons to humility, and its failure to produce that effect is itself a stage in the judgment [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran]. **[Study Quran]** records the theological debate the verse has generated: some read it as proof that God arranges the circumstances that encourage belief but does not compel it, since the plagues' purpose was stated as persuasion and the Egyptians remained free to refuse; others question that inference. And it notes the difference between the two treatments of the same events: the Qurʾān's account has the Egyptians persist, while the Biblical account has Pharaoh's heart increasingly hardened through the successive plagues [Study Quran]. **[Qurṭubī]**'s citation of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer against Quraysh — "make it for them years like the years of Joseph" — connects the sūrah's Egyptian famine to the Arabian drought of the Prophet's own day and to the same theology of warning through want [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "And We have already sent messengers to nations before you, then We seized them with poverty and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves" (6:42; cf. 6:43–44); "And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of famine and a shortage of fruits, that perhaps they might remember" (7:130); "And We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood — distinct signs — but they were arrogant and were a criminal people" (7:133); "Corruption has appeared throughout the land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, so He may let them taste part of what they have done, that perhaps they will return" (30:41) [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrah's last word on the argument from want: before God drowns a tyrant, He thins his harvest. The years and the dwindling fruit are not the punishment — 7:133's plagues and the sea are still ahead — but the last honest instruction the Egyptians will get in the language of the stomach, addressed to a court that had already refused the language of the staff and the hand. **[Saʿdī]**'s sentence is the one that closes the verse's door: it did not profit them and did not avail; rather they persisted in wrong and corruption [Saʿdī]. And the commentators' note that adversity softens hearts — sometimes, but for Pharaoh's not at all — turns the verse into a question aimed past Egypt at the reader: the same providence that gives rain and takes it away is speaking about the same Lord all along, and the only variable is who is listening [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].
## 7:131

*"But when good came to them, they said, 'This is ours'; and if an evil struck them, they augured ill of Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their omen is with God — but most of them do not know."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the account of a people who read their own weather religiously and got it exactly wrong: when comfort, fertility, ease and abundant fruits came to the people of Pharaoh, and they saw what they loved in their worldly life, they said, "This is ours" — we are the ones most entitled to it — and they were not grateful; and when an evil struck them, meaning drought and barrenness and affliction, they augured ill of Moses and those with him: they would say, our share of ease and plenty departed from the moment Moses came to us [Ṭabarī]. The early reports he gives make the charge explicit. Mujāhid: "good" is well-being and ease; "this is ours" is "we are more deserving of it"; "evil" is affliction and punishment; "they augured ill" is "they took ill omens from Moses." Ibn Zayd's version is the sentence the Egyptians are made to say: "Nothing has struck us but because of you, O Moses, and those with you — we saw no evil and nothing struck us until we saw you!" And he sets beside it the case of the earlier people: the people of Ṣāliḥ said, "We augur ill of you and of those with you," and God answered, "Your omen is with God; rather, you are a people being tested" (27:47) [Ṭabarī]. Then the correction: "Unquestionably, their omen is with God" — the shares of ease and plenty and of good and evil that fall to the people of Pharaoh and others are only with God, not with Moses, and it is because most of them do not know that they augured ill of Moses and those with him [Ṭabarī]. Ibn ʿAbbās: their afflictions are with God; and by another chain, "the affair is from God" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same and adds the linguistic history of the superstition: *al-ḥasanah* is fertility and abundance, *al-sayyiʾah* is drought and disease; the verb "they augured ill" is originally *yataṭayyarū*, the *tāʾ* assimilated into the *ṭāʾ*, and Ṭalḥah read it *taṭayyarū* as a past-tense form. The root is *al-ṭiyarah* and the driving of birds (*zajr al-ṭayr*): the Arabs would take good omens from the *sāniḥ*, the animal that came from the right, and ill omens from the *bāriḥ*, the one from the left; they augured from the voice of the crow, interpreting it as separation, and from the responses of birds to one another and their calls at unusual times; so too with gazelles, with the proverb "Who will give me a *sāniḥ* after a *bāriḥ*?" — but since their strongest practice concerned birds as a whole, every augury came to be called *taṭayyur*. He notes the same superstition among the non-Arabs: they would take ill omens from seeing a boy led off to school in the morning and good omens from a boy returning from his teacher; ill from seeing a water-carrier with a full skin and good from an empty one; ill from a porter heavy with a load and good from one who had set his load down. Then the ruling: Islam came forbidding augury and the taking of omens from the sound of any bird, whatever it was and in whatever condition, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Leave the birds at their perches" [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the same psychology in a sentence: whenever good came to them — a fertile season and provisions — they said, "This is for us," because we deserve it; and if evil afflicted them — drought and famine — they considered it an omen about Moses and those with him, saying the hardship was because of them and what they had done [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** connects the verse to the Qurʾān's other treatments of the same self-serving reading of events: in 27:47 the Thamūd similarly considered Ṣāliḥ an ill omen, and in 4:78–79 certain Jews or hypocrites in Medina considered any good that befell the city to be from God but any evil to be on account of the presence of the Prophet; the Qurʾānic response there is that all good is from God and all evil is from oneself, and here that their ill omen lies with God — meaning that all good or bad fortune happens according to God's will and wisdom (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** draws the doctrinal conclusion: when a people are stamped with the wrath of Allah they lose their faculty of distinguishing right from wrong; Pharaoh's people did not take lesson from the warning but ascribed the calamity to a bad presage from Moses and his people. The Arabic word *ṭāʾir*, used for omen, signifies a bird, and the Arabs held the superstition that a bird coming down to their right or their left meant a good or bad fate; the verse implies that good and bad fate come from Allah, that everything in this world happens under His will, and that no one brings good or bad fate to anyone — it is sheer ignorance to believe such things and base one's activities on such baseless assumptions [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]** spells out the missing thankfulness and the misplaced blame: when good came, they said "this is ours" — we deserve it — and did not thank God for it; when evil came, they said it had only come because of Moses's coming and the Children of Israel following him; and God replied that their omen is with God by His decree and power, not as they said — rather it was their own sins and their disbelief that were the cause — but most of them do not know, and that ignorance is why they said what they said [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** compresses the whole into four lines: whenever a good thing such as fertility befell them they said, "This belongs to us," that is, we deserve it, and did not give thanks; and whenever an evil thing such as drought smote them they augured ill of Moses and those with him; surely their ill augury is with God who brings it on them, but most of them do not know that whatever befalls them is from Him [Jalālayn].

**Language.** The verse turns on the Arabic vocabulary of omens. *Ṭāʾir* is a bird, and *taṭayyur* is the reading of birds for signs — a practice the commentators describe in detail: the *sāniḥ* from the right and the *bāriḥ* from the left, the crow's call, the untimely bird-cry [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. *Ṭāʾiruhum* in the verse is therefore a pun with a verdict inside it: "their bird" — their omen, their fate, the thing that flies toward them — is with God, not with the man they blame for it [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And the two terms *ḥasanah* and *sayyiʾah* are not moral categories here but states of circumstance, comfort and hardship, so that the verse's accusation is about how a people interprets its own condition: prosperity is read as entitlement, adversity as someone else's fault, and God is left out of both halves of the ledger [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** uses the verse to state the Islamic ruling on augury: the Prophet ﷺ forbade taking omens from the voice of any bird in any condition — the report he cites is "leave the birds at their perches," an instruction to abandon the practice rather than to read anything from it — and the verse supplies the reason, since what people call the bird's message is God's decree, which no bird carries and no omen predicts [Qurṭubī]. **[Maʿārif]**'s application is the same in the moral key: since all things happen under God's will, basing one's decisions on omens is ignorance; the practice was one of the marks of the *jāhiliyyah*, and the verse exposes its logic — attributing to the arrival of a prophet what belonged to one's own sins [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And if good befalls them, they say, 'This is from God'; but if evil befalls them, they say, 'This is from you [O Muhammad].' Say: All is from God" (4:78); "Whatever good comes to you is from God, and whatever evil comes to you is from yourself" (4:79); "They said: We consider you and those with you an ill omen. He said: Your ill omen is with God — rather, you are a people being tested" (27:47); "And when a good thing came to them they said, 'This is ours'" (cf. 41:50); "Corruption has appeared on land and sea for what the hands of people have earned" (30:41) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** The verse describes something recognizably modern: a people who credit themselves for their prosperity and blame their prophets for their problems. The Egyptians had the most dramatic possible sequence of events to read correctly — a staff become serpent, a hand become light, water become blood — and their interpretive habits survived all of it: what went well was earned, what went badly was Moses's fault. Ignoring God in the two halves of life is not two errors but one, and the sūrah states the cost plainly: the ones who cannot see who is speaking in their weather will shortly meet Him in their sea [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

## 7:132

*"And they said, 'Whatever sign you bring to us to bewitch us by it, we will not believe in you.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as the declaration the people of Pharaoh made to Moses: whatever sign and indication you bring us, "to bewitch us by it" — to turn us away from what we are upon of Pharaoh's religion by it — "we will not believe in you," that is, we will not accept that you are in the right in what you call us to [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the stubbornness the sentence states: they declared to Moses that they would not cease and would not move from their falsehood — "we have settled it in our minds that you are a sorcerer; so whatever sign you bring, we have resolved that it is magic, and so we will not believe you nor accept you as true." This is the furthest limit of stubbornness, he says: that it should reach the point for the disbelievers where the states are equal to them whether signs come down or not [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** identifies the verse as the encapsulation of one of the key ideas of the whole account: no miraculous sign, no matter how powerful or convincing, can change the hearts of those who stubbornly refuse to believe; in 7:146 this stubbornness is engendered by pride, since God "turns away from His signs" those who, like Pharaoh and his notables, wax arrogant upon the earth; and it cites 6:25 and 10:96–97 for the idea that some are impervious to all signs of God [Study Quran]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** renders the claim in the same terms and places it in his section on God's punishment of the people of Pharaoh for their rebellion: they said, whatever miracle, proof and evidence you bring us, we will neither accept it from you nor believe in you or in what you came with [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the sentence as the sequel to the statement of ill omens: "Whatever sign you bring to us in order to enchant us therewith, we are not going to believe in you" [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** carries it and adds the consequence in the narrative: and they said to Moses, "Whatever sign you bring us to cast a spell upon us therewith, we will not believe in you" — and so Moses invoked God against them [Jalālayn]. **[Qurṭubī]**, working through the verse's words in the passage, notes the sense they attached to the signs — that Moses was working magic on them to turn them from their religion — and the flatness of their refusal: they will not believe [Qurṭubī].

**Language.** *Mahmā* — "whatever," "whenever" — is the particle of indefinite condition the exegetes analyze as *mā* strengthened by *mā*, "what thing soever"; the verse thus makes their refusal universal in advance: not "this sign does not convince us" but "no sign will." *Li-tasḥaranā* — to bewitch us, to spell us — states their interpretation of the signs as an operation on their minds, the very charge the sorcerers themselves had abandoned when they confessed that what they saw was not their craft [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the phrase *fa-mā naḥnu laka bi-muʾminīn* places the negative on faith itself: they are not going to be believers in him, whatever happens in the sky, the river or the field [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Belief.** The verse establishes a limit case for the theology of signs: a miracle does not compel faith. **[Study Quran]**'s citation of 7:146 and 10:96–97 makes the point systematically — the very function of the signs is to encourage belief among those already inwardly disposed to it and to distinguish them from those who refuse; the heart that has resolved to explain everything cannot be cornered by evidence [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** states the corollary: when a people reach the point where signs and their absence are the same to them, there is nothing left for the signs to do but testify against them [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And of them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it" (6:25); "Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment" (10:96–97); "I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right; and if they should see every sign, they will not believe in it" (7:146); "And if they were to see a piece of the sky falling, they would say, 'Clouds gathered in heaps'" (52:44) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrah's study of the point at which argument stops being possible. The Egyptians had watched an act that their own experts identified as beyond their art, and their conclusion was not "we were wrong" but "it is a bigger spell." **[Saʿdī]**'s description — sign and no-sign have become the same to them — is the definition of a closed mind, and the Qurʾān presents it not as a flattering intellectual failing but as a moral one, traceable to pride (7:146). What follows in the sūrah is therefore no longer a debate: it is a sequence of plagues, five of them, each of which reads to the Egyptians as an omen rather than an address [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:133

*"So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood — signs made distinct — but they were arrogant and were a criminal people."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with a dispute over the first term: "the flood" (*al-ṭūfān*). Some said it was water: Ibn ʿAbbās said that when Moses came with the signs, the first of the signs was the flood — God sent the sky upon them; Abū Mālik said "the flood is water"; al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same, and in another report from him it is drowning; Mujāhid said the flood is water, and the plague in every case. Others said it is death: Mujāhid is reported saying "the flood is death in every case," and ʿĀʾishah is reported saying that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "The flood is death" — a report whose chain the editor of the printed *Jāmiʿ al-Bayān* marks as containing al-Minhāl b. Khalīfah, an unreliable transmitter *(weak)* [Ṭabarī]. Then the plagues themselves in Qurṭubī's and Ibn Kathīr's expansions: the locusts ate their crops and their fruits until they even ate the roofs and the doors, so that their houses collapsed, and nothing of them entered the homes of the Children of Israel; the *qummal* — Ibn ʿAbbās called it the grain-bug, others said it is small wingless locusts, and al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd b. Jubayr said it is small black insects — consumed what the locusts had left; the frogs filled their vessels and their food and tormented them severely; and the blood: it is said it was nosebleeds, or, as many of the exegetes said, the water they drank turned to blood, so that they had nothing to drink but blood and nothing to cook with but blood [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** also preserves Saʿīd b. Jubayr's narrative of the sequence, which the other sources summarize: when Moses demanded the release of the Children of Israel and Pharaoh refused, God sent the flood — a rain that continued until they feared it was a torment; they asked Moses to pray and promised faith and release; he prayed and God lifted it; they did not believe, nor did they send the Children of Israel with him. That year God caused the earth to grow produce, fruits and grass as never before; they said, "This is what we hoped for"; so God sent the locusts, which fed on the grass; when they saw that no vegetation would be saved, they again asked Moses to pray, promised, and broke their word; then the grain-bugs, so that a man would take ten bags of grain to the mill and get back barely three [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** records the reports on duration and on the five plagues as a matter of *islām*'s law as well: each punishment lasted seven days and then three weeks of relief (Ibn ʿAbbās), four hundred years... no — he gives Nūf al-Shāmī's report that Moses remained among the people of Pharaoh forty years after defeating the sorcerers, and Ibn ʿUthmān's that it was twenty years, showing them the signs of the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood [Qurṭubī]. He then turns to a set of legal questions raised by the passage: on killing locusts when they descend on a land and cause destruction, some said they are not to be killed, arguing that it is a great creature of God's creatures eating from God's provision and no revealed law restricts it, and citing the report "Do not kill the locusts, for it is the greatest army of God"; while the jurists, all of them, held that they are to be killed, since leaving them is the ruin of property, and the Prophet ﷺ permitted fighting a Muslim who intends to take one's property, so a locust that ruins property is more deserving of it; the same reasoning, he notes, is why killing snakes and scorpions is permitted. And he records the ḥadīth of the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against the locusts: "O Allah, destroy its great ones and kill its small ones and ruin its eggs and cut off its rear and withhold its mouths from our livelihoods and our provisions; You are the Hearer of supplication" — a man asked, "O Messenger of God, how do you pray against an army from the armies of God to cut off its rear?" and he said, "The locust is the *nathrah* of the fish in the sea." He cites Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: ʿAbdallāh b. Abī Awfā said, "We fought seven battles with the Messenger of God ﷺ and we used to eat locusts with him," and reports the consensus that if a locust is taken alive and its head cut off it is lawful, the act standing as its slaughter (dhakāh), with the jurists differing whether it needs a further cause of death when hunted — the majority holding it does not, its rule being that of fish, Mālik holding that it does, and al-Layth and Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib disliking the eating of locusts found dead; and he records the ḥadīth of al-Dāraquṭnī from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Two dead things and two bloods have been made lawful for us: the fish and the locust, the liver and the spleen," and the report that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to exchange locusts on plates. Finally he carries the report of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, "God created a thousand nations: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land, and the first of these nations to perish is the locust; and when the locust perishes, the nations follow one another like the beads of a necklace when its thread is cut" — recorded by al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm in *Nawādir al-Uṣūl*, with his note that the locust is the first of these nations to perish because it was created from the clay left over from the clay of Ādam *(Isrāʾīliyyāt-flavored transmission)* [Qurṭubī]. **[Study Quran]** situates the list: this verse gives five punishments sent against Pharaoh and his people in response to their failure to believe in the One God and in Moses's prophethood and their continued oppression of the Israelites; four of the five — locusts, lice, frogs and blood — are identical to four of the ten plagues visited upon Pharaoh's people in the Biblical account (Exodus 9–11); 17:101 states that Moses was given nine clear signs, which are understood to include the miracles of his staff and hand, not only the punishments. "Flood" translates *ṭūfān*, related to "typhoon," the word also used of the flood of Noah (29:14), usually connoting a complete deluge bringing sudden death; some commentators interpret it as death that comes from all sides or by all means, since the root means "to surround," a view supported by a ḥadīth in which the Prophet glossed *ṭūfān* simply as death (Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabarī). According to one report, the rain persisted for eight days and flooded the houses of the Egyptians but did not enter those of the Israelites (al-Zamakhsharī). "Lice" translates *qummal*, which may denote a variety of tiny insects, including fleas or ticks (Ṭabarī); according to some, the locusts consumed most of the crops in the fields, and when this did not cause Pharaoh to repent, the *qummal* consumed the rest (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). Pharaoh's continued stubbornness led to the frogs, which filled the houses of the Egyptians and ruined them (Ṭabarī), and the blood, which was what any water drawn by the Egyptians turned into, while water drawn from the same sources by Israelites was clean (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), similar to the Biblical plague of blood (Exodus 9). According to one report, each punishment lasted a week, and when it was lifted on account of Pharaoh's plea and Moses's supplication, Pharaoh's state of repentance lasted only a month, after which he resumed his disbelieving and oppressive ways (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The verse describes these as "signs made distinct," which some interpret as signs any reasonable person would know came from God (al-Zamakhsharī), and others as successive signs, distinct from one another in time (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the five with their effects: the flood is the abundant water that drowned their trees and crops and harmed them greatly; the locusts ate their fruits, crops and plants; the *qummal* — it was said to be the *dubāʾ*, that is, small locusts, though the apparent meaning is the well-known louse; the frogs filled their vessels and disturbed them and harmed them severely; and the blood, which was either nosebleed or, as many of the exegetes said, their drinking water turned to blood so that they drank nothing but blood and cooked with nothing but blood. And their description as "signs made distinct": proofs and clarifications that they were liars and wrongdoers, and that what Moses brought was true; "but they were arrogant" when they saw the signs, and "were" in their prior affair "a criminal people" — which is why God punished them by leaving them in their error and misguidance [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** supplies the numerical frame: Moses stayed in Egypt for twenty years, preaching and conveying God's message, and was given nine miracles during that stay; two were performed before Pharaoh and his people, the third was the famine of 7:130, and the remaining six are in this passage, of which the five punishments of this verse are termed signs distinct from one another — according to Ibn ʿAbbās each lasted for a fixed period followed by a period of relief, and Ibn al-Mundhir cites from him that each lasted seven days starting from Saturday, then came three weeks of relief; al-Baghawī, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, adds that when they were first relieved of the famine at Moses's prayer they did not keep their promise to believe, so Moses prayed that they be inflicted with a painful punishment that would serve as a lesson for his people and their descendants — and the strange thing about the flood, he says, was that the lands and houses of the Israelites were not affected by its water [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders the plagues with their shapes: the flood of water which penetrated their houses and which for seven days would come up to people's necks as they sat; the locusts which consumed their crops and fruits, likewise engulfing them for seven days; the lice, like woodworm or ticks, which would follow and consume what the locusts left; the frogs, which infested their houses and food supplies; and the blood flowing in their water — distinct clear signs, but they were too scornful to believe in them and were a sinful folk [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Ṭūfān* is the flood that surrounds, from a root of encircling — **[Study Quran]** notes its connection to "typhoon" and its use for the flood of Noah, and the commentators' two readings: water that overwhelms, or death that comes from every side; the ḥadīth-gloss "the flood is death" is the tradition's compressed reading of the word *(weak chain)* [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Qummal* is the disputed insect — grain-bug, louse, tick, wingless locust — and the exegetes leave it general because the Arabic word covers a family of tiny vermin [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. And *āyāt mufaṣṣalāt* — "signs made distinct" — is glossed two ways: signs so clear that any reasonable person would recognize their origin, or signs separated from one another in time so that each arrived with its own interval [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The passage carries an unusual concentration of legal tradition. **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** both record the ḥadīth of ʿAbdallāh b. Abī Awfā in the two Ṣaḥīḥs — "we fought seven battles with the Messenger of God ﷺ and we used to eat locusts with him" — and the report of al-Dāraquṭnī from Ibn ʿUmar, "Two dead things and two bloods have been made lawful for us: the fish and the locust, the liver and the spleen"; **[Qurṭubī]** adds the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against the locust ("destroy its great ones, kill its small ones, ruin its eggs, cut off its rear") with his reply to the questioner that the locust is the "sneeze" of the fish of the sea, and the notice that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to exchange locusts on plates. **[Ṭabarī]** carries the report of ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet ﷺ said al-ṭūfān is death, with the editor's warning about its chain, and the ʿUmar report of the thousand nations whose first to perish is the locust — a report **[Qurṭubī]** transmits with al-Ḥakīm's explanation that the locust was created from the leftover clay of Ādam, material that stands in the category of transmitted lore rather than of sound ḥadīth [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] *(weak)* *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)*.

**Rulings.** Two rulings the commentators derive directly from this verse. First, on the killing of locusts in a land they infest: **[Qurṭubī]** reports the disagreement in full — a group forbidding it on the ground that the locust is a creature of God and the text contains no license, and the jurists in general permitting it because leaving them ruins people's property, an argument he presses by analogy with the permitted killing of snakes and scorpions [Qurṭubī]. Second, on eating locusts: **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** both report the consensus that a locust taken alive and killed is lawful, the act of taking serving as its *dhakāh*, with the schools differing over locusts found dead — the majority treating them like fish, Mālik requiring a cause of death, and al-Layth and Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib disapproving [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And **[Maʿārif]**'s report that the Israelites' land and homes were untouched by the flood adds the pattern that runs through the whole passage: the plagues distinguish between the two peoples, as the signs distinguish between the two readings of the same events [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years and a shortage of fruits" (7:130); "And We had already given Moses nine clear signs" (17:101); "Then We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood, distinct signs; but they were arrogant and were a criminal people" (7:133, the verse itself); "So We sent upon them the flood" (cf. 29:14, of Noah's flood); "And We did not send a sign except that it was greater than its sister" (cf. 43:48) [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].

**Reflection.** The list is the sūrah's most concrete demonstration of what it means for a people to be seized by their own water, weather and vermin. Each plague strikes the base of Egyptian life — the river, the field, the home, the food, the jar — and each is described by the commentators as affecting the Egyptians and passing over the Israelites, which is to say that the afflictions were themselves a kind of scripture written in the land. What the verse notes last is what mattered most: "they were arrogant, and were a criminal people." The signs were distinct, and their response was to raise their heads. **[Saʿdī]**'s sequence — they were arrogant when they saw the signs, and they had been criminals before — locates the permanence of the problem not in the plagues but in the people, which is why the fifth plague is followed by a promise they will break [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:134

*"And when the punishment fell upon them, they said, 'O Moses, call upon your Lord for us by what He has entrusted to you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and send with you the Children of Israel.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the setting: when the *rijz* — the punishment — fell upon them and God's wrath settled on them, they went to Moses with this plea [Ṭabarī]. And he gathers the tradition on what exactly the *rijz* was. Some said it was a plague. **[Ṭabarī]** records Saʿīd b. Jubayr's narration in full: Moses commanded his people of the Children of Israel — this after the five signs of the flood and what God mentioned in the verse had come to Pharaoh's people, and they had not believed and had not sent the Children of Israel with him — that every man among them should slaughter a ram and dye his palm in its blood and strike it on his door; the Copts said to the Children of Israel, "Why are you treating this blood on your doors?" and they answered, "God will send a punishment upon you, and we will be safe while you perish"; the Copts said, "And does God know you only by these marks?" and they said, "So our prophet commanded us!" And in the morning seventy thousand of Pharaoh's people had been stricken, and by evening they were unable to bury one another. Then Pharaoh said, "Call upon your Lord for us by what He has entrusted to you; if you lift the plague from us, we will believe you and send with you the Children of Israel" — and he called upon his Lord and He lifted it from them, and the most faithful of them all was Pharaoh, who said to Moses, "Take the Children of Israel wherever you wish" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same identification through Ibn Jubayr — it was a plague that killed seventy thousand of the Copts in a single day — and the alternative: what is meant by the *rijz* is the previously mentioned signs themselves; and he notes the recitation of the word *al-rijz* with *ḍammah* as a known variant [Qurṭubī]. On the plea's wording: "by what He has entrusted to you" — *mā* in the sense of *alladhī*, that is, by the knowledge He deposited with you, or by what He singled you out with by making you a prophet; and it is said the phrase is an oath, "by His covenant with you," with *mā* serving as a connective [Qurṭubī]. Then the pledge: "if you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and send with you the Children of Israel" — a people whom, as the exegetes note, the Egyptians were using as forced labor [Qurṭubī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the episode in its wider Qurʾānic pattern: the pleas of the drowning and the terrified in 6:63–64, 10:22–23, 29:65, 30:33 and 31:32 are examples of the human tendency to call on God in moments of peril and to make promises of worship and belief that are soon broken when the peril has passed. Pharaoh and his notables beseech Moses: "call upon your Lord by the covenant He has made with you," referring to the special relationship they understood Moses to have with God, given his ability to perform miraculous signs (al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī); and it records the commentators' alternative that the *rijz* refers to the various punishments collectively, with these verses describing the reaction to each one [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** states what the pledge was worth: they said, "O Moses, call upon your Lord for us by what He has entrusted to you," interceding through Moses by the covenant of revelation and law that God had placed with him; "if you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and send with you the Children of Israel" — and in that they were liars, intending nothing but the removal of what had befallen them, and supposing that once it was lifted no other would strike them [Saʿdī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the verse in his narrative of the plagues' sequence: when the punishment struck them they said, "O Moses, invoke your Lord for us because of His promise to you; if you remove the punishment from us, we will indeed believe you and let the Children of Israel go with you" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** records the sixth plague under the Arabic word *rijz*, which signifies plague or pestilence, with more than seventy thousand Egyptians reported killed in it, relief coming through Moses's prayer — and then notes that they broke their promise again as before [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]**'s report of the blood on the doorposts, transmitted from Saʿīd b. Jubayr, has no other purpose in the tafsīr than to mark the plague as passing over Israel even as it fell on Egypt, and the exegetes read it as the same event the Bible calls the plague on the firstborn, an identification **[Study Quran]** makes explicitly [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: and when the chastisement fell upon them they said, "O Moses, pray to your Lord for our sake by the covenant which He has made with you to remove the chastisement from us if we believe. Indeed, if you remove the terror from us, verily we will believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you" — with the *lām* of oaths [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Al-rijz* is the passage's key noun, and **[Study Quran]** notes that it can mean filth and defilement as well as divine punishment — a doubleness worth carrying: what descended on Egypt was at once a plague and a pollution, and its removal is described as "lifting" (*kashf*) as though it were a covering laid over the land [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī]. "By what He has entrusted to you" — *bi-mā ʿahida ʿindaka* — turns on the verb *ʿahida*, to entrust, to covenant; **[Qurṭubī]** offers both readings, the knowledge deposited with Moses and the office conferred on him, and the further possibility that the phrase functions as an oath in the name of God's covenant with His prophet [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. And their promise is put in the doubled future of oaths — *la-nuʾminanna laka wa-la-nursilanna maʿaka* — "we will surely believe you and we will surely send with you"; **[Saʿdī]** hears in the formality of the oath the very proof that it was worth nothing, since the oath was framed to end a plague and not to change a heart [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** Two matters the commentators attach here. First, the plea itself: the Egyptians invoke Moses's standing with God — "call upon your Lord for us by what He has entrusted to you" — an acknowledgment, extracted by pain, that Moses's relationship with his Lord is real and effective, and a demonstration of the chapter's theme that even the enemies of a prophet know where the power lies when they are frightened [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. Second, the pattern of the peril-pledge: **[Study Quran]** gathers the Qurʾānic parallels (6:63–64; 10:22–23; 29:65; 30:33; 31:32) to show that the promise made under duress and broken in safety is a fixed feature of human behavior in the Qurʾān's account, and it reads the present episode as one more instance of that pattern rather than as a unique Egyptian perfidy [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them with a favorable wind... they call upon God, sincere in their religion: If You save us from this, we will surely be among the thankful" (10:22; cf. 29:65; 31:32); "Say: Who saves you from the darkness of the land and sea, when you call upon Him in fear and hope, saying, 'If He saves us from this, we will surely be among the thankful'?"
