(6:63–64); "And when they ride upon the ship, they call upon God, sincere in their religion; but when He delivers them to the land, behold, they associate others with Him" (29:65); "So when they ride upon the ship, they call upon God" (cf. 30:33); "And they said: Whatever sign you bring to us to bewitch us by it, we will not believe in you" (7:132) [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse is a portrait of the religion of emergency. The Egyptians had told Moses in the previous verse that no sign would ever make them believe; now, with a plague in their houses, they negotiate — and their offer contains the whole future of the story: faith and the release of Israel, the two things Moses had asked from the beginning. **[Saʿdī]**'s verdict that they were liars with no intention beyond the lifting of the plague is the sūrah's own verdict, delivered by the rest of the narrative [Saʿdī]. What is new here is not their sincerity but their theology: driven by pain, they speak of God as real, of Moses's covenant as effective, and of Egypt's policy as negotiable — and the next verse records what happens to all three of those discoveries the moment the water runs clean again [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

## 7:135

*"But when We removed the punishment from them for a term they were to reach, behold — they broke their word."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the sequel already told in the reports of the previous one: when the punishment was lifted — through the supplication of Moses — and the respite ran until the appointed time God had fixed, they broke the covenant they had made with Moses [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the clause its precise sense: "to a term they were to reach" means the term decreed for them, that is, the limit whose end was their drowning; their removal of the punishment was not permanent but temporally bounded; and "they broke their word" means they undid what they had bound on their own souls [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** makes the same twofold point about the lifting and the breaking: "when We removed the punishment from them to a term they were to reach" — that is, to a span whose duration God had decreed for them, and not to a lifting that was forever but one that was timed — behold, they break the covenant they had made with Moses and promised him: faith in him and the sending of the Children of Israel with him. So they neither believed him nor sent the Children of Israel with him; rather they continued in their disbelief, wandering blindly, and in torturing the Children of Israel without pause [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** notes that verse 135 confirms God's response to the plea of verse 134 — the punishment was lifted, but only for a term they were to fulfill, a term that some understand as a period of respite before they would be destroyed completely (al-Rāzī) — and that their "reneging" refers to their obstinate refusal to recognize Moses's prophethood or release the Israelites, as they had promised [Study Quran]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** carries the verse in the running narrative of the plagues: "But when We removed the punishment from them for a fixed term, which they had to reach, behold, they broke their word" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** records the same in his account of the sixth plague: they were relieved of the punishment by the prayer of Moses, and again they broke their promise as before; and when they showed no sign of understanding, they were finally caught by the last punishment — death, leaving behind their lands, houses and possessions to chase Moses and his people, and to be drowned in the sea [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: but when We removed the terror from them, to a term which they should reach, lo, they were already reneging, breaking their covenant and persisting in their disbelief [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]**'s report from Saʿīd b. Jubayr preserves the detail that makes the verse's irony visible: after the plague was lifted, "the most faithful of them all was Pharaoh," who said to Moses, "Take the Children of Israel wherever you wish" [Ṭabarī].

**Language.** *Yankuthūn* — they break, they untwist — is the Qurʾān's verb for the violation of a covenant, and its basic image is the undoing of a spun thread; the sūrah uses the same image elsewhere of the woman who unravels her yarn after spinning it strong (16:92) [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. The phrase *ilā ajalin hum bālighūh* — "to a term they were to reach" — states the limit of the reprieve without naming it, and the commentators fill it with the drowning: the term they were to reach was the sea [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. The construction with *idhā* — "behold, they break" — expresses the immediate resumption of the old behavior the moment the pressure lifts, which is the verse's psychological observation [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** The verse states a principle the commentators generalize from the incident: a reprieve is not an acquittal, and the removal of a punishment does not signal that the offender has changed. **[Qurṭubī]**'s reading of the term as the decreed limit whose end was the drowning makes the reprieve itself part of the sentence — the space granted them was the road by which they walked into the sea [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. And **[Saʿdī]**'s detail that after breaking the covenant they continued "torturing the Children of Israel without pause" ties the verse to the social reality the whole passage has been about: the promise to release the enslaved people was broken along with the promise to believe, and the two were one promise from the start [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And do not be like she who untwists her yarn after spinning it into strength" (16:92); "And fulfill the covenant of God when you have taken it, and do not break oaths after their confirmation" (16:91); "Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification and sever what God commanded to be joined" (2:27; cf. 13:25); "So when they forgot that by which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every good thing until, when they rejoiced in that which they were given, We seized them suddenly" (6:44) [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran].

**Reflection.** There is a whole doctrine of history in the phrase "for a term they were to reach." God did not ignore the Egyptian plea, and He did not accept the Egyptian promise; He granted time, and the time belonged to the decree that was already running. The verse thus closes the long exchange of plagues with the observation that mercy misread becomes the instrument of judgment: the relief that should have produced gratitude produced only the opportunity to break a word. And the report of Pharaoh's momentary fidelity — "take the Children of Israel wherever you wish" — tells the reader that the promise was not impossible for him to keep; he simply kept it only as long as the water tasted of blood [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif].
## 7:136

*"So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the reckoning after the broken covenant: when they broke their pledges, "We took retribution from them" — We took satisfaction from them by visiting Our vengeance upon them, which is His punishment — "and drowned them in the sea," *al-yamm* being the sea itself, as the poet Dhū al-Rummah says in describing a wilderness and the darkness of night as though they were a sea on whose shores the Byzantines murmur, and as al-ʿAjjāj says of the surging of a sea watered by the sea. Then the reason: "because they denied Our signs" — because of their denial of Our proofs and marks which We showed them — "and were heedless of them," that is, heedless of the vengeance We brought down on them before it fell, or heedless of the signs, turning away from them so that they became like those who do not heed [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives *al-yamm* as *al-baḥr*, the sea, and reads the last clause in both ways the grammar allows: heedless of the vengeance, the *hāʾ* referring back to the retribution just mentioned, or heedless of the signs, meaning they did not take admonition from them until they became as those who ignore them [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the narrative: when the people of Pharaoh rebelled and transgressed even though God had inflicted them with consecutive signs, one after another, He took retribution from them by drowning them in the sea that Moses had parted by God's power, and which Moses and the Children of Israel passed through; in their pursuit Pharaoh and his soldiers went into the sea chasing him, and when they had all entered, the sea closed in on them and they all drowned, because they had denied the signs of God and were heedless of them [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** supplies the scene the sūrah tells elsewhere, and which he lays out in its sequence from Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ: when the appointed time of their destruction came, God ordered Moses to travel with the Children of Israel by night and informed him that Pharaoh would follow him with his armies; Pharaoh dispatched gatherers through the cities to collect the people to follow the Children of Israel, saying, "These are a small band, and they have enraged us, and we are all vigilant and armed" (26:54–56); and so God brought them out of gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station — thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit it (26:57–59) — and they pursued them at sunrise; and when the two hosts saw one another, Moses's companions said, "We are surely overtaken," and he said, "No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me" (26:61–62); and God revealed to him, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it split, and each part was like a great mountain, and there God brought near the others, and saved Moses and those with him all together, and then drowned the others (26:63–66). And then the verse's own statement: "We drowned them in the sea because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them" — because of their denial of the signs of God and their turning away from what those signs pointed to of the truth [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** supplies the lexical and narrative context: God's taking vengeance means that He punished them for their evil deeds and because they were heedless of the signs and clear proofs of Moses's prophethood (al-Ṭabrisī); the Qurʾān, like the Bible, recounts that Pharaoh and his hosts were drowned in the sea that Moses had miraculously parted, and when they pursued through the parted waters the sea returned to its state and drowned them (see 2:50; 8:54; 10:90; 17:103; 26:65–66; 28:40; 43:55; 44:24; 51:40). And it notes that *yamm*, rather than the more common Arabic word for sea, *baḥr*, is used in the Qurʾān only in connection with the Mosaic narratives (20:39, 78, 97; 28:7, 40; 51:40) — similar to the Hebrew word used in the Biblical account — and that it may refer to a sea of unfathomable depths, or to the loud roar or vastness of the sea (al-Zamakhsharī) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the sequence as the sixth and final punishment: when they broke their promise again and showed no sign of understanding, they were finally caught by the last punishment — death; leaving behind all their lands, houses and possessions they chased Moses and his people, and were drowned in the sea [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: so We exacted retribution from them and therefore drowned them in the sea — *al-yamm* denotes salt waters — for the reason that they denied Our signs and were heedless of them, not reflecting upon them [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Al-yamm* is the verse's chosen word for the sea, and **[Study Quran]**'s observation that the Qurʾān uses it only in the Mosaic narratives — in contrast to the general word *baḥr* — sets the drowning in a specialized vocabulary that matches the Hebrew of the Exodus account; the exegetes gloss it as the deep, or the roaring sea [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī]. *Intaqamnā* — We took retribution — is the verb of exacting satisfaction for a wrong; **[Ṭabarī]** glosses it as taking satisfaction by the infliction of vengeance, and the retribution's instrument is the very water that had been the stage of the deliverance [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And the two reasons given — denial of the signs, heedlessness of them — are the sūrah's standard pair: the first is a verdict on the will, the second on the attention; the last clause may be read, as **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** both note, as heedlessness of the coming punishment rather than of the signs, in which case it describes not ignorance but unconcern [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "And We parted the sea for you and saved you, and We drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on" (2:50); "And We took revenge upon the people of Pharaoh — We drowned them in the sea" (cf. 43:55); "And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his hosts followed them in insolence and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said, 'I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit'" (10:90); "Then We drowned the rest. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not to be believers" (26:66–67); "So We seized him and his hosts and threw them into the sea; then see how was the end of the wrongdoers" (28:40) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Rulings.** **[Study Quran]**'s gathering of the drowning passages shows the event's fixed place in the Qurʾān's argument: the deliverance of the enslaved and the destruction of the enslaver are one act, recounted wherever the sūrahs need to state that God's help of the weak is not theoretical [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr]. And **[Saʿdī]**'s narration preserves the point of the scene's staging — Israel watching, the sea closing, the tyrant's army gone — which **[Ibn Kathīr]** likewise notes as the public vindication that added disgrace to the punishment and comfort to the hearts of the believers [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** The verse's two reasons deserve to be read together: they denied the signs, and they were heedless of them. The Egyptians had seen more divine evidence in a few years than most nations in the Qurʾān are granted — a serpent, a luminous hand, a river turned to blood — and the sūrah's diagnosis of their end is not that they lacked information but that they never attended to it. And the instrument of their end is the element through which their victims had just walked dry: the sea that opens for the delivered closes on the pursuer, so that the same water is mercy and judgment in a single night [Study Quran] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]**'s summary is the plain historical verdict: they left behind lands, houses and possessions to chase an unarmed people, and were drowned [Maʿārif].

## 7:137

*"And We made the people who were being weakened inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed. And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because they were patient. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and what they used to erect."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the fulfillment of the promise given in 7:128–129: We made the people whom Pharaoh and his people were weakening — slaughtering their sons, sparing their women, and subjecting them to forced labor and enslavement, of the Children of Israel — inherit the eastern and western parts of the land. "The eastern parts of the land" he identifies with al-Shām, that portion of it facing east; and "the western parts which We blessed," meaning the land in which We made good permanent and lasting for its people. He explains the verb "We made inherit": God gave it to the Children of Israel as an inheritance after bringing about the destruction of the Amalekites who were in it. Then he records the early authorities: al-Ḥasan said, "al-Shām"; Qatāda the same; Muʿammar from Qatāda likewise. He then disposes of a grammatical opinion — that "the eastern and western parts" is accusative in place of an omitted *fī*, "those who were weakened in the east and west of the land," with "which We blessed" as the object of "We made inherit" — on the ground that it makes no sense: the Children of Israel were not being weakened except by Pharaoh and his people, and Pharaoh had no authority outside Egypt, so it is not valid to say they were being weakened in the easts and wests of the earth. Then the promise: "the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel" — God brought His promise to the Children of Israel to completion as He had pledged it: their establishment in the land and His aid of them against their enemy Pharaoh; and "His good word" is His saying, "And We desired to do a favor to those who were weakened in the earth, and to make them leaders, and to make them the inheritors" (28:5) [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** works through the grammar precisely as Ṭabarī does: al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ held that the original was "in the easts of the land and its wests" with the *fī* dropped and the noun therefore put in the accusative; but the evident meaning is that they inherited the land of the Copts, so that the phrase is a plain direct object, since one says "I inherited the property" and "I made him inherit the property," the verb taking two objects when it carries the causative *hamza*. The land, he says, is the land of al-Shām and Egypt, and its easts and wests are the directions of east and west within it, so that the land is specified — from al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and others; while it is also said that what is meant is the whole earth, since from the Children of Israel came David and Solomon, who ruled the earth. "Which We blessed" means with crops, fruits and rivers. "And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel" is His saying, "And We desired to do a favor to those who were weakened in the earth and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors" (28:5). "Because they were patient" — because of their patience under Pharaoh's harm and under God's command after they believed in Moses. And "We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people were making and what they used to erect": *ʿarasha yaʿrishu* is to build; Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said it means the palaces and other structures they were building; al-Ḥasan said it is the trellising of the vine; and he records the recitations: Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read *yaʿrushūn* with *ḍammah* on the *rāʾ*, which al-Kisāʾī calls the dialect of Tamīm, and Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAblah read *yuʿarrishūn* with the *rāʾ* doubled [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the inheritance and the identification: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatāda commented that "the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof which We have blessed" refers to the Shām region, and Mujāhid and Ibn Jarīr agreed; and he explains "the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their endurance" by God's other statement, "And We wished to do a favor to those who were weak and oppressed in the land, and to make them rulers and to make them the inheritors, and to establish them in the land, and We let Pharaoh and Hāmān and their hosts receive from them that which they feared" (28:5–6); and "We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people produced" means their agriculture and buildings, with Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid saying that *yaʿrishūn* means "they built" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the inheritance as the answer to the enslavement: "We made the people who were being weakened in the land" — the Children of Israel, who were servants of the house of Pharaoh, made to taste the worst punishment — inherit "the eastern and western parts of the land," and by the land here he understands the land of Egypt itself, in which they had been humiliated: God gave them all of it and established them in it. "Which We blessed, and the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because they were patient" — this is what Moses had said to them: "Seek help from God and be patient; indeed the earth belongs to God; He gives it in inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the outcome belongs to the reverent" (7:128). "And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people were making" — of towering buildings and decorated dwellings — "and what they were erecting": those houses of theirs became empty because of their wrongdoing — "in that is a sign for a people who know" (cf. 10:24) [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the verse as the fulfillment of Moses's words at 7:128: God bequeaths the land to those who were oppressed — the Israelites — as a reward because they were patient under Pharaoh's oppression; and it notes the more general sense, that those who face adversity with patience and the anticipation of divine succor will be granted deliverance. "The land that We blessed" is thought by many to refer to the area encompassing Syria and Palestine (al-Shām), since this is the land understood elsewhere as ordained for the Israelites (5:21) — though not necessarily only for the Israelites, since it is holy and blessed for all peoples (21:71) — while others claim that the land here refers to the domain of Pharaoh in Egypt (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī), or to both Egypt and Syria/Palestine (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī); it is called blessed because it has been endowed with fertility and abundance. "The most beautiful Word" that was fulfilled for the Children of Israel refers to their triumph over Pharaoh (Ṭabarī) and is also considered the fulfillment of God's promise in 28:5–6 [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** draws the theological point out of the pronouns: the verse did not say "the people who were weak," it says those who were *taken* as weak — implying that those who have God as their support can never be weak in the real sense, though they may seem so in their apparent condition; people finally come to realize that they are not weak, because dignity and honor belong to God. The term "inheritance" is used for their domination in the land to indicate that, like a son who is the real inheritor of his father's land, the Israelites were the real inheritors of the land and wealth of Pharaoh's people. The plural "easts and wests" may denote the different points of sunrise and sunset in winter and summer; and the "land," according to the exegetes, is the land of Egypt and Syria, which came under the Israelites' domination after the people of Pharaoh and the Amalekites were destroyed; "which We had blessed" refers to the lands of Syria and Egypt, with traditions on the blessing of Egypt and ʿUmar's word that the Nile is the prince of rivers and Ibn ʿUmar's that Egypt has nine parts of blessing out of ten, the tenth divided through the earth. Then the promise: the sublime word of your Lord was fulfilled — either the promise made through Moses in 7:129 or the promise made to the Israelites in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, "And We desired to bestow a favor upon those who were deemed weak in the land... and to show Pharaoh and Hāmān and their hosts that which they feared" (28:5–6); and in fact both promises are the same. This favor, he says, was the reward of their patience, as the verse specifies "because they stood patient" — and the description carries the implication that any people or individual following the same example, at any time and place, shall get the same reward. He quotes al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: when a person who has been wronged tries to take revenge on his own by doing wrong to his opponent, God leaves him alone to manage his own affairs, ending in success or failure; whereas when one seeks God's help against the affliction from others and remains patient, God opens the door of success upon him — and he notes the same kind of promise made to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in Sūrat al-Nūr (24:55) [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders the verse with its identifications: and We bequeathed upon the people who were oppressed through bondage — the Children of Israel — the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof which We had blessed with water and trees, meaning Syria; and the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled — His saying, "Yet We desired to be gracious to those who were oppressed in the land" to the end of the verse (28:5) — for the Children of Israel because they endured patiently the persecution of their enemy; and We destroyed utterly what Pharaoh and his folk had been creating by way of architecture, and what they had been erecting, reading *yaʿrishūn* or *yaʿrushūn*, of edifices [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Yustadʿafūn* — being weakened, treated as weak — is the passive intensive of the root of weakness, and **[Maʿārif]** builds his reflection on its form: the verse says "those who were *taken* as weak," not "those who were weak," because the weakness was imposed by a tyrant and did not describe their real condition before God [Maʿārif]. *Awrathnā* — We made to inherit — is the causative of the verb of inheritance; **[Qurṭubī]** notes that with the causative *hamza* the verb takes two direct objects, which is why "the eastern and western parts" is accusative as a plain object and not, as some grammarians held, a place-adverbial with an omitted preposition [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. *Yaʿrishūn* — they erect, they build trellises and structures — is the disputed verb of the last clause, read *yaʿrishūn*, *yaʿrushūn* and *yuʿarrishūn*; **[Qurṭubī]** reports al-Ḥasan's view that the reference is to the trellising of vines and Ibn ʿAbbās's and Mujāhid's that it is building, and the difference is between architecture in general and the specific arbors of Egyptian agriculture [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Rulings.** Two principles the commentators state here. First, the inheritance of the land is presented as the reward of patience: **[Saʿdī]** and **[Maʿārif]** both emphasize the causal clause "because they were patient," and **[Maʿārif]** generalizes it — any people or individual who follows the same example at any time or place shall receive the same reward, and he cites al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's counsel that the wronged person who takes private revenge is left to himself, while the one who seeks God's help and waits is granted victory [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. Second, the destruction of Pharaoh's works — **[Saʿdī]**'s "towering buildings and decorated dwellings" and **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s "agriculture and buildings" — is read as the end of a civilization's monuments: what the Egyptians built as the expression of their permanence was dismantled, and the people they had enslaved were given the ground itself [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And We desired to bestow a favor upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them the leaders, and to make them the heirs, and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Hāmān and their hosts that which they feared" (28:5–6); "And He made you heirs of their lands and their houses and their wealth and a land you had not trodden" (33:27); "And We have already written in the Scripture, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants" (21:105); "God has promised those who have believed among you and done righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth" (24:55); "And enter the land which God has ordained for you" (5:21) [Study Quran] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the hinge on which the whole Egyptian narrative turns into a theology of history. The people who had been counted as raw material — their sons killed, their daughters kept for service, their labor conscripted — are named here as heirs, and the lands they inherit are not merely Egypt's fields but the whole horizon of east and west that the sūrah's language of blessing can hold. Compared with the passage immediately before it, the sentence is almost serene, and its serenity comes from the causal clause at its center: *bi-mā ṣabarū*, because they were patient. The sūrah has shown what impatience looked like — the complaint of 7:129, the calf of 7:148 — and it shows here what patience received. And the last clause, the demolition of everything Pharaoh's people had made and erected, is the sūrah's quiet epitaph on a civilization that built for forever and was swept away in a single morning [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

## 7:138

*"And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people clinging to their idols. They said, 'O Moses, make for us a god as they have gods.' He said, 'Indeed, you are a people behaving ignorantly.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the charge the verse carries, and his reading is sharp: God says that He carried the Children of Israel across the sea — *bāʾtu bihim* — after the signs they had seen and the lessons they had witnessed at the hands of God's prophet Moses; and those signs did not restrain them, nor did those lessons and clear proofs admonish them, until they said — while witnessing proofs that would properly have moved even cattle to remember! — passing by a people clinging to idols, that is, standing over images they worshipped besides God: "Make for us, O Moses, a god to worship and an idol to take as a god, just as those people have idols." And Moses said to them: you are a people ignorant of the greatness of God and of the obligation of His right upon you, and you do not know that worship may not be given to anything besides God, the One, the Overpowering [Ṭabarī]. He records the identification of the idolaters: Ibn Jurayj said their idols were images of cattle, and when the Sāmiri's calf came, it was made to seem to them one of those cattle — and that was the beginning of the calf affair. Qatāda said the people were of Lakhkhm; it is also said they were of the Canaanites whom Moses was commanded to fight [Ṭabarī]. Then comes the tradition that makes this one of the most theologically pointed passages in the sūrah: Abū Wāqid al-Laythī said, "We went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ toward Ḥunayn, and we passed by a lote tree. I said, 'O Prophet of God, make for us this one a *dhāt anwāṭ*, as the disbelievers have a *dhāt anwāṭ*' — and the disbelievers used to hang their weapons on a lote tree and stay around it" — and the Prophet's answer, preserved in full in **[Qurṭubī]**: "God is greatest! You have said as the people of Moses said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.' You will surely follow the ways of those before you, handspan by handspan and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered a lizard's hole you would enter it too." And this occurred on the way to Ḥunayn [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. **[Study Quran]** fills in the scene: the Children of Israel were brought across the sea when Moses miraculously parted it with his staff by divine command (2:50; 20:77; 26:63); and shortly thereafter — according to some, even before their feet were dry from their walk across the divided sea (al-Zamakhsharī) — they came upon a people clinging to idols. Commentators speculate that these may have been the Canaanites (Ṭabarī), or Lakhmites who had settled in the area (Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī), or descendants of Abraham's idolatrous people (al-Jalālayn); their idols were said to be in the form of a calf (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), which is also the form of the idol later made by the Israelites (7:148). In response, Moses derides them as an ignorant people, *qawm tajhalūn*, the word for ignorant being derived from the same root as *jāhiliyyah*, the pre-Islamic pagan era in Arabia; in both cases ignorance refers to ignorance of the greatness of God, of the duty to worship Him, and of the prohibition against worshipping anything else (Ṭabarī). "As for these" refers to the idolaters whom the Israelites had come upon, whose practices would perish [Study Quran]. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the readings and the identification: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read *yaʿkifūn* with *kasrah* on the *kāf*, the rest with *ḍammah*, and both mean to stay at a thing and cling to it; Qatāda said those people were of Lakhkhm, settled at al-Raqqah; and it is said their idols were images of cattle, which is why the Sāmiri brought out a calf for the Israelites. He then records the ḥadīth of *dhāt anwāṭ* in full, with the Prophet's ﷺ comparison to the words of Moses's people and his warning that the community would follow the ways of those before it, and notes that this occurred at the Prophet's departure for Ḥunayn [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the request as the fruit of a moment's folly in the midst of miracles: after God had saved them from Pharaoh and destroyed him while the Children of Israel watched, they came upon a people keeping to idols, standing by them, seeking blessing from them and worshipping them; and they said, in their ignorance and folly, to their prophet — after God had shown them what He had shown them of signs — "O Moses, make for us a god as they have gods," that is, legislate for us that we take idols as gods as these have. And Moses said to them: "Indeed, you are a people behaving ignorantly" — and what ignorance is greater than to be ignorant of one's own Lord and Creator, and to wish to make equal to Him someone who owns no benefit, no harm, no death, no life and no resurrection? [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the social observation: after their miraculous victory over Pharaoh and a life of ease and comfort, they began to show the signs of ignorance as people of wealth show when given a life of luxury and opulence; the first impertinent request they made was that Moses make them a god like the gods of the people they saw being worshipped on their way. Moses was greatly annoyed by their ignorance and said that the labor of worship of those people was to go to waste [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the verse in his sequence of the crossing and what followed [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: and We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon — they passed by — a people cleaving in devotion to idols of theirs, constantly worshipping them; they said, "O Moses, make for us a god, an idol for us to worship, just as they have gods." He said, "Truly you are an ignorant folk, for repaying God's grace to you with what you have said" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Yaʿkufūna* — clinging, cleaving, staying put — is the verb of devoted station before a thing; the readings with *kasrah* and *ḍammah* on its second root letter are both authentic and both mean the same [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]. *Jahl* — ignorance — in the Qurʾān's usage is rarely a lack of information and almost always a moral condition; **[Study Quran]** notes that Moses's word *tajhalūn* shares the root of *jāhiliyyah* and that the ignorance in question is ignorance of God's greatness and of the prohibition of worship to another [Study Quran] [Saʿdī]. And the phrase "as they have gods" — *kamā lahum ālihatun* — states the request's whole logic: not "give us a god" but "give us one like theirs," a request for parity with a people who had just been passed on the road [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The verse's most consequential tradition is the ḥadīth of Abū Wāqid al-Laythī, transmitted through al-Zuhrī: the request at the lote tree before Ḥunayn, and the Prophet's ﷺ reply, "God is greatest! You have said as the people of Moses said, 'Make for us a god as they have gods.' You will surely follow the ways of those before you, handspan by handspan and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered a lizard's hole you would enter it too" — a report the commentators cite as the verse's demonstration that the tendency it describes is not confined to ancient Israel [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī].

**Rulings.** The commentators draw two lessons. First, the request is an act of *shirk* in intention even though it is not carried out, and Moses's rebuke treats the wish itself as ignorance of God's greatness — **[Saʿdī]**'s rhetorical question, what ignorance is greater than to equate with one's Creator a thing that owns no benefit, no harm, no death, no life and no resurrection, is the standard formulation of the doctrine of *tawḥīd* against it [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. Second, the passage warns the later community: the Prophet's ﷺ response to the same request in his own time shows that the pattern of following "those before you" is a standing danger, and that the community's protection against it lies in the same rebuke Moses gave [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "They said: O Moses, make for us a god as they have gods. He said: Indeed, you are a people behaving ignorantly" (7:138); "And they took, after him, the calf, a mere body that lowed" (7:148; cf. 20:88); "So he brought out for them a calf, a mere body that lowed, and they said: This is your god and the god of Moses, and he forgot" (20:88); "Then you took the calf [for worship] after him, and you were wrongdoers" (2:51; cf. 2:92–93; 4:153) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse's placement is its message. Israel had just crossed a sea on dry ground, with the walls of water on either side and the Egyptian army closing behind them — and the first recorded sentence they speak on the other shore is a request to be given an idol. The commentators all note the speed of it, and **[Study Quran]**'s report that some placed the request before their feet were dry gives the scene its full pathos: the miracle had not finished happening, and the request for a stone had already been made [Study Quran]. What the verse diagnoses is the ease with which a delivered people converts its deliverance into an entitlement and then looks for something visible to carry; and by recording the Prophet's ﷺ alarm at the same request in his own community, the tradition makes the passage a standing warning rather than a settled account of the past [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif].

## 7:139

*"'Indeed, these — destroyed is what they are in, and vain is what they have been doing.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as God's report of Moses's word to his people, stated in the verse before: Moses said to them, these people who cling to these idols, God will destroy what they are upon of practice and ruin it, and will make them lose by it, requiting them with humiliating punishment; and "vain is what they were doing" — their worship of idols — because it will vanish and come to nothing, since it will not profit them when God's command comes and settles among them, nor defend them from God's might when it descends, nor rescue them from His punishment when He punishes them in the hereafter; so their work is in the position of something that never was [Ṭabarī]. He records the early glosses: al-Suddī, "destroyed what they are in" means ruined (muhlik); Ibn ʿAbbās: loss (khusrān); Ibn Zayd: the two halves are one, like a doubled divine name — "forgiving, merciful," "pardoner, forgiving" — and the Arabs say of a wretched man that he is "perishing" and "losing" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the passage's brief comment on the same lines [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the argument: therefore Moses said to them, "these — destroyed is what they are in, and vain is what they were doing" — because their calling upon these idols is vain, and the idols are vain in themselves; so their action is vain and its end is vain [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the sentence as Moses's verdict on the people the Israelites had just asked to imitate: "As for these" refers to the idolaters whom the Israelites have come upon — the Canaanites or Lakhmites, whose idols were in the form of a calf — and their practices shall perish, while "that which they used to do" is described as vain, since it neither brings them benefit nor averts harm [Study Quran]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Maʿārif]** carry the verse as part of Moses's rebuke: the labor of worship of those people was to go to waste, and how could he think of making for them a god other than Allah, who had given them excellence over the peoples of all the worlds [Maʿārif] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: "Truly as for these, their way will be destroyed and what they have been doing is in vain" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Mutabbar* — destroyed, shattered — is a strong word, from a root of breaking and perishing, used of things ground to pieces; **[Ṭabarī]**'s first gloss, "ruined," and Ibn ʿAbbās's "loss" both preserve the sense of a thing whose substance is gone [Ṭabarī]. *Bāṭil* — vain, void — is the Qurʾān's standing word for what is false and for what does not last; the verse applies both terms at once, so that the idolaters' way is not merely wrong but non-existent in the ledger of the end. And the verse's final phrase, "what they were doing" — *mā kānū yaʿmalūn*, in the imperfect of habitual practice — covers the whole of their religious labor, not one act of it; the verdict is on a life's work [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Belief.** The verse states the *tawḥīd* argument as a claim about futility rather than about punishment: whatever is worshipped besides God has no power to carry the worshipper anywhere, so the worship itself dissolves. **[Saʿdī]** puts it in two clauses — their supplication to idols is vain, and the idols are vain in themselves, therefore the action is vain and its end is vain — which makes the verse a compact summary of why *shirk* is irrational before it is ever counted as a sin [Saʿdī]. And **[Ṭabarī]**'s expansions — that the worship will not profit them, nor defend them from God's might, nor rescue them from His punishment — give the same claim its eschatological teeth: the vanity of idols is proved on the day they are needed [Ṭabarī].

**Cross-references.** "That is because God is the Truth, and that which they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and that God is the Most High, the Most Great" (22:62; cf. 31:30); "And those whom they invoke besides God create nothing and are themselves created" (16:20); "Like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty man deems to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing" (24:39); "The example of those who take allies other than God is that of the spider who takes a home — and indeed, the weakest of homes is the home of the spider" (29:41) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** Moses's reply to the request for an idol is not a sermon on the oneness of God; it is a prediction about the idols' fate. He does not tell his people that the object of their imitation is evil — he tells them that it is passing away, and that the labor spent on it will prove to have been spent on nothing. It is the same method the sūrah uses everywhere: the truth of worship is settled by what survives the end, and by that measure the gods of the road are already demolished [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And the sentence has an edge on the future, because the people who heard it a few verses after crossing the sea will themselves build a calf within a few chapters of their journey — and the verdict Moses pronounced on the idols of others will be pronounced on their own [Study Quran].

## 7:140

*"He said, 'Shall I seek for you a god other than God, when He has favored you above the worlds?'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as Moses's second word to his people, closing the request: shall I seek for you a god other than God, and make for you an object of worship that you worship, when God — who is your Creator — has favored you over the worlds of your age and time? Will I seek for you a god that neither profits nor harms, that you worship, and leave the worship of the One who has favored you over creation? This is ignorance from you [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** unfolds the interrogative as an argument from God's perfection and their preference: "shall I seek for you a god other than God" — that is, shall I seek for you an object of worship other than God, who is perfect in His essence, His attributes and His acts — "when He has favored you over the worlds," which requires you to meet His favor and His preference with gratitude, and gratitude means singling God out alone with worship and disbelieving in whatever is called upon besides Him [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the sense of the final clause: that God has favored the Israelites above the worlds may mean that He favored them above all other people of their time, or that the miraculous signs and the deliverance through Moses were not granted to any other people (al-Rāzī); and it points to 2:47 and to 7:141's account of the deliverance from the house of Pharaoh, with the slaying of sons and sparing of women, as the concrete content of the favor [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** reads the verse as the second half of Moses's rebuke: how could he think of making for them a god other than Allah while He had given them excellence over the peoples of all the worlds — that is, the people who believed in Moses were superior to all the people of that age — and he then notes that the next verses remind them of their pitiable condition and their persecutions at Pharaoh's hands, when their sons were killed and their daughters saved to serve as maidservants: shall they be as ungrateful to their Lord as to take abject stones as gods and make them partners with Allah? [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** keeps the verse in the flow of Moses's answer to the request [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the same reading in the passage's brief comment [Qurṭubī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: he said, "Shall I seek other than God as a god for you to worship — where 'shall I seek for you' is originally 'for you' with the preposition — when He has favoured you above all the worlds of your time, in the ways He has mentioned?" [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]**'s closing lines fix the tone: the question is rhetorical and the answer is meant to be obvious; the verse is not a deliberation but a rebuke, and its last clause supplies the reason — a people singled out by the Lord of the worlds does not go looking for a stone [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Language.** *Abghīkum* — shall I seek for you — is the verb of seeking, and its placement at the head of the sentence makes the absurdity grammatical: the object sought is "a god other than God," and the subject of the search is a prophet who has just been shown the Lord's power at the sea [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]. The phrase *faddalakum ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — favored you above the worlds — is the sūrah's standing description of Israel's election (cf. 2:47, 122; 45:16), and the exegetes read it with the qualification the context supplies: the preference is over the peoples of their time, and its content is the signs and the deliverance granted them through Moses [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. The verse ends without a further clause, so that the question hangs: the argument is that favor and idolatry are incompatible, and the incompatibility is left for the listener to feel [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī].

**Rulings.** The verse states the logic of gratitude as a religious obligation: **[Saʿdī]**'s "which requires you to meet His favor with gratitude, and gratitude means singling God out alone with worship" makes *shukr* the practical form of *tawḥīd*, so that the request for an idol is not only ignorance but ingratitude [Saʿdī]. And **[Maʿārif]**'s reading places the argument in the arc of the passage: the Israelites are reminded in the following verses of what they were saved from, so that the rebuke is grounded in memory — the people asking for a god of stone had been slaves, and the God who freed them is the one they were proposing to supplement [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I have bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds" (2:47; cf. 2:122); "And We certainly gave the Children of Israel the Scripture and the judgment and prophethood, and We provided them with good things and preferred them over the worlds" (45:16); "And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, killing your sons and letting your women live" (7:141; cf. 2:49; 14:6); "And We delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment — from Pharaoh" (44:30–31) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

**Reflection.** The verse's logic is the oldest argument in the sūrah and the newest, and it is stated as a question rather than a thesis: shall I look for you a god other than the One who has already carried you? The Israelites had been given a preference that cost them nothing to receive and everything to misunderstand; the request for an idol was, at bottom, a wish to be religious in the manner of their neighbors rather than in the manner of their deliverance. Moses's answer refuses the wish by pointing to the ledger of favors already received, and by leaving them to conclude that a people who have crossed the sea on dry ground cannot plausibly need a stone to remind them who did it [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].
## 7:141

*"And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment — killing your sons and letting your women live; and in that was a great trial from your Lord."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the reminder that follows the rebuke: God says to the Jews of the Children of Israel who lived among the emigrants of the Messenger of God ﷺ — remember, together with this saying of yours which you said to Moses, after you had seen the signs and the lessons, and after the favors which went before from Me to you and the gifts that preceded — the deed you did, when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were upon his way and his path in disbelief. They were afflicting you with the worst torment, that is, imposing upon you the ugliest and most evil punishment: they were killing your sons, the males among your children, and letting your women live, that is, sparing the females. And in that — in their imposing the worst torment upon you — was a trial from your Lord and a great favor: an examination from God for you, and a great blessing, since the affliction and the deliverance together proved you and shaped you [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same reminder in the setting of Moses's discourse: Moses reminded the Children of Israel of God's blessings, such as saving them from Pharaoh and from his tyranny and the humiliation and disgrace they suffered; and he reminded them of the glory and the vengeance against their enemy, when they watched that enemy suffering in disgrace, destroyed by drowning and meeting utter demise [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the completion of the rebuke of the previous two verses: having told them that the way of the idolaters is destroyed and their own God is the One who favored them above the worlds, God reminds them of the blessing in detail — the rescue from the people of Pharaoh, the affliction of the worst torment, the killing of the sons and the sparing of the women to serve them — and says that in that there was a trial from their Lord: either the great and mighty blessing of the deliverance itself, or the punishment coming from the enemy as a trial and testing for them [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** notes the variant reading *anjākum*, "He delivered you," in place of the standard *anjaynākum*, "We delivered you"; the punishment is "the worst kind of chastisement, namely slaying your sons and sparing your women"; and the *balāʾ* is either a grace or a tribulation from your Lord — so will you not take heed of the admonition and desist from what you are saying? [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** puts the verse in the flow of the whole passage: after their miraculous victory over Pharaoh and their life of ease and comfort, the Israelites had begun to show the signs of ignorance as people of wealth show when given luxury and opulence; and now the next verses remind them of their pitiable condition and their persecutions at the hands of Pharaoh, when their sons were killed and their daughters were saved to serve as maidservants — Allah relieved them of this disgraceful chastisement through His prophet, so shall they be so ungrateful to their Lord as to take abject stones as gods and make them partners with Allah? They must repent to Allah for their transgression [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the verse in the passage's comment; and **[Study Quran]**'s note on 7:140, that the preference over the worlds has as its concrete content this deliverance, applies directly to the reminder here [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran].

**Language.** Two words carry the verse. *Yasūmūnakum* — they were afflicting you, literally "they were pasturing you on" — is used of driving a herd to pasture, so that the torture is described as a diet imposed on a herd [Ṭabarī]. And *balāʾ* is the verse's pivot: it means trial and testing, and it is used of both halves of the experience — the enslavement was God's test of Israel, and the deliverance was God's gift to Israel, and **[Saʿdī]** preserves both readings side by side, since the same event can be a trial in its pain and a blessing in its outcome [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. The phrase *āl Firʿawn* — the house of Pharaoh — is read by **[Ṭabarī]** as the confession rather than the family: they were the ones on his way and his path in disbelief [Ṭabarī].

**Cross-references.** "And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, killing your sons and letting your women live; and in that was a great trial from your Lord" (2:49); "And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh" (14:6, where Moses says it to his people); "He is the One who made you successors in the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees, to test you by what He has given you" (6:165, on *balāʾ* as the test of gifts); "And We tested them with good times and adversities that perhaps they might return" (7:168) [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The placement of this verse is its lesson. In 7:138–140 the Israelites asked for an idol and were told that their neighbors' gods were doomed and that their own God had favored them; here the sūrah tells them what that favor had been. Gratitude, the passage implies, is a work of memory: the people who wanted a golden object to carry were the people who had forgotten the morning they walked through the sea. **[Maʿārif]**'s diagnosis of the sequence — ease and comfort breeding the signs of ignorance in a newly wealthy people — is one of the most sober observations in the commentaries, and it explains why the sūrah's cure for the wish for idols is a recital of what God has already done [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

## 7:142

*"And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was fulfilled at forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, 'Take my place among my people, and do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the plain sense: God says that He made an appointment with Moses for His intimate discourse of thirty nights, and completed the thirty with ten nights, making forty; and Moses, when the time of his Lord's appointment came, said to his brother Aaron, "Be my deputy among my people until I return." He notes the derivation of the deputyship: *khalafahu yakhlufuhu khilāfah*. "And do right" — that is, set them right by carrying them to the obedience of God and His worship; and **[Ṭabarī]** preserves Ibn Jurayj's sharp specification of what that reform entailed: part of his setting things right was that he was not to leave the calf to be worshipped. "And do not follow the way of the corrupters" — do not walk the path of those who work corruption in the earth by their disobedience to their Lord and who aid the people of disobedience in their rebellion, but walk the way of those who obey their Lord [Ṭabarī]. He then sets the historical placement: the appointment of God with Moses came after the destruction of Pharaoh and the deliverance of the Children of Israel from him — after they had crossed the sea and come to the good land, where God sent down the manna and the quails, He commanded His prophet to meet Him; Moses, wishing to meet his Lord, appointed Aaron as his deputy over his people and promised them that he would come to them after thirty nights — a promise from himself, not from God's command or appointment — and when the thirty nights were up, the enemy of God, al-Sāmirī, said to the people: "Moses is not coming to you; nothing will set you right but a god you can worship!" Aaron adjured them: do not do it; wait out this night and this day, and if he comes, well; if not, do what you see fit. They agreed. But the next morning, not seeing Moses, al-Sāmirī repeated his word to them; and God then added ten more to the appointed term, and the time of Moses's Lord was completed at forty nights. Aaron adjured them again to wait their day; al-Sāmirī came the third time with the same speech, and Aaron again restrained them — and when they did not see Moses, the report breaks off in the manuscript at that point [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** works through the verse in three questions. First, the appointment itself was part of the honor done to Moses: the promise of the intimate discourse was a gift of rank. The exegetes identify the years: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Masrūq said the thirty nights are Dhū al-Qaʿdah and the ten are the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah; Moses was commanded to fast the month and to be alone in it for worship, and when he had fasted it he was troubled by the smell of his own mouth and cleaned his teeth with a stick — it is said with the wood of the carob tree — whereupon the angels said, "We used to breathe from your mouth the fragrance of musk, and you have spoiled it with the tooth-stick," and so ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijjah were added, or, by another report, God revealed to him: "O Moses, I will not speak to you until your mouth returns to what it was; do you not know that the smell of the fasting person is dearer to Me than the smell of musk?" God spoke to Moses on the morning of the day of sacrifice, the day on which Ishmael was ransomed from slaughter and the day on which the pilgrimage of Muhammad ﷺ was completed. Then the arithmetic: the benefit of saying "forty nights" after saying "thirty and ten" is that no one should suppose the ten were counted inside the thirty; and the apparent difference with 2:51, where God says forty, is no contradiction, since forty in one expression and thirty-and-ten in another is the same sum told two ways, as the Arabs count "ten and four" for fourteen — the night of the full moon. Second, our scholars, says **[Qurṭubī]**, have drawn from this verse the standing practice of fixing a term for an appointment, and the wisdom of gradualism: Ibn al-ʿArabī's rule is that when a term is set for a purpose and the term expires with the purpose unmet, an extension is added for the sake of insight and excuse; and God made this clear to Moses, setting thirty then adding ten to complete forty. Then the failure: Moses was late in those ten days, and they did not grasp the legitimacy of delay and postponement until they said Moses had strayed or forgotten, and they broke his covenant and substituted after him and worshipped a god other than God. Third, the verse proves that dating was by nights rather than days — "thirty nights" — because the nights are the beginnings of the months, and by nights the Companions used to reckon their days; Ibn al-ʿArabī's sentence is quoted by **[Maʿārif]** as well: the reckoning of the sun is for benefits in worldly matters, and the reckoning of the moon is for religious observances [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** fills in the setting: Moses spent forty nights on Mount Sinai, the sacred mountain (95:2; cf. 2:63, 93; 4:154; Exodus 24:18), during a period corresponding to Dhū al-Qaʿdah and the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, concluding on the day of the Feast of Sacrifice (Ṭabarī); during this time Moses fasted and engaged in intimate discourse with God (al-Mawdūdī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī); some report that he fasted the first thirty days and the Torah was revealed to him during the final ten (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭūsī); and according to some, Moses originally told the people he would be away thirty days, but God had him stay an additional ten so as to test the faith of the Israelites when he did not return after the thirty (al-Qummī). "Take my place" translates *ukhlufnī*, related to *khalīfah*, "representative" or "successor," the term used for the leaders of the Muslim community after the death of the Prophet; Aaron is instructed to set matters aright (Ṭabarī) or to correct the corrupt among them (Ṭūsī) [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** explains the purpose of the appointment from God's side and Moses's: when God had completed His favor to them by deliverance from their enemy and established them in the land, He wished to complete it by sending down the Book containing the legal rulings and the pleasing doctrines; so He appointed Moses for thirty nights and completed them with ten — forty nights — so that Moses might prepare and ready himself for God's promise, and so that the descent of the Book might have a great place in their hearts and they might long for it. And when Moses went to the appointment of his Lord, he said to Aaron, out of his care for the Children of Israel and his compassion for them: "Take my place among my people" — be my deputy among them and do what I was doing; "and do right" — follow the way of righteousness; "and do not follow the way of the corrupters," who are those who act in disobedience [Saʿdī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that God here reminds the Children of Israel of the guidance He sent them by speaking directly to Moses and revealing the Torah, which contained their law and the detail of their legislation; that Moses fasted the thirty nights and cleaned his teeth with a twig at the end, so God commanded him to complete the term with ten more, making forty; that when it finished he was to return to the Mount, as God says elsewhere, "O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy and made a covenant with you on the right side of the Mount" (20:80); and that Moses left his brother Aaron with the Children of Israel, commanding him to use wisdom and avoid mischief — which was only a reminder, for Aaron was an honorable and noble prophet with grace and an exalted standard with God [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** gathers the practical readings of the passage. The fixing of a period teaches gradualism, since it is God's practice to do things by degrees; He created the universe in six days though He could have created it in an instant, and the Torah likewise was given after a fixed period. Ibn al-ʿArabī's observation, transmitted from **[Qurṭubī]**, is that the extension of a term is an education in granting respite: it teaches those in authority to give their subordinates time when they fall short. And **[Maʿārif]** reports the fast and the tooth-stick in the same form as the others, adding the ruling: these reports cannot be used to establish that cleaning the teeth while fasting is prohibited or disliked, first because the report is cited without a chain of narrators, and second because it could have been a command specific to Moses and not to others; the permissibility of the tooth-stick for the fasting person is proved by the Prophetic practice, and al-Bayhaqī has reported from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The best trait of the one who fasts is the tooth-stick," a tradition whose status in *al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr* is that of *ḥasan*. Then the application to the covenant: the Israelites had been told thirty days and grew restless at the ten additional nights, which is where their haste showed itself and where the calf came in — the delay was the trial [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the narrative compactly: the thirty nights were Dhū al-Qaʿdah; Moses disliked the bad odour of his mouth after the fast and cleaned his teeth; God therefore commanded him to fast ten more nights of Dhū al-Ḥijjah so as to speak to him despite the odour, since the odour of the faster is dear to God; and Moses said to his brother Aaron when departing to the Mount for the communion: "Be my deputy over my people and be righteous among them in their affair, and do not follow the way of the agents of corruption" by consenting with them to acts of disobedience [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Wāʿadnā* — "We appointed" — is read *waʿadnā*, "We promised," by some; the difference between an appointment and a promise is slight here because both fix a time [Jalālayn]. *Ukhlufnī* is the imperative of deputyship, from the same root as *khalīfah*, and **[Study Quran]** notes that its use here gives the verse its place in the vocabulary of succession in Islamic law and history [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī]. *Mīqāt* is the appointed time, and the phrase "the appointed time of his Lord was fulfilled at forty nights" states the completion of a term already fixed, not the discovery of a new one [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the tense of the final instruction — *lā tattabiʿ sabīl al-mufsidīn* — is a continuing prohibition, which is why **[Maʿārif]** reads it as a directive against helping or encouraging the mischievous rather than a warning that Aaron might become one of them [Maʿārif].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the tradition that makes the verse's deputyship a matter of legal memory: in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ, the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAlī when he left him behind in one of his campaigns, "Are you not pleased to be to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?" He then reports the uses made of it: the Imāmī and other Shīʿī groups used it to claim that the Prophet ﷺ appointed ʿAlī over the whole community, and some of them went so far as to declare the Companions disbelievers for not implementing what they took to be an explicit designation — a claim **[Qurṭubī]** rejects outright, arguing that the deputyship of Aaron was a deputyship during life, like a trust that ends with the end of the one who appointed it, not a perpetual succession; that the Prophet ﷺ appointed Ibn Umm Maktum and others over Madinah without that implying any permanent succession; and that Aaron was in any case a partner with Moses in the prophethood itself, so the report gives them no support for what they seek [Qurṭubī]. **[Maʿārif]** draws the administrative lessons from the same material: it is incumbent on one who holds an office to appoint a deputy when he must be absent, as the Prophet ﷺ appointed deputies, including ʿAlī and ʿAbdallāh b. Umm Maktum, on different occasions (cited from Qurṭubī); and it is a religious requirement to leave instructions with one's deputy, which Moses did [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s caution about Aaron belongs here too: the command to avoid mischief was a reminder rather than a suspicion, since Aaron was an honorable prophet [Ibn Kathīr].

**Rulings.** Two rulings the commentators extract. First, the legitimacy of delegation and of leaving instructions: **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of the Prophetic practice and Ibn Jurayj's specification that the deputy's duty includes preventing the worship of the calf give the verse the shape of a job description — the deputy must set things right, not merely keep the seat warm [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. Second, the discipline of terms and patience with delay: **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Maʿārif]** both use the verse to show that setting a deadline and even extending it is a divine *sunnah* meant to teach rulers to deal with subjects by granting time; and the catastrophe in the passage is traced precisely to a people who could not wait ten extra nights [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, and then you took the calf [for worship] after him, and you were wrongdoers" (2:51); "And We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations, as enlightenment for the people" (28:43); "O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy and made a covenant with you on the right side of the Mount" (20:80); "And We called him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near for intimate conversation" (19:52); "By the Mount and by a Book inscribed" (52:1–2); "By the fig and the olive, and by Mount Sinai" (95:1–2) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse looks like a schedule and functions like a test. Forty nights on the mountain, during which the people are left with a deputy and a promise; and the sūrah's whole disaster happens in the gap between what was said and what was meant — Moses told them thirty, God had decreed forty, and in the ten days of waiting the calf was born. Nothing in the passage suggests that God sprang the extra ten on Moses as a trick; everything in the commentaries presents them as a fixed part of the term, and the failure as belonging to the people's impatience [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. The further note — that the ten days of delay were themselves a test of the Israelites' faith — makes the appointment a mirror of the whole story: the people who had walked through the sea could not sit still ten nights for a book [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].

## 7:143

*"And when Moses came to Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, 'My Lord, show me, that I may look upon You.' He said, 'You shall not see Me, but look at the mountain: if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me.' And when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down in a swoon. And when he recovered, he said, 'Glory be to You! I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the reason for Moses's request from the early authorities. Al-Suddī: when Moses's Lord spoke to him and confided in him, he longed to look at Him, and said, "My Lord, show me, that I may look upon You"; and God, answering him, said, "You shall not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you shall see Me." In al-Suddī's report the mountain was ringed about with angels, and the angels with fire, and the fire with angels again, before the Lord appeared to it [Ṭabarī]. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, explaining "and We brought him near for intimate conversation" (19:52), said that one who had met the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ told him that the Lord brought him so near that he heard the scraping of the pen — and it was at that point, out of longing for Him, that Moses said, "My Lord, show me, that I may look upon You"; and God said, "You shall not see Me, but look at the mountain" [Ṭabarī]. Another report: when Moses was held back beyond the thirty nights until he heard the speech of God, he longed to look at Him and said the words of the verse; and God said, "You shall not see Me — and no human being has the capacity to look at Me in this world; whoever looks at Me dies." Moses said, "My God, I have heard Your speech and I long to look at You; and to look at You and then die is dearer to me than to live and not see You!" So God said, "Look at the mountain: if it stays in its place, you will see Me." Ibn ʿAbbās glossed "show me" as "give me." And Ibn Isḥāq records what he found among the People of the Book, noting honestly that the Scriptures of the Jews contain much regression and story on this matter that did not come to us in the Book of God [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the doctrinal spine of the passage. Moses asked for the vision out of longing after God had made him hear His speech; and "you shall not see Me" means in this world. He rejects the interpretation that Moses was asking for a sign of power rather than for God Himself, because the verse says "to You" and because God's answer is "you shall not see Me" — had he asked for a sign, God would have given it as He gave all the other signs, and Moses had no need to ask for another. As for the mountain: God set before him an example drawn from what is stronger than his own frame and more firmly fixed — if the mountain stays still, you will see Me; if it does not, you cannot bear My vision, as the mountain cannot bear it. He then reports the striking opinion of al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ from Abū Bakr b. al-Ṭayyib: that Moses did see God and for that reason fell down in a swoon, and that the mountain saw its Lord and became dust by a perception God created in it — an inference from "if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me," followed by "when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down in a swoon." *Tajallā* means He appeared and was disclosed, from the usage *jalawtu al-ʿarūs*, "I displayed the bride"; Qutrub and others said what appeared was His command and His power. The readers of Madinah and Baṣrah read *dakkan*, and the readers of Kūfah read *dakkāʾ*, meaning He made it like a leveled earth. "And Moses fell down in a swoon" — that is, unconscious, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and Qatāda; some said dead, since *ṣaʿiqa* is used of the thunderstruck. Qatāda and al-Kalbī put the day precisely: Moses fell down in a swoon on Thursday, the day of ʿArafah, and was given the Torah on Friday, the day of the sacrifice. And when he came to himself he said, "Glory be to You! I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers" — Mujāhid said the repentance was from having asked for the vision in this world; others, from having asked without permission; and the Muslim community is agreed that this "turning" was not from a sin, since the prophets are protected from sin [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** frames the same material by the word *lan*. "You shall not see Me" — the *lan* by no means indicates that seeing God will never occur, as the misguided Muʿtazilites claimed; the hadiths of mutawātir grade from the Messenger of God ﷺ affirm that the believers will see Allah in the Hereafter, and he cites 75:22–23, "Some faces that Day shall be radiant, looking at their Lord." In earlier Scriptures it was reported that God said to Moses: "O Moses, no living soul sees Me but perishes, and no solid thing but is demolished." Then: when the Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. In his *Musnad*, Aḥmad recorded from Anas b. Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ, reciting "when his Lord appeared to the mountain," held out the tip of his little finger "like this" — a report al-Tirmidhī graded *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb* and al-Ḥākim graded sound by the criterion of Muslim; and al-Suddī reported from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās that only the extent of the little finger appeared from Him, and the mountain was made dust and Moses fell down in a swoon. When Moses recovered, he said, "Glory be to You" — praising, glorifying and honoring God, since no living soul could see Him in this life and remain alive; "I turn to You in repentance," meaning, according to Mujāhid, from asking to look at You; "and I am the first of the believers" — among the Children of Israel, per Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, a view Ibn Jarīr preferred; or, by another report from Ibn ʿAbbās, the first to believe that no one shall see You in this life [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** builds the meaning step by step: when Moses came to the appointment set for the sending down of the Book, and his Lord spoke to him of His revelation, His command and His prohibition, he longed for the vision of God, his soul drawn to it out of love for his Lord and desire to see Him, and he said, "My Lord, show me, that I may look upon You." God said, "You shall not see Me" — that is, you are not able to see Me now, for God created the creatures in this abode upon a constitution in which they cannot bear or withstand the vision of God; and he notes that there is in this no proof that they will not see Him in Paradise, since the Qurʾānic texts and Prophetic traditions prove that the people of Paradise will see their Lord and enjoy gazing at His noble face, and that God will create them in a complete constitution with which they can see Him. God therefore tied the vision in this verse to the mountain's stability: "but look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me." And when the Lord appeared to the mountain — the deaf, solid mountain — He made it crumble like sand, shaken by the vision of God and unable to withstand it; and Moses fell in a swoon, and it became plain to him that if the mountain could not stand for the vision of God, Moses is even less able. He sought his Lord's forgiveness for what had issued from him of the question that did not accord with the situation, and said: "Glory be to You" — declaring You free and great beyond what does not suit Your majesty; "I turn to You in repentance" — from all sins and from ill manners before You; "and I am the first of the believers" — he renewed, upon him be peace, his faith in what God had completed for him of that which he had not known before [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** isolates the doctrine carried by the wording: the phrase *lan tarānī*, "you shall never see Me," itself indicates that the vision of Allah is not impossible, only that Moses in his present physical disposition could not endure it — for had it been impossible the phrase would have been *lan urā*, "I cannot be seen" (al-Mazharī); this allows that the vision is a rational possibility while this verse and the consensus of the majority of scholars preclude its occurrence in this world; and the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim states, "None among you shall see his Lord until he dies." The second phrase, "but look at the mountain," is a physical demonstration that in his present state the addressee cannot endure the impact of such an experience, and God then demonstrated it by a flash of His appearance on Mount Sinai, which could not stand it and was smashed to pieces. On *tajallā*: the word signifies exposure or disclosure, and the spiritual masters hold that it signifies seeing something indirectly through some other means, like seeing a thing reflected in a mirror — so the word cannot signify "seeing," which is also inferred from the verse itself, since it negates the possibility of seeing while mentioning the occurrence of the manifestation. And he cites the ḥadīth of Anas in Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim: the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and, placing his thumb on the tip of his little finger, said that only that much of Allah's light was exposed to the mountain, which made it burst into pieces [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** sets the verse in the debate: it speaks directly to the issue of the human ability or inability to "see" God and seems to support the view that God cannot be seen by human beings in this world, at least in the ordinary sense — consistent with 6:103, "Sight comprehends Him not, but He comprehends all sight." Moses's desire was engendered by the intimacy he had experienced; God spoke to him without intermediary, and, according to a legendary report, was so close that Moses could hear the scratching of the pen across the tablets as they were written by God; overcome with spiritual ecstasy, he yearned to be nearer and asked. Some argued that Moses, who knew God transcends form and body, asked this only to satisfy the Israelites who had said, "We will not believe you till we see God openly" (2:55); others suggest he was asking not for a physical vision but for such complete spiritual knowledge of God as would be like seeing Him directly. Some commentators understand "you shall not see Me" to mean that God is not seen in this world but may be in the next, invoking 75:23; others argue the emphatic form indicates He will not be seen even in the next world. In the Biblical account Moses is told that none can see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20), and some commentators mention this, or note that had Moses not looked at the mountain when God manifested Himself, he would have died. For Sufis this may be connected with the idea that the vision of God in this life is possible only after the "death of the ego."
