On the mountain's crumbling: it indicates that seeing God with the physical eye is as impossible as the mountain being able to withstand God's self-manifestation; it demonstrates the annihilating power of that vision, since even the mountain, so much larger and stronger than Moses, was incapable of bearing it. Moses fell in a swoon out of sheer awe or as the result of being passed over by one of the angels; *ṣaʿiqa* might also be translated "thunderstruck," from the same root as the thunderbolt that struck the Israelites for asking a similar question in 2:55; some indicate Moses actually died and was brought back to life, though others argue *afāqa* connotes arousal from unconsciousness rather than from death. Upon recovering, Moses turns in repentance for having asked to see God; and "I am the first of the believers" may mean the first among the Israelites of his time to believe, or the first to believe that God could not be seen physically, or the foremost believer of his time. Finally, the Sufi tradition: al-Sulamī, commenting on this verse, indicates that "nothing can withstand the witnessing of God save the hearts of the gnostics," which God has adorned with spiritual knowledge of Himself and illuminated with His light — though even this witnessing really describes God's witnessing Himself, "for the Real is witnessed by none but Himself" [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** keeps the essentials and the famous gloss: Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke with him without an intermediary, with speech he heard from all directions; he said, "My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may behold You"; God said, "You shall not see Me" — the use of "you shall not see Me" instead of "I shall not be seen" implies that seeing God is possible — "but behold the mountain, which is stronger than you are: if it remains fixed in its place, then you shall see Me"; and when his Lord manifested of His light the equivalent of half a nail of a little finger, as stated in a hadith verified by al-Ḥākim, the mountain was leveled to the ground, and Moses fell down senseless at the awesomeness of what he had seen; and when he recovered he said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You for having asked what I was not commanded to ask, and I am the first of the believers of my time" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Lan tarānī* — "you shall not see Me" — is the verse's most contested construction, and the exegetes read its grammar as doctrine. **[Jalālayn]**, **[Maʿārif]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** all note that the wording speaks of the object's inability rather than of God's being unseeable, which is the linguistic ground on which the Ashʿarite and Sunnī position rests: had the meaning been that God cannot be seen at all, the natural Arabic would have been "I shall not be seen" [Jalālayn] [Maʿārif] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Tajallā* is disclosure, from the root of displaying a bride or drawing a sword from rust; **[Qurṭubī]** gives those derivations, and **[Maʿārif]**'s Sufi point is that in this very verse manifestation occurs while vision is denied, so the two cannot be the same thing [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. *Dakk* and *dakkāʾ* are the two readings of the leveled mountain, the first a verbal noun of crushing, the second an adjective for a flattened rise of earth [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]. And *ṣaʿiqa* is the swoon or death that comes over one struck by a thunderbolt — **[Study Quran]** notes that the Israelites who demanded to see God were struck with a thunderbolt of the same root (2:55), so that Moses's experience and his people's demand are variants of one encounter between human capacity and divine self-disclosure [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Three traditions the commentators carry here. First, the finger hadith: al-Tirmidhī's and al-Ḥākim's report from Anas b. Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ, reciting this verse, indicated the tip of his little finger — that much of God's light was exposed to the mountain and it shattered [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif] [Jalālayn]. Second, the Bukhārī and Muslim report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not prefer me above the Prophets; verily, on the Day of Resurrection people will be struck unconscious, and I shall be the first to awake, and I will find Moses holding onto a pillar of the Throne; I will not know whether he woke up before me or received his due because of his unconsciousness on the Mount" — a report **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** both cite in this place, and which **[Qurṭubī]** uses to guard the rank of Moses while affirming the Prophet's ﷺ own station [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī]. Third, the transmission of the listening of the pen: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib said that God wrote the Tablets for Moses while Moses heard the scraping of the pens; Saʿīd b. Jubayr said God brought him near until he heard the scraping (Ṭabarī, and the report of al-Rabīʿ b. Anas in Ṭabarī's chain from someone who met the Companions) [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** also records from Abū Bakr b. Abī Shaybah from Kaʿb: God divided His speech and His vision between Muhammad and Moses — Moses He spoke to twice, and Muhammad ﷺ saw Him twice — a report that stands in the category of transmitted lore rather than of sound ḥadīth *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* [Qurṭubī].

**Belief.** The passage became one of the great proof-texts of Islamic theology, and the commentators are aware of it: **[Ibn Kathīr]** says explicitly that the *lan* does not prove the impossibility of the vision, against the Muʿtazilites, and cites 75:22–23 and the mutawātir hadiths on the vision of the believers in the Hereafter; **[Maʿārif]** reports the majority position that the vision is rationally possible but precluded in this life, with the ḥadīth "none among you shall see his Lord until he dies"; **[Qurṭubī]** states that the Muslim community is agreed that Moses's "turning" was not from a sin, since the prophets are protected, and that Ahl al-Sunnah hold the vision permissible while the innovators deny it, citing ʿAlī b. Mahdī al-Ṭabarī's argument that had Moses's request been impossible he would not have made it — as it would not have been permitted to say to God, "Do You have a consort and a child?"; and **[Saʿdī]** warns explicitly against drawing from the verse a denial of the Hereafter vision, since "you shall not see Me" here means "you are not able now," and the Paradise vision is established by other texts [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "Sight comprehends Him not, but He comprehends all sight, and He is the Subtle, the Aware" (6:103); "Some faces that Day shall be radiant, looking at their Lord" (75:22–23); "And when you said, O Moses, we will not believe you till we see God openly; so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on" (2:55); "We brought him near for intimate conversation" (19:52); "If We had sent down this Qurʾān upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split asunder out of fear of God" (59:21); "Truly We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they declined to bear it and feared it" (33:72); "And they say, Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord? Say: The signs are only with God" (cf. 6:37) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** This is the sūrah's mountain of mercy and its lesson about capacity. Moses, the man who had spoken with God, asks for the one thing that the intimacy of speech cannot supply, and the answer comes as a demonstration rather than a refusal: the mountain, larger and older than he, is dust at a fraction of the manifestation, and Moses falls where it falls. The traditional reading of the exchange is careful to protect everything at stake — the reality of the vision as God's gift, the impossibility of bearing it in this body, the sincerity of Moses's longing, and the absence of any sin in his swoon and recovery [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. What the verse gives the ordinary reader is a measure: the man who had heard God speak still staggered when God drew near, and the words with which he came to himself were not a complaint but a confession — "Glory be to You; I turn to You; and I am the first of the believers" [Study Quran].

## 7:144

*"He said, 'O Moses, I have chosen you above the people with My messages and My speech. So take what I have given you, and be among the grateful.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the exchange as an honor conferred after the swoon: God said to Moses, "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people" — that is, I selected you from among them — "with My messages" to My creation, which I sent with you to them, "and with My speech": I spoke to you and confided in you apart from all My creation. "So take what I have given you" — take My command and My prohibition and hold to it, and act by it — "and be among the grateful" to God for what He has given you of prophethood and for the intimate dialogue He has singled you out for, through obedience to His command and prohibition, and by hastening to His good pleasure [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the compensation for the withheld vision: when God had prevented him from seeing Him after he had so longed for it, He gave him much good, saying, "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people" — selected, drew near, preferred and singled you out with great virtues and noble traits — "with My messages," which I give only to the best of creation, "and with My speech," to you without any intermediary; and this is a distinction peculiar to Moses, the one who speaks with God, by which he is known among his brothers the messengers. "So take what I have given you" — of blessings, and take what I have given you of command and prohibition with an expanded breast, receiving it with acceptance and submission — "and be among the grateful" to God for having singled you out and preferred you [Saʿdī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same and adds the ranking: God chose Moses above the people of his time by His message and by speaking to him; and he adds the necessary qualification, that there is no doubt that Muhammad ﷺ is the chief of all the children of Adam, the earlier and the later, which is why God made him the final prophet and messenger whose law remains dominant until the Hour; after Muhammad ﷺ, the next in honor and virtue is Ibrāhīm, then Moses son of ʿImrān, who spoke to the Most Merciful directly. And he reads "take what I have given you" as an instruction to take the speech and the conversation and be grateful for it — and not to ask for what is beyond his capacity to bear [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** notes that this verse recounts the consolation given to Moses after he was denied the vision, and indicates the great blessing for which he should be among the thankful (al-Qushayrī, al-Rāzī); that being chosen above mankind indicates his status among the people of his time, as 20:13 again calls him chosen and as 3:42 calls Mary "chosen above the women of the worlds"; that the Prophet Muhammad also bears the name al-Muṣṭafā, from the same root; that Moses is distinguished by the messages he received, meaning the Torah, and by God's having spoken directly to him (cf. 4:164), as Exodus 33:11 and Deuteronomy 34:10 likewise describe him speaking with God face to face; that for this distinction Moses carries the honorific *Kalīm Allāh*, "he with whom God spoke"; and that the Prophet Muhammad is also said to have spoken to God without intermediary at the lote tree of the boundary (53:14) during the Night Journey and Ascension [Study Quran]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the verse and, in his comment on the vision before it, preserves the argument that Moses's standing was such that God's answer came to him as correction rather than rebuke [Qurṭubī]. **[Maʿārif]** states the theological point the verse carries: that Allah spoke directly to Moses is confirmed by the Qurʾān in clear terms; the first time God spoke with Moses was when he was entrusted with prophethood, and this was the second time, at the occasion of giving him the Torah, and the wording of the present verse indicates that this later discourse had some additional characteristics compared with the first; as to the nature and character of that discourse, no one but God can ascertain it, and only those suppositions that do not contravene the law may be entertained, none of them as definite. The best practice in this regard, he says, is the one followed by the Companions and their disciples and the elders after them: they left such matters to Allah and never tried to make ungrounded suppositions to resolve them [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse plainly: God said to him, "O Moses, I have elected you, chosen you from among mankind — the people of your time — for My messages, read in the plural or the singular, and for My speech, that is, for My having spoken to you; so take what I have given you of bounty, and be of the thankful for My favors" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Iṣṭafaytuka* — I have chosen you — is the intensive form of the verb of selection, the same root that yields the Prophet's ﷺ title *al-Muṣṭafā*; **[Study Quran]** notes the echo, and the parallel with the choosing of Mary in 3:42, which shows that the Qurʾān's language of election is not exclusive to one prophet or one community [Study Quran]. *Bi-risālātī wa-bikalamī* — "with My messages and My speech" — is a single election described by its two instruments, and **[Maʿārif]**'s remark that the second is the distinctive one is borne out by the tradition: the title *Kalīm Allāh*, the one whom God addressed, belongs to Moses alone, though the Prophet ﷺ was also honored with speech at the lote tree [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. And "be among the grateful" — *min al-shākirīn* — places gratitude in the plural, as the Qurʾān usually does with commands of worship: the honor is given to one man, and the response it calls for is membership in the company of those who give thanks [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ranking — Muhammad ﷺ the chief of the children of Adam, then Ibrāhīm, then Moses — is his own synthesis rather than a Prophetic text, and he offers it in the context of the hadith he cites at 7:143 from Bukhārī and Muslim forbidding the preferment of one prophet over another in a way that breeds dispute [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report from Kaʿb, that God divided speech and vision between Moses and Muhammad — Moses spoke to God twice and Muhammad ﷺ saw Him twice — belongs to the transmitted lore and is best cited as such *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* [Qurṭubī].

**Rulings.** Two practical conclusions the commentators state. First, the response to divine honor is gratitude expressed as obedience: **[Ṭabarī]** defines *shukr* here as obedience to the command and prohibition and haste to God's pleasure, not merely verbal thanks [Ṭabarī]. Second, and pointedly, **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads "take what I have given you" as including a limit — be grateful for it and do not ask for what is beyond your capacity to bear, which is the verse's connection to the request that preceded it [Ibn Kathīr]. And **[Maʿārif]**'s methodological rule belongs among the rulings of the passage as well: the attributes and acts of God that the law does not explain are to be left as they are, in the manner of the Companions, without ungrounded supposition [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed" (20:13); "And to Moses God spoke directly" (4:164); "And mention in the Book Moses; indeed he was chosen, and he was a messenger and a prophet" (19:51); "And God has chosen Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImrān above the worlds" (3:33); "O Mary, indeed God has chosen you and purified you" (3:42); "So remember Me and I will remember you, and be grateful to Me and do not deny Me" (2:152) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the answer to a prayer that was not granted, and its shape is worth noticing. God does not explain why the vision is withheld; He simply tells Moses what he has been given — messages, speech, election — and asks him to take it and be grateful [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. The request was for a sight that would have ended him; the gift, restated, is a relationship that had already been ongoing. For the reader who comes to this passage after the mountain crumbled, the exchange has the proportions of the whole sūrah: ask for the last thing, and be shown what is in your hands; and the answer to the unanswered prayer is a command to be thankful for what the unanswered prayer presupposed [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

## 7:145

*"And We wrote for him upon the Tablets an admonition concerning all things, and an elaboration of all things: 'So take hold of them with strength, and command your people to hold to the best of them. I will show you the abode of the defiant.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains each phrase: We wrote for Moses in his tablets — the definite article standing in place of the possessive, as in the poetic line "and the dreams are not far off" where the meaning is "his dreams" — of every thing, that is, of reminder and awakening to the greatness of God and the might of His authority; an admonition for his people and for those commanded to act on what was written; and an elaboration of every thing, that is, an explanation of every one of God's commands and prohibitions. He then reports the early glosses: Mujāhid and Saʿīd b. Jubayr, "an elaboration of every thing" is what they were commanded and forbidden; al-Suddī, it is the lawful and the unlawful; and Wahb b. Munabbih, in a report of what the Tablets contained: Do not associate anything with Me from the inhabitants of the heaven or the inhabitants of the earth, for all of that is My creation; do not swear falsely by My name, for the one who swears falsely by My name I will not purify; and honor your parents. On "take hold of them with strength," he gives the two glosses: Ibn ʿAbbās said "with seriousness," al-Suddī said "with seriousness and effort," and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas said "with obedience to God"; and he refers the reader to the same phrase in 2:63, where he had already set out the disagreement. "And command your people to hold to the best of them": Ibn ʿAbbās said Moses was commanded to take it more strictly than his people were commanded. Then Ṭabarī answers the obvious objection — if the Tablets contain what is best, what is left for the people to take less than the best of? — with the reply that there is no permission in the verse for the people to leave part of what is in the Tablets; rather the Tablets contain commands and prohibitions, and God commanded them to act on what they were commanded and to leave what they were forbidden, and acting on the command is "better" than acting on the prohibition. Finally, "I will show you the abode of the defiant": he records three interpretations — Mujāhid's, "their destination in the hereafter," al-Ḥasan's, "Hell"; Qatāda's, "I shall bring you into the land of Shām and show you the dwellings of the unbelievers who inhabit it, the giants and the Amalekites"; and the third view, that it is the abode of the people of Pharaoh, namely Egypt, in a report whose text is lost in the manuscript. Ṭabarī's own preference is the first: what precedes this clause is a command to Moses and his people to act on what is in the Torah, and the most fitting close to such a command, in God's wisdom, is a warning to those who waste it and turn aside from His way, rather than news of something whose account has not been given [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** identifies "the Tablets" as those of the Torah, and reports the traditions about their making and their fate. It is reported that Gabriel took hold of Moses with his wing and carried him up until he brought him near enough to hear the scraping of the pen when God wrote the Tablets for him. On their material: Mujāhid said they were of green emerald; Ibn Jubayr, of red ruby; Abū al-ʿĀliya, of chrysolite; al-Ḥasan, of wood, sent down from heaven; and it is said they were of a solid rock which God softened for Moses, who cut it with his hand and split it with his fingers, and it obeyed him as iron obeyed David. Muqātil said the writing was engraved like the engraving of a seal. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas said the Torah came down as seventy camel-loads. On the writing itself, the attribution to God is a mark of honor, since it was written by His command, written by Gabriel with the pen with which the Reminder was written and whose ink was drawn from a river of light; or, it is said, the writing was a script God made appear and created in the tablets. And the word *lawḥ* has at its root the sense of something that gleams with the meanings it contains. He notes that the reports say there were two tablets, the plural being used because the dual is a kind of plural, and then the crucial report from Ibn ʿAbbās about what happened to them: the Tablets broke when Moses threw them down, and all but a sixth of them was raised up; or, in another form of the report, a seventh remained and six sevenths were raised, and in the portion that was raised was "the elaboration of every thing," while in the portion that remained were "the guidance and the mercy" (7:154). Abū Nuʿaym the ḥāfiẓ reported from ʿAmr b. Dīnār: Moses fasted forty nights, and when he threw down the Tablets they broke, so he fasted another forty, and they were returned to him. On "of every thing," he reports al-Thawrī's reading — of what they need in their religion, of the rulings and the clarification of the lawful and the unlawful — and the counter-view that the phrase is one of magnification and not intended as a universal: one says, "I entered the market and bought everything," and "such a person has everything," though nothing in the world holds everything; the Qurʾān likewise says of a wind that "it destroys everything" (46:25) and of the Queen of Sheba that "she was given of everything" (27:23), where universal literalness is not intended [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same identification and adds a transmission of the debate: the Tablets contained the Torah, which God described as "enlightenment for the people" (28:43); and it was also said that God gave Moses the Tablets before the Torah, and God knows best; "hold to these with firmness," meaning be firm in obedience; and he cites Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah, from Abū Saʿd from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, that Moses was commanded to adhere to the toughest of what was ordained on his people; and "I shall show you the home of the rebellious" means you will witness the recompense of those who defy My order and deviate from My obedience — the destruction, demise and utter loss they will suffer [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** notes that God wrote the Torah upon the Tablets, indicating that it was originally a written revelation, as in Exodus 31:18, where the Tablets were "written with the finger of God"; that commentators generally consider there to have been two Tablets, as in the Biblical narrative, although the grammatical plural has led to speculation that there could have been more than two, some saying seven or ten (al-Zamakhsharī); that various reports indicate the Tablets were made of emerald, ruby or wood and were brought to Moses by the Archangel Gabriel (al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭūsī, al-Zamakhsharī), while others say they were of stone cut by Moses himself, similar to Exodus 34; that the Tablets contained an elaboration of all things, meaning all that the people needed to know for the purposes of their religion (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) or that, like the Qurʾān, they were revealed as a clarification of all things (16:89); and that Moses is commanded to take hold of them with strength — to obey in earnest the commands and prohibitions given in them (Ṭabarī) [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the same in the language of benefit: God wrote for Moses in the Tablets of everything that the servants need — an admonition that stirs souls to desire good deeds and warns them against evil deeds, and an elaboration of every thing of legal rulings, creed, morality and manners. "So take hold of them with strength" — with seriousness and effort in establishing them; "and command your people to hold to the best of them," namely the obligatory and recommended commands, for these are the best of it; and in this there is a proof that God's commands in every revealed law are complete, just and good. "I shall show you the abode of the defiant" — after God has destroyed them and left their dwellings as a lesson after them, by which the believers who are granted success and who are humble take heed [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** draws out the two surviving questions of geography and canon: "the abode of the defiant" is a promise that the Israelites would soon take over Egypt or Syria, and the two views about which land is meant turn on the question whether the Israelites had returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people — if they had, and ruled the land, as the verse on inheriting the land indicates, then this verse refers to Syria, since Egypt had already been taken before the events of Sinai; if they had not, the reference may be to Egypt and Syria both. And he adds a note on the Tablets: the phrase "We wrote for him on the Tablets" makes clear that the Torah was given to Moses inscribed on them, while another view holds that these Tablets were given to him before the revelation of the Torah and were not part of it, cited by ʿAllāmah Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī from Ibn Kathīr [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the details of the Tablets and the command: they were made from the lote-tree of Paradise, or of chrysolite, or emerald, and they were either seven or ten; the writing was about all things one needs in religion, as an admonition and a detailing of all things; "take it" has an implicit "We said" before it; take it firmly, seriously and earnestly, and enjoin your people to adhere to the fairest precepts in it; "I shall show you the abode of the wicked" — of Pharaoh and his followers, that is Egypt — that you may take an example from them [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Alwāḥ* is the plural of *lawḥ*, and **[Qurṭubī]** notes the root's suggestion of gleaming: the tablet is so called because meanings shine in it. *Bi-quwwah* — with strength — is the same phrase used of the Israelites at Sinai in 2:63 ("take what We have given you with strength"), and the exegetes gloss it as seriousness, effort, and obedience [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Bi-aḥsanihā* — "the best of them" — is the verse's smallest puzzle, and **[Ṭabarī]** resolves it by distinguishing commands from prohibitions: to act on what is commanded is "better" than to act on what is forbidden, so the instruction is not a license to select [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And *dār al-fāsiqīn* — the abode of the defiant — is *dār* in the sense of a final dwelling, which is why the majority of the glosses read it eschatologically and why the land-readings must specify which land had not yet been entered [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif].

**Rulings.** Three matters the commentators attach to the verse. First, the Tablets as written revelation: **[Study Quran]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** both use the verse to establish that the Torah was originally given in writing, and **[Maʿārif]** reports the minority view that the Tablets preceded the Torah itself [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. Second, the fate of the broken Tablets: **[Qurṭubī]** preserves Ibn ʿAbbās's report that when Moses threw them down they broke and six sevenths or all but a sixth were raised, with the "elaboration of every thing" in the portion raised and "the guidance and the mercy" in what remained, and ʿAmr b. Dīnār's report that Moses fasted another forty nights and the Tablets were returned to him — reports that bear directly on how the community read the loss and restoration of revelation [Qurṭubī]. Third, the warning function of "I will show you the abode of the defiant": whether it means Hell, the land of the giants, or Egypt, the exegetes agree that it is a threat attached to the command to act on the Book, which is why **[Ṭabarī]** prefers the eschatological reading — the command to hold fast to revelation closes with a view of those who let it go [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the criterion, that you might be guided" (2:53); "And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel" (17:2); "And We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations, as enlightenment for the people and guidance and mercy" (28:43); "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be righteous" (2:63); "And this is a blessed Book which We have revealed, confirming what came before it" (6:92, on the confirmation of prior Books); "Then We gave Moses the Scripture, complete for the one who would do good, and an elaboration of all things" (6:154) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrah's statement about what revelation is: not a collection of reminders only, but an admonition and an elaboration — a text that both moves the heart and settles the details [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī]. And it is given with a requirement of strength, which is the mirror image of the request for a vision: Moses could not bear to see, but he could be commanded to take hold, and the two halves of his experience on the mountain — the sight that would have undone him and the book he was told to carry with firmness — form the passage's theology of human capacity [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. The closing threat, whether it points to the fire or to the lands of the giants, makes the text's reception the measure of the reader: the abode shown is the resting place of those who did not hold on [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif].
## 7:146

*"I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right; and if they should see every sign, they will not believe in it. And if they should see the way of right judgment, they will not take it as a way; but if they should see the way of error, they will take it as a way. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the disagreement over what the "turning away" means, and he records three positions. Some said it means "I shall remove from them the understanding of the Book": Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah said it means "I shall take away from them the understanding of the Qurʾān and turn them away from My signs." Ṭabarī notes that Ibn ʿUyaynah's gloss implies, in his view, that this passage is a warning addressed to the disbelievers among those to whom our Prophet ﷺ was sent, and not to the people of Moses — since the Qurʾān was revealed to our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and not to Moses. Others said it means "I shall turn them away from considering the proofs": Ibn Jurayj said it is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the signs within them — "I shall turn them away from reflecting on them and taking heed." And Ṭabarī gives his own preferred reading: God has informed us that He will turn away from His signs — and His signs are His proofs and His marks pointing to the truth of what He commanded His servants and made obligatory upon them of His oneness and His justice and the rest of His ordinances; the heavens and the earth and every existing thing of His creation are among His signs, and the Qurʾān is also among His signs. He has stated comprehensively that He turns away from His signs "those who are arrogant upon the earth without right," and they are the ones against whom God's word has been decreed that they will not believe; they are turned away from understanding all of His signs and from taking heed and remembering by means of them, because if they were enabled to grasp some of it and guided to take heed, they would be admonished and turn back to the truth — but that is not to be from them, since God said, "And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it," and there is no changing of God's words. On the phrase "arrogant upon the earth without right" he explains: their arrogance is their exaltation and their refusal to believe in God and His messenger and to submit to His command and prohibition — while they are God's servants, whom He nourishes with His blessing and provides with His provision morning and evening [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the sense as deprivation: God says that He shall deprive the hearts of those who are too proud to obey Him, and who are arrogant with people without right, of understanding the signs and proofs that testify to His might, His law and His commands; and just as they acted arrogantly without justification, God disgraced them with ignorance. He cites 6:110, "And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe in it the first time," and 61:5, "So when they turned away, God turned their hearts away." Then he takes up Ibn ʿUyaynah's gloss and Ṭabarī's comment on it: Ṭabarī said Ibn ʿUyaynah's statement indicates that this part of the verse is addressed to this community; Ibn Kathīr corrects this reading of Ibn ʿUyaynah — what he meant is that this occurs in every community, and that there is no difference between one community and another in this regard, and God knows best. And on "if they see every sign they will not believe in it," he cites 10:96–97: "Truly, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment." "And if they see the way of right judgment they will not take it as a way" — even if the way of guidance and safety appears before them they will not take it; but the way that leads to destruction and misguidance they adopt; and the reason: "that is because they denied Our signs" in their hearts, "and were heedless of them," gaining no lessons from them [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the portrait of "the others," set against the humble who profit from the signs: God says, "I shall turn away from My signs" — from consideration of the signs in the horizons and in the souls, and from understanding the signs of the Book — "those who are arrogant in the earth without right": those who are arrogant against God's servants, against the truth, and against the one who brings it. Whoever has this characteristic, God deprives him of much good, forsakes him, and he does not understand from God's signs what would benefit him; rather, the realities may be inverted for him and he may find the ugly beautiful. "And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it," because of their turning away and their opposition and their enmity toward God and His messenger; "and if they see the way of right judgment" — that is, guidance and uprightness, the path leading to God and to the abode of His honor — "they will not take it as a way," they neither follow it nor desire it; "and if they see the way of error" — that is, misguidance, which leads its follower to the abode of misery — "they will take it as a way." And the cause of this deviation: "that is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them" — their rejection of God's signs, their heedlessness of what is intended by them, and their contempt for them are what necessitated their walking the way of error and abandoning the way of right judgment [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** sets out the theological stakes: that God will turn away from His signs those who are arrogant may mean that He will prevent them from understanding the revelation given to them (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), perhaps by sealing their hearts so that they do not understand, or by allowing them to be distracted by worldly desires; "signs" here may indicate all of God's signs and proofs, including those present in nature and those found in the human soul, in addition to scriptural revelation, so that God's turning them away means that He prevents them from contemplating them or benefiting from them — since some signs benefit only those whose hearts are already in a state of belief (al-Rāzī). It notes that Ashʿarite theologians appealed to this verse for the view that God might prevent certain people from believing, while Muʿtazilites and others interpreted God's turning people from His signs as a punishment for having freely chosen to be arrogant and to deny the signs beforehand (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī). On the word: "wax arrogant" translates *yatakabbarūn*, literally to make oneself out to be grand and by implication to belittle others; God is the Proud (*al-Mutakabbir*, from the same root, 59:23), but all others wax arrogant "without right," since God alone has the right to assert His greatness and superiority over all beings — so the attribute is positive when applied to God and often negative for creatures; alternately, waxing arrogant without right might refer to asserting one's superiority over others when it is not merited, as with Iblīs at 7:12–13. And "the way of right judgment" means the path of guidance, truth, and correct knowledge and action, leading to felicity in this world and the next [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** draws two lessons. First, from the phrase "without truth" or "unjustly": the qualification indicates that assuming arrogance in response to the arrogant is a justified act, since it is arrogance in appearance and not in reality — a known dictum runs, "Arrogance with the arrogant is an act of humility." Second, the effects of arrogance: by saying "I shall keep away from My verses those who show arrogance," the verse implies that people who have an offensive sense of superiority over others are deprived of knowledge and understanding and are rendered incapable of benefiting from the signs of Allah; and "the signs of Allah" may refer to the revealed verses of the Torah, the Evangel and the Qurʾān as well as to the signs inherent in the heavens and the earth. The false sense of superiority is therefore the worst habit, keeping man away from deliberation over the signs of Allah and from awareness of the truth; and he quotes Rūḥ al-Bayān, that arrogance is such a wicked habitude as raises a wall between man and the knowledge from Allah, since divine knowledge comes only through the mercy of Allah and His mercy visits those who are humble, with Rūmī's line: water flows down toward the slope, and solution goes where difficulty appears [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse in compressed form: I shall turn away from My signs — the proofs of My power, in the way of creations and otherwise — those who behave arrogantly in the earth without right, by humiliating them so that they do not magnify themselves; and if they see every sign they do not believe in it, and if they see the way of right judgment — the path of rectitude, the guidance that has come from God — they do not adopt it as a way to follow, and if they see the way of error — misguidance — they adopt it as a way; that turning away is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them [Jalālayn]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the passage's comment on the verse in the same lines [Qurṭubī].

**Language.** *Sa-aṣrifu* — I will turn away — is a verb of diverting, and the commentators divide over what is diverted: the understanding (Ibn ʿUyaynah), or the people themselves from reflection (Ibn Jurayj), or the signs from the people in the sense that they are prevented from profiting by them (Ṭabarī's synthesis); the three are finally one mechanism viewed from three angles [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. *Al-rushd* — right judgment, maturity of guidance — is the Qurʾān's word for the path that leads straight; its opposite here is *al-ghayy*, the way of error, a word that carries the sense of being lost into ruin. The pairing of the two is exact: the verse gives the arrogant a test of sight, and they fail it in both directions [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And "without right" — *bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq* — is the qualification that distinguishes the arrogance condemned here from the grandeur of God and the justified firmness of the rightly guided, which is why **[Maʿārif]** can speak of a legitimate, apparent "arrogance" toward the arrogant [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

**Belief.** The verse became a locus of the classical dispute over divine guidance and the human will, and the exegetes report it as such. **[Study Quran]** states the two positions: the Ashʿarites appealed to the verse for the view that God might prevent certain people from believing, while the Muʿtazilites interpreted the turning away as a punishment for arrogance freely chosen beforehand. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s construction falls on the second side of the tension without denying the first: the deprivation is described as a just requital of pride — as they acted arrogantly without justification, God disgraced them with ignorance [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr]. And **[Saʿdī]** insists that the heedlessness named at the end is the human's own act, so that the causal chain of the verse runs from their denial and neglect to their deprivation, not the reverse [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right" (7:146, the verse itself); "And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe in it the first time" (6:110); "So when they turned away, God turned their hearts away" (61:5); "Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment" (10:96–97); "And He is the Proud, the Compeller" (cf. 59:23, from the same root as arrogance); "He is the First and the Last..." — and on Iblīs's arrogant claim of superiority: "I am better than him" (7:12) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Reflection.** The verse explains a phenomenon the sūrah has been documenting in the Egyptians across many verses: the capacity of a person to watch a miracle and draw no conclusion. Its answer is that the blindness is not in the evidence but in the posture. The proud man has already placed himself above the thing he is being shown, and a sign cannot instruct someone who must not be instructed [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation that realities may be inverted for such a person — that he may come to find the ugly beautiful — describes the shape of the punishment exactly: it is not the removal of the signs but the loss of the organ that reads them [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

## 7:147

*"Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter — their deeds have come to naught. Are they recompensed for anything except what they used to do?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the general verdict that absorbs the specific case: "those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter" — and the meeting of the Hereafter is the meeting with God in the next abode; so these are the arrogant upon the earth without right, and every denier of God's proofs and His messengers and His signs, every repudiator of the claim that he will be raised after his death, and every denier of meeting God in his hereafter — their works have gone and come to nothing, while their burdens have come to them and been established, because they worked for other than God and wearied themselves in what does not please God, so their works became a curse upon them. And "are they recompensed for anything except what they used to do?" — are they rewarded with anything but the reward of what they did? Their reward for their deeds becomes eternal abiding in the fire, whose enclosure surrounds them, since their works were in obedience to Satan rather than in obedience to the Most Merciful; we seek refuge with God from His anger [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same and adds the condition that makes the verse precise: it indicates that whoever does this, remaining on this path until death, then all his deeds are in vain; and "are they recompensed except what they used to do" means that We only recompense them according to the deeds they performed, good for good and evil for evil — as you bring forth, you reap the harvest [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** explains the two elements: "the meeting of the Hereafter" refers to the Day of Resurrection and Judgment; those who deny this key element of belief and the signs of God will have their deeds come to naught — that is, they will not benefit from them or receive reward for them, nor will their deeds, however seemingly good, be able to shield them from punishment for their denial and disbelief; elsewhere the Qurʾān states that disbelievers, idolaters, hypocrites and those who persecute the prophets and the righteous will have their deeds come to naught (2:217; 3:22; 5:5; 5:53; 9:17; 18:105), and it notes the similar rhetorical questions at 10:52 and 27:90 [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** states the reason the works vanish: they are invalid because they stand on no foundation — their condition, which is faith in God's signs and belief in His recompense, is missing. And "are they recompensed except what they used to do?" — the works of one who does not believe in the Day of Judgment have no reward hoped for in them and no goal at which they terminate, and therefore they dissolve and become void [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** identifies the works that come to naught in this life: their works — the good deeds they performed in the world, such as the maintenance of kinship ties or voluntary almsgivings — have failed and are invalid and will not be rewarded, since they are not binding in this case; and "shall they be requited for anything but what they used to do" of denial and acts of disobedience? [Jalālayn]. **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Maʿārif]** carry the verse in the flow of the passage's discussion of the arrogant and the heedless [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Ḥabiṭat* — "came to naught," literally "failed," from a root used of a beast's belly swelling so that it cannot be eaten, and of food going to waste: the image is of works that rot on the vine. **[Ṭabarī]**'s phrase is exact — the works went and the burdens stayed — and it preserves the double ledger the verb carries: what the doer measured as achievement is deleted from one page and entered on another [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the question with which the verse ends — *hal yujzawna illā mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — is a rhetorical identity rather than a debate: the recompense is the deed, visited on the one who did it [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Belief.** The verse ties the validity of deeds to belief in the meeting with God, a doctrine the Qurʾān states repeatedly and that the commentators here state in the technical language of conditions: the deed that is done without faith lacks its condition, so it is not received [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s qualifier — remaining on that path until death — preserves the other side of the doctrine, that the cancelation of deeds belongs to the state in which a person dies, not to the number of their lapses [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "Say: Shall We inform you of those who will lose most through their deeds? Those whose efforts were misguided in the life of the world while they thought they were doing well — those are the ones who denied the signs of their Lord and the meeting with Him, so their deeds have come to naught" (18:103–105); "God has made the deeds of the disbelievers worthless" (cf. 47:8–9); "Those who deny God and His messengers, and wish to make a distinction between God and His messengers... it is they who are the disbelievers" (4:150–151); "And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should — those are the ones whose striving is appreciated" (cf. 17:19); "So when they forgot that by which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every good thing" (6:44) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** The verse is placed immediately after the anatomy of arrogance, and its function is to close the ledger: the proud man may look active, but the Qurʾān's accounting has him losing everything he does, because what he built had no market in the world he denied [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran]. The line "as you bring forth, you reap the harvest" that **[Ibn Kathīr]** cites sums up the verse's logic [Ibn Kathīr]; and **[Saʿdī]**'s observation about the absence of a goal gives an ordinary reader the sharpest form of it — a deed without an end cannot survive the end of the world [Saʿdī].

## 7:148

*"And the people of Moses, after he had departed, took a calf from their ornaments, an image that lowed. Did they not see that it did not speak to them nor guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the scene: the Children of Israel, the people of Moses, took — after Moses had left them, going to his Lord for the intimate discourse and to fulfil the promise his Lord had made him — a calf from their ornaments, the calf being the young of the cow, and they worshipped it. Then God explains what that calf was: a body with a lowing, the *khuwār* being the sound of cattle. And God says that they went astray by something by which no one of sound intellect would go astray, because the Lord whose is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and their governance cannot be a body with a lowing that speaks to no one and guides to no good. Yet these people of whom God tells the story said, "This is our god and the god of Moses," and clung to it in worship out of ignorance, straying from God and going astray. He notes the two dialects of *ḥulī* — with the *ḥāʾ* vowelled *u*, which is the original, and with *i* — and that whichever the reciter reads is correct, since both are widely transmitted and their meanings do not differ. On the question: "did they not see that it does not speak to them and does not guide them to a way?" — the verse reproaches those who devoted themselves to the calf made from their ornaments that it neither speaks to them nor shows them the road, and that these are not the attributes of their Lord, whose is worship in truth, but His attributes are that He speaks to His prophets and messengers and guides His creation to the way of good and forbids them the way of destruction; and "they took it," that is, they took the calf as a god, and by taking it as a worshipped lord they were wronging themselves, through worshipping other than the one who deserves worship and attributing divinity to other than the one who possesses it [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** supplies the narrative and the lexical detail. The readings of *ḥuliyyihim*: the people of Madinah and Baṣrah read *ḥulī*, the people of Kūfah read *ḥilī* with ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb read *ḥaly* lightened; al-Naḥḥās explains that the word is a plural whose singular is *ḥaly*, on the analogy of *thady* and *thudiyy*. Then the story: the Samiri, whose name was Mūsā b. Ẓafar, was so named after a village called Sāmirah; he was born in the year of the killing of the sons and his mother hid him in a cave of a mountain, where Gabriel fed him, and so he knew him; and when he crossed the sea he took — riding a mare that desired the stallion, in order to precede Pharaoh into the sea — a handful from the trace of the horse's hoof, which is the meaning of his saying, "I seized a handful of the trace of the messenger" (20:96). Moses had promised his people thirty days, and when he was late in the additional ten and the thirty nights had passed, al-Sāmirī said to the Children of Israel — and he was obeyed among them — "You have with you ornaments from the ornaments of the people of Pharaoh; they are unlawful for you; bring them and we shall burn them." And a report says that after the drowning the Israelites took the ornaments as spoils from the people of Pharaoh and Aaron said to them that the ornaments were spoils which were not lawful for them, so he gathered them in a pit he had dug, and al-Sāmirī took them. And another report says they had borrowed the ornaments on the night they intended to leave Egypt, pretending to the Copts that they had a wedding or a gathering. And al-Sāmirī had heard their saying in the earlier passage — "make for us a god as they have gods" — and those gods of theirs were in the shape of cattle; so he fashioned for them a calf, a body, meaning solid, though they heard from it a lowing; or, it is said, God turned it into flesh and blood; or, it is said, when he threw the handful of dust from the trace into the fire upon the ornaments it became a calf with a lowing — it lowed once and did not repeat — and he said to the people: "This is your god and the god of Moses, and he forgot" (20:88) — meaning Moses forgot his god here and went off seeking him and was lost concerning him, so come and let us worship this calf. And God said to Moses while He was speaking with him: "We have tried your people in your absence, and al-Sāmirī has led them astray" (20:85). Moses said, "My Lord, this Samiri brought out for them a calf from their ornaments — but who made it a body and who made it low?" And God said, "I did." Moses said, "By Your might and majesty, none but You led them astray." God said, "You have spoken truly, O wisest of the wise" — which is the sense of "it is nothing but Your trial" (cf. 7:155). And al-Qaffāl said the Samiri contrived to hollow the calf and face it to the wind, so that what came from it mimicked the lowing, and he made them think it happened because of the dust thrown into the body which he had taken from the earth beneath the legs of Gabriel's horse — a talk with incoherence in it, says al-Qushayrī. And on "did they not see that it does not speak to them nor guide them to a way": the verse makes clear that the object of worship must be characterized by speech, and to guide them to a way means to a proof; "they took it" means as a god; and "they were wrongdoers" — wrongdoers against themselves in what they did of taking it, or they became wrongdoers in the sense of associators, by making the calf a god [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the sequence: God describes the misguidance of those who worshipped the calf that al-Sāmirī made for them from the ornaments they had borrowed from the Copts; he made the shape of a calf with those ornaments and threw into it a handful of dust from the trace of the horse that the angel Gabriel was riding, and the calf seemed to moo. This occurred after Moses went for the appointed term with his Lord, where God told him what had happened while he was on Mount Ṭūr. Then the two views of the scholars of tafsīr: whether the calf actually became alive and mooing, or remained made of gold while the air entering it made it appear to be mooing — two opinions, and God knows best. It was reported that when the statue mooed, the Jews began to dance around it and fell into misguidance because they adored it; and they said that this is your god and the god of Moses, but Moses forgot it. God answered them: "Did they not see that it could not return them a word, and that it had neither power to harm them nor to do them good?" (20:89). So here God condemned the Jews for falling into misguidance, worshipping the calf and ignoring the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Lord and King of all things: they worshipped besides Him a statue made in the shape of a calf that seemed to moo, but neither spoke to them nor brought them any benefit — rather, their very sense of reason was blinded because of ignorance and misguidance [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** concentrates the folly: the companions of Moses, after his departure, took from their ornaments a calf, a body; al-Sāmirī fashioned it and cast upon it a handful from the trace of the messenger, so that it had a lowing and a sound; they worshipped it and took it as a god, saying, "This is your god and the god of Moses, so he forgot," and went seeking him. This is of their folly and their feeble insight: how could the Lord of the earth and the heavens be confounded for them with a calf, one of the most deficient of creatures? Therefore God said, explaining that there is in it no attribute of essence or of act that would require it to be a god: "did they not see that it does not speak to them" — and the absence of speech is a great deficiency, so they are more complete than this animal or lifeless object that does not speak — "nor guide them to a way," that is, it does not point out to them a path in religion nor secure for them any worldly interest; because it is established in reason and in the natural constitution that taking as a god one that does not speak and neither benefits nor harms is among the falsest falsehoods and the ugliest follies; hence "they took it, and they were wrongdoers," in that they placed worship in other than its place and associated with God what He has not sent down an authority for. And in this there is a proof that whoever denies the speech of God has denied one of God's divine characteristics, since God mentioned that the absence of speech is a proof that the one who does not speak is not fit for divinity [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the context: cf. 2:51–54, 92–93, and especially 20:86–97 for the most extensive account in the Qurʾān of the Israelites making and worshipping the calf; the Biblical account is in Exodus 32. While Moses was away — still speaking with God on the mountain — the Israelites took a calf from their ornaments, meaning that they fashioned from precious metals, usually understood to be gold, an idol in the form of a calf and made it an object of worship, saying, "This is our god and the god of Moses" (20:88). Although Aaron was left in charge, the commentators indicate that Aaron did not participate in making or worshipping the calf, which was directed by another Israelite referred to as al-Sāmirī, the "Samaritan," as indicated in 20:87, 95–97; rather, Aaron tried to stop this action (see 20:90). The calf is described as a body that lowed — leading some to think it possessed a supernatural power, although 20:95–96 indicates that the lowing was the result of a kind of sorcery on the part of al-Sāmirī; others suggest the calf was fashioned with carefully placed holes and hollows, and when the wind blew through them it generated a lowing sound (al-Rāzī). Despite the lowing, the calf spoke not unto them nor guided them to any way. The Qurʾānic narrative offers a further reflection on the nature of prophetic guidance and miracles as contrasted with sorcery: unusual feats are not themselves indications of spiritual power or worthy of worship and are no substitute for divine revelation; true prophethood and its signs can be distinguished from the mere conjuring of a sorcerer, because the former bring guidance and clarity while the latter, like the feats of the sorcerers at 7:116, are ultimately powerless and illusory. They were wrongdoers in that they wronged themselves by taking a powerless idol as an object of worship (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī). And the Sufi commentators understand the calf, and the Israelites' willingness to worship it despite God's tremendous favor toward them, to be indicative of a tendency in human beings to allow worldly phenomena to distract them from the worship of God — a reminder that none are free of this temptation toward idolatry save those who have "slain their souls" by conquering its worldly passions [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** narrates the story in the same shape: when Moses did not turn up after thirty days from the Mount, the Israelites, a hasty and impatient people, began to make a fuss about it; among them was al-Sāmirī, a prominent man with beliefs in superstitions, who said that the jewels and ornaments of the Egyptians in their possession were not permissible for them — noting that plunder taken from the enemy after their defeat was also not permissible for the Israelites — so the people gathered all their jewels and handed them over, and he melted them and forged a golden calf. He had collected some dust from under the hooves of the horse of the Archangel Gabriel, and Allah had made this dust to have the effect of a kind of life; al-Sāmirī mixed it with the molten metal while preparing the calf, and this made the calf emit a sound like the mooing of a cow. Having designed this satanic invention, he invited the people to worship the calf and said it was god: Moses had gone to the Mount to speak with God, while God had come to them in the form of this calf. Al-Sāmirī already enjoyed a place of respect among them, and this unusual demonstration increased their trust in him, so they started worshipping the calf and took it as their god [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse's details: the people of Moses, after he had departed for the communion with God, made from their ornaments — which they had borrowed from the people of Pharaoh on the pretext of a wedding celebration and which remained in their possession — a calf which the Samaritan had fashioned for them, a mere living body of flesh and blood that lowed, the calf having been transformed into that when the dust the Samaritan had collected from where the hoof of Gabriel's steed had trodden was placed in its mouth, for it has the effect of giving life to that in which it is placed; the second direct object of the verb "they made" has been omitted and would be "as a god." Did they not see that it did not speak to them nor guide them to any way? So how could it be taken as a god? Yet they took it as such, and were evildoers for taking it so [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Jasad* — a body — is the word for a physical frame, and its use here makes the calf's materiality the argument: the thing they worshipped was an object with a sound, and the very nouns the verse chooses — body, lowing — are the vocabulary of an animal, not of a god [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. *Khuwār* is the lowing of cattle specifically, and the verse's point is the disproportion between the noise and the claims made for it: it lowed, but it did not speak, and speech is the minimum the verse requires of anything called divine [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. *Ḥulī* — ornaments, jewelry — is the plural whose vowel patterns the readers vary, all of them correct and all of them the same word [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the phrase "they took it" (*ittakhadhūhu*) is the Qurʾān's standing verb for taking a god, used here without its object to let the act speak for itself [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The verse's material is largely narrative from the earlier scriptures and the reports of the exegetes: the biography of al-Sāmirī, born in the year of the slaughter of the sons and hidden in a cave where, in the report of **[Qurṭubī]**, Gabriel fed him so that he recognized him when he took the dust from his horse's hoof; the borrowing of the ornaments under the pretext of a wedding; and the exchange **[Qurṭubī]** transmits in which Moses asks who gave the calf its body and its lowing, and God answers, "I did," and Moses confesses, "By Your might, none but You led them astray" — a report that stands in the category of transmitted lore rather than sound ḥadīth *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī].

**Rulings.** Two rulings the commentators state from the verse's reasoning. First, the criterion of divinity: **[Qurṭubī]** says the verse proves that the object of worship must be characterized by speech, and **[Saʿdī]** turns the same point into a doctrine about God's attribute — whoever denies God's speech has denied one of His divine characteristics, since the verse uses the calf's speechlessness as the proof of its unfitness [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. Second, the internal evidence of the story about how idolatry was manufactured: a claimant with prestige, a claim about unlawful wealth that required the people to surrender their gold, and a trick of sound. **[Study Quran]** draws out the contrast between sorcery and revelation that the whole episode carries: a miraculous-looking effect is not a proof of divinity, and the sign of true prophethood is guidance rather than spectacle [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf after him, and you were wrongdoers" (2:51); "And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief" (2:93); "So he brought out for them a calf, a body that lowed, and they said, This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot" (20:88); "Did they not see that it could not return them a word and had no power to harm or benefit them?" (20:89); "And Aaron had said to them before, O my people, you are only being tried by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrah's own answer to the request made at 7:138, and the distance between the two is a few chapters of a journey and one absence. The people who asked for a god "as they have gods" now have one: a body with a sound, made of the gold they had carried out of Egypt, and it speaks to no one [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. The commentaries' repeated observation that it lowed once and did not repeat itself says everything about the relationship between the spectacular and the divine, and **[Study Quran]**'s Sufi note draws the general lesson the episode is meant to teach: the temptation is not confined to idolaters of gold, and no one is free of it except the one who has conquered the passions of the self [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:149

*"And when they were smitten with remorse and saw that they had gone astray, they said, 'If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the idiom first: "when it was dropped into their hands" means when those who had worshipped the calf regretted it, upon Moses's return to them, and submitted to Moses and his judgment; and the Arabs say of anyone who regrets a matter that has passed or gone before him, or who is helpless before something, that "it has been dropped into his hands," with the two forms *suqiṭa* and *usqiṭa* both correct. He derives the expression from capture: a man strikes another or throws him down, and hurls him from his hands to the ground in order to bind him, so that the one thrown is "dropped into the hands" of the one who threw him; and from that the phrase was applied to everyone helpless before a thing, whose helplessness has humbled him and who regrets what he said. "And they saw that they had gone astray" — they saw that they had swerved from the straight path and departed from the religion of God and disbelieved in their Lord — so they said, repenting to God and turning back to Him from their disbelief: "If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers," meaning: if our Lord does not incline toward us with His mercy for our repentance and cover our sins with it, we will be among the perishing whose works are void. He then records the readings: the majority of the readers of Madinah, Makkah, Kūfah and Baṣrah read "If our Lord does not have mercy upon us" with the *yāʾ* of the third person and the nominative — as a report; while the majority of the readers of Kūfah read "If You do not have mercy upon us, our Lord," with the *tāʾ* of address and the accusative, in the sense "if You do not have mercy on us, O our Lord," as direct address from them to their Lord, supporting this with the reading "Our Lord, if You do not have mercy upon us and forgive us" — which shows the address — and noting that this is the reading of Ubayy b. Kaʿb and in the codex of ʿAbdallāh b. Masʿūd. Ṭabarī's own preference is the report-form with the *yāʾ* and the nominative, because nothing precedes it that requires it to be taken as address [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** adds to the idiom: it is said of the remorseful and bewildered person that it has been dropped into his hand; al-Akhfash says both *suqiṭa fī yadihi* and *usqiṭa* are used; and one who reads it as a verb with the remorse as its subject has the meaning "the remorse fell." Then the explanation that earned its place in the commentaries: remorse occurs in the heart, but the hand is mentioned because it is said of one who has obtained a thing that "it has come into his hand," since dealings are for the most part by the hand — as God says, "That is for what your two hands have sent forth" (22:10) — and also because remorse, even if it settles in the heart, shows its effect on the body, since the remorseful person bites his hand and strikes one hand against the other, as in "he began to turn his palms over" (18:42) and "the day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands" (25:27), and the remorseful person puts his chin in his hand. And another explanation: it is from capture, as Ṭabarī said. "And they saw that they had gone astray" — that is, they had been turned around by their disobedience to God; and "they said, If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers": they took up the acknowledgment of servitude and the seeking of forgiveness. And on the reading: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "if You do not have mercy upon us, our Lord, and forgive us," with the *tāʾ* of address; in it is the sense of appeal and humility and earnest supplication in the asking and the prayer; and *rabbanā* is accusative by the omission of the vocative particle, which is also more eloquent in supplication and submission — so their reading is more eloquent in self-abasement and pleading, and therefore preferable [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the verse as the account of their turning: "and when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said, If our Lord has not mercy upon us and forgive us, we will certainly become among the losers" — or among the destroyed; and he describes it as their recognition of their sin and their way of seeking salvation from Allah, the Most Mighty and Majestic [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the sequence: when Moses returned to his people and found them in this state and told them of their misguidance, they regretted; *suqiṭa fī aydīhim* — from sorrow and remorse for what they had done; and they saw that they had gone astray, so they turned to God in appeal and humility, saying: if our Lord does not have mercy on us — by guiding us to Him, granting us His worship and enabling us to righteous deeds — and forgive us what issued from us of worshipping the calf, we shall surely be among the losers, who have lost this world and the Hereafter [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** explains the idiom and the theology: "wrung their hands" in remorse might be literally translated "[remorse] fell into their hands," that is, settled into their hearts (al-Rāzī); some suggest the image is an allusion to the tendency of the remorseful to bite their hands, as if attacking the site of their remorse (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī); alternately, that remorse "fell into their hands" may mean that they now realized it was their responsibility to make amends and set matters right with their own hands (al-Rāzī). And the statement itself: the Israelites' words are one of immediate and utter contrition, casting themselves upon the mercy of God rather than offering excuses — identical to what is uttered by Adam and Eve at 7:23, and by Noah at 11:47 [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: when they became remorseful and saw that they had gone astray — and this was after Moses's return from the communion — they said, "Unless our Lord is merciful to us and forgives us," reading both verbs either in the third person or in the second person, "verily we shall be among the losers" [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** keeps the verse in the flow of the narrative of the calf and the return [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Suqiṭa fī aydīhim* is one of the Arabic idioms the exegetes most enjoy explaining, and both explanations preserved — the hand as the organ of dealings and remorse's visible effects, and the origin in capture — end at the same meaning: the failing person has nothing left but his own hands, and his remorse is now a possession he cannot put down [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. *Khāsirīn* — losers — is used in the Qurʾān of those whose loss is total rather than partial; and **[Saʿdī]** reads the word with both worlds in view: the losers are those who lose this world and the Hereafter [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And the conditional *la-in lam yarḥamnā* with the doubled *lām* of the answer gives the sentence the force of a vow: the outcome of the whole affair hangs on one act of divine mercy, and they say so [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī].

**Readings.** The two readings of the verse are famous and both are transmitted: the majority reading with the *yāʾ* — "if our Lord does not have mercy upon us" — as statement, preferred by **[Ṭabarī]** because nothing before it requires address; and the Kūfan reading with the *tāʾ* — "if You do not have mercy upon us, our Lord" — supported by the codex of Ubayy b. Kaʿb and that of Ibn Masʿūd, and preferred by **[Qurṭubī]** because address is more eloquent in supplication and self-abasement [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn].

**Cross-references.** "They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers" (7:23); "He said: My Lord, I seek refuge with You from being among the ignorant" (cf. 11:47 for Noah's appeal); "They will say: Yes, by our Lord. He will say: Then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve" (cf. 6:30); "Indeed, the losers are those who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection" (39:15); "And whoever is given his record in his left hand will say: Would that I had not been given my record" (69:25) [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr]. This verse's sentence is nearly identical in wording to the repentance of Adam and Eve at 7:23, which the sūrah has already set before the reader [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The sūrah allows the calf-worshippers one grace, and it is the grace of seeing clearly. Their sentence contains neither excuse nor complaint: they name their own straying, and they stake their whole future on mercy they have no claim to [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran]. The commentators note the echo of Adam's words at 7:23 — the same formula of surrender — and the pairing is the sūrah's point: the first man and the calf-worshippers meet at the same floor of utter contrition, and the door works the same way for both [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:150

*"And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said, 'How evil is what you did in my place after me! Were you impatient for the command of your Lord?' And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him. He said, 'Son of my mother! Indeed, the people deemed me weak and were about to kill me, so make not the enemies rejoice over me, and do not place me with the wrongdoing people.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets the scene and then the word: Moses returned to his people of the Children of Israel angry and grieved, because God had informed him that his people had been tried and that al-Sāmirī had led them astray, so his return was in that state. And *al-asaf* is intensity of anger and rage against the one who has angered a person; Abū al-Dardāʾ said it is a station beyond anger, more intense — and the proof is in the Book of God: "he went to his people angry, and he went grieved" — while al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan said "grieved" means sorrowful; and Ibn ʿAbbās noted that *al-asaf* has two faces, anger and grief, citing 43:55, "when they angered Us" (*āsaffūnā*), meaning "they made Us angry." "How evil is what you did in my place after me" — evil is the deed you did after my separation from you, the succession you gave me among my people and my religion which your Lord commanded you. "Were you impatient for the command of your Lord?" — did you outstrip the command of your Lord for yourselves and go away from it? and he explains the Arabic: *ʿajila* a thing is to precede it, *aʿjala* a person is to hurry him, and "do not hurry me, O so-and-so" is "do not go away from me and leave me." Then the Tablets and the seizure of Aaron: he records that the scholars disagreed on why Moses threw down the Tablets. Some said he threw them in anger at his people who had worshipped the calf: Ibn ʿAbbās, from Saʿīd b. Jubayr, said Moses took hold of his brother's head, dragging him toward him, and threw down the Tablets out of anger; and from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās: when he came near them, being close by, he heard voices, and said, "I hear the voices of people at play"; and when he saw them clinging to the calf, he threw down the Tablets and broke them, and seized his brother's head, dragging him toward him. Then the other view: some said Moses threw the Tablets because he found in them virtues recorded for a people other than his own, and this was hard on him. **[Ṭabarī]** preserves Qatāda's report: Moses said, "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation that is the best nation brought forth for mankind, commanding right and forbidding wrong — make them my nation!" and the answer came: "That is the nation of Aḥmad." And in the fuller form: "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation whose gospels are in their breasts, reciting them" — while those before them read their book from sight, so that when they lifted it away they had memorized nothing and recognized nothing; Qatāda adds that God gave this community a measure of memory that He gave to no other community — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation that believes in the first Book and the last Book, and fights the fringes of misguidance until they fight the one-eyed liar" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation whose charities they consume in their own bellies and are yet rewarded for them" — whereas other nations, when a charity was accepted from one of them, God sent fire upon it and it consumed it, and if it was returned, birds and beasts ate it; God says: "I take the charity of your rich for your poor" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation one of whom, when he intends a good deed and does not do it, is credited with a good deed; and if he does it, it is written tenfold to seven hundredfold" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation one of whom, when he intends an evil deed, is not charged with it until he does it, and when he does it only one evil deed is written" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation who are the responders and the responded-to" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." "My Lord, I find in the Tablets a nation who are the intercessors and the interceded-for" — "make them my nation!" — "That is the nation of Aḥmad." And it was mentioned to us that the prophet of God Moses cast down the Tablets and said, "O God, make me of the nation of Aḥmad!" And God gave Moses two things He gave no other prophet: "O Moses, I have chosen you above mankind with My messages and My speech" (7:144), and Moses was satisfied; then the second: "And of the people of Moses there is a nation who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:159), and Moses was fully satisfied. **[Ṭabarī]** then gives his own verdict: the more fitting view is that the cause of Moses's throwing the Tablets was his anger at his people for their worship of the calf, because God has told us so in His Book in that order — "and when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said, How evil is what you did in my place after me; were you impatient for the command of your Lord?
