And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him" — and because of the report that when God wrote the Torah for Moses in the Tablets, He brought him near until he heard the scraping of the pen, a report from ʿAlī and from Saʿīd b. Jubayr; and he adds the report that the Torah was seven sevenths: when Moses threw down the Tablets they broke, and six sevenths were raised, and among what was raised was "the elaboration of every thing" — and what remained was the guidance and the mercy [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** supplies the grammar and the law of anger. *Ghaḍbān* does not take the feminine ending because its feminine is *ghaḍbā* and because the *alif* and *nūn* stand in the place of the *alif* of the feminine; it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier; and *asif* is intensely angry. Abū al-Dardāʾ: *al-asaf* is a station beyond anger, more intense than it. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī: he returned sorrowful at what his people had done; and al-Ṭabarī said God had told him before his return that they had been tried by the calf, and that is why he returned angry. Ibn al-ʿArabī: Moses was among the most angry of men, but he was quick to recover, and that balanced it. Ibn al-Qāsim said: I heard Mālik say, "When Moses was angry, smoke would rise from his hood and the hair of his body would lift his cloak" — anger being a live coal that burns in the heart — and for that reason the Prophet ﷺ commanded the angry person to lie down, and if his anger does not leave him, to bathe, so that his lying down smothers it and his bathing extinguishes it. And his quickness to anger was the reason he struck the angel of death and put out his eye — a report that has already been discussed in Sūrat al-Māʾidah. Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm said: Moses could allow himself that because he was the one with whom God spoke, as though he saw that whoever dared to wrong him or stretched a hand toward him with harm had committed a grave offense — the report being that the angel argued with him: from where will you take my soul? From my mouth, with which I have spoken with my Lord? From my hearing, with which I heard the speech of my Lord? From my hand, with which I took the Tablets from Him? From my foot, with which I stood before Him speaking with Him at the Mount? From my eye, with which my face shone for His light? — and the angel returned to his Lord silenced. Then the Prophetic rulings: in Abū Dāwūd's *Muṣannaf* from Abū Dharr, the Messenger of God ﷺ said to us, "When one of you is angry and he is standing, let him sit; if the anger leaves him, fine; otherwise let him lie down." And it was also reported from Abū Wāʾil the storyteller: we entered upon ʿUrwah b. Muḥammad al-Saʿdī and a man spoke to him and angered him; he got up and then returned having performed ablution, and said: my father told me from my grandfather ʿAtiyya that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Anger is from Satan, and Satan was created from fire, and fire is only extinguished by water; so when one of you is angry, let him perform ablution" — a chain ʿAtiyya's descent that the exegetes note for what it is *(weak)*. Then the words: "How evil is what you have left behind me" is a censure of them, meaning how evil the deed you did after me; the verb *khalafahu* is used of acting for a man in his family and his people after his departure, in good or in evil. "Were you impatient for the command of your Lord?" — did you outstrip it; *al-ʿajalah* is advancing a thing before its time and is blameworthy, while *al-surʿah* is doing a thing at its first time and is praiseworthy; and "the command of your Lord" may mean the appointment of your Lord, that is, the promise of forty nights, or hastening the wrath of your Lord, or hastening to worship the calf before a command came to you from your Lord. Then the two issues of throwing the Tablets: first, it was from the anger and grief that came over him when he looked down on his people clinging to the worship of the calf and on his brother for his neglect of their affair, as Saʿīd b. Jubayr said — and for this it was said, "information is not like observation"; and no attention is paid to what is reported from Qatāda, if it is authentically from him, that the throwing was because of what he saw in the Tablets of the virtue of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ and that it was not for his own nation — a base opinion that should not be attributed to Moses. Then the second issue: some ignorant ones among the Sufis used this as proof of the permissibility of throwing their clothes about when their ecstasy intensifies at the singing; some of them throwing them whole, some tearing them and then throwing them, saying these are in a state of absent-mindedness and so are not to be blamed, since Moses, when grief overcame him at his people's worship of the calf, threw down the Tablets and broke them, and did not know what he was doing. Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī answered: who can establish that Moses threw them with the throw of a breaker? What is mentioned in the Qurʾān is that he cast them down — where do we get that they broke? And then, if it were said they broke, where do we get that he intended to break them? And then, if we established that from him, we would say he was in a state of overpowering emotion, such that had there been before him a sea of fire he would have waded into it — and who can establish that absent-mindedness for these people, who know the singer from others and avoid a well if it were before them? Then how can the states of the prophets be measured against the states of these fools? And Ibn ʿAqīl was asked about their ecstasy and their tearing of clothes and said: it is an error and forbidden, and the Messenger of God ﷺ forbade the wasting of wealth. Someone said to him: but they do not know what they are doing; he said: if they attended these places knowing that ecstasy would overpower them and take away their minds, they are sinners for what they brought upon themselves of tearing and other destruction, and the address of the law does not fall away from them, because they were addressed before attending with avoiding the place that leads to that — just as they are forbidden to drink intoxicants; so this ecstasy, which the Sufis call "finding," if they are truthful contains a natural drunkenness, and if they are lying they are corrupting while sober, and there is no safety in it in either state, and avoiding doubtful places is obligatory. Then the seizure of Aaron: he seized him by the head, that is, by his beard and the hair of his forelock; and Aaron was three years older than Moses and more beloved to the Children of Israel than Moses, because he was gentler of temper. The scholars give four interpretations of the seizing: first, that it was customary among them, as the Arabs would seize a man by the beard in honor and veneration, not in humiliation; second, that it was in order to tell him secretly that the Tablets had come down to him, since they came down in this communion and he wanted to hide it from the Children of Israel before the Torah — hence Aaron said, "Do not take me by my beard nor by my head," lest what Moses was confiding should be mistaken by the Israelites for humiliation; third, that he did it because it had occurred to him that Aaron leaned with the Children of Israel in what they did with the calf — and the like of that is not permissible for prophets; fourth, that he drew his brother to himself to learn what he had, and Aaron disliked it lest the Israelites think he had humiliated him; so his brother explained to him that they had deemed him weak — meaning the calf-worshippers — and had nearly killed him. And when Moses heard his excuse he said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother" — me for the anger for which I threw down the Tablets, and my brother because he thought him remiss in denouncing them even though no remissness had occurred from him; and al-Ḥasan said: all of them worshipped the calf except Aaron — for had there been a believer there other than Moses and Aaron, he would not have confined himself to "forgive me and my brother," but would have prayed for that believer too [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the sequence and the lesson: when Moses returned to his people after conversing with his Lord he became angry and full of regret; and Abū al-Dardāʾ said that *asaf* is the severest kind of anger. "How evil is that which you did during my absence" — evil it is that which you committed after I departed by worshipping the calf; "did you hasten in the matter of your Lord?" — Moses said, you wanted me to rush back to you, though this was God's decision. This verse, he says, demonstrates the meaning of the hadith "information is not the same as observation," and it indicates that Moses threw down the Tablets because he was angry at his people, according to the majority of the scholars of the early and later generations. And he seized his brother by the head and dragged him toward him, for Moses feared that Aaron might not have tried hard enough to forbid them from their evil action, as the other passage states: "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, that you followed me not? Have you then disobeyed my order? He said: O son of my mother, seize me not by my beard nor by my head! I feared lest you should say, You have caused a division among the Children of Israel and have not respected my word" (20:92–94). Here Aaron said, "O son of my mother, indeed the people deemed me weak and were about to kill me, so make not the enemies rejoice over me, nor put me among the people who are wrongdoers" — do not place me on the same level as they are, as if I were one of them. And he said "son of my mother" so that Moses would feel more mercy and leniency toward him, even though Aaron was also the son of Moses's father. And when Moses was satisfied that his brother was innocent, he said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy" (7:151) [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the psychology: when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved — filled with anger and rage against them because of the completeness of his jealousy for God and the perfection of his counsel and his compassion — he said, "How evil is the state in which you have succeeded me after my departure," for it is a state leading to eternal ruin and endless misery. "Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" — He had promised you the sending down of the Book, and you rushed ahead under your own corrupt opinion to this ugly characteristic. And he cast down the Tablets — he threw them out of anger — and seized the head of his brother Aaron and his beard, dragging him toward him, and said to him: what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, that you did not follow me — did you disobey my order to you, my saying, "Take my place among my people and set things right and follow not the way of the corrupters"? And Aaron said, as in the other sūrah, "O son of my mother, take me not by my beard nor by my head; I feared that you would say, You have caused a division among the Children of Israel and have not awaited my word" (20:94); and here he said, "O son of my mother, the people deemed me weak" — they despised me when I said to them, "O my people, you have only been tried by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90) — "and they were about to kill me; so do not gladden the enemies over me," by rebuking me and touching me with harm, for the enemies are eager to find in me a stumble or to discover in me a slip; "and do not place me with the wrongdoing people," by treating me as they are treated. And the phrase "son of my mother," mentioning the mother alone, is a softening for his brother — though he was his brother by his mother and his father both [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the setting and the details: cf. 20:86; Moses returned to his people already angry and aggrieved even before seeing them, because God had made him aware of their having gone astray while he was still on the mountain (20:83–85). "Aggrieved" translates *asifan*, which may connote sadness but also intense anger (al-Mawdūdī, Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī); his anger was at his people, but also perhaps at himself for having left them, and his grief was both for his people's grave error and for his having to leave the intimate discourse with God, since the narrative of 20:83–85 suggests he had to cut short his time on the mountain to address the matter. "How evil is the course you have followed after me" may have been directed at the Israelites generally or at the leaders among them, including Aaron (al-Zamakhsharī); "after me" may mean while Moses was away (Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī) or after Moses had set the example of true monotheism (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī). "Would you hasten the command of your Lord" — it addresses their impatience concerning, and their ultimate hastening of, Moses's return from his appointed meeting with God, since the forty-day stay was reportedly ten days longer than his people had expected; it may also refer to their hastening God's judgment upon them through their actions, a repeated Qurʾānic warning to disbelievers (6:57–58; 10:50–51); and more broadly the question might chastise them for impatience regarding God's fulfillment of His promise, as in 20:86: "Did your Lord not make you a goodly promise? Did the pact seem too long for you?" Moses throws down the Tablets in anger (Ṭabarī) and shock (al-Zamakhsharī) upon seeing his people's idolatrous worship, breaking them (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), as in the Biblical account (Exodus 32:19). He then seizes his brother Aaron in anger for having failed in his charge of preserving the Israelites in righteousness; for another narrative of the confrontation, see 20:92–94. Aaron pleads with Moses, calling him son of my mother rather than just "my brother," in a bid to evoke Moses's tenderness and mercy (Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī); he excuses his own actions by arguing that the people deemed him weak, meaning that they no longer recognized his authority (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī) — as suggested by their having followed the directives of al-Sāmirī while ignoring Aaron's pleas for them to desist (20:90) — and were moreover prepared to slay him; and he asks Moses not to let their enemies rejoice in his misfortune, that is, to gloat over his further humiliation at the hands of Moses, and not to place him with the wrongdoing people, that is, not to consider him guilty of idolatry and so punish him along with the others (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** adds the apologetic point: Allah had informed him of their perversion on the Mount, and now seeing them in that state with his own eyes filled him with indignation; "how bad is the thing you have done in my absence" means they should have waited until the Book of Allah came to them, though some commentators say it means they hastily decided that Moses was dead. Then he turned to Aaron, his deputy: he wanted to free his hand in order to grab him, so he quickly put down the Tablets and grabbed his brother's head — and this has been termed "having dropped" them; the Arabic word *ilqāʾ* signifies dropping or throwing, which gives rise to the doubt that Moses showed disrespect to the Tablets. It is obvious, he says, that throwing the Tablets of the Torah would be a great sin, and equally obvious that all the prophets are innocent and free of sins; the implication is therefore that he put away the Tablets as quickly as he could in order to free his hands, which seemed like having been dropped, and the Qurʾān has described it with this word as a gesture of warning [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: when Moses returned to his people angry because of them and bitterly grieved, he said, "Evil is the manner of succession you have followed in my place, this idolatry of yours; would you hasten the judgment of your Lord?" And he cast down the Tablets — and they were broken into pieces — and he seized his brother by the head, that is, by the hair with his right hand, and by the beard with his left, dragging him toward him in anger. He said, "O son of my mother" — read *ibna ummī* or *ibna umma*, meaning the standard form of saying "my mother," the mention of her being more affectionate in appealing to his heart — "the people judged me weak and were close to killing me; do not make my enemies gloat over my misfortune by your humiliating me, and do not count me among the folk who have done evil" by worshipping the calf in your reproach of them [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Ghaḍbān asifan* is a double description that the exegetes parse closely: *ghaḍab* is anger, and *asaf* is either its intensification (Abū al-Dardāʾ: a station beyond anger) or its twin in grief (al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan: sorrowful) — and **[Ṭabarī]** keeps both, since Ibn ʿAbbās's appeal to 43:55 shows the root covering anger and grief at once [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. "*Biʾsa mā khalaftumūnī*" — how evil is what you succeeded me with — turns on the verb *khalafa*, which is used of acting for a man in his family and people after his departure, in good or in evil; so the verse's charge is technical: you were my successors and this is the succession you handed in [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Aʿajiltum amr rabbikum* — did you outstrip your Lord's command — is the verse's decisive verb, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s distinction between *al-ʿajalah* (advancing a thing before its time, blameworthy) and *al-surʿah* (doing a thing at its first time, praiseworthy) is the most quoted line in the commentaries on the passage: the people were not fast, they were early [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. And "son of my mother" — *ibna umm* — is the plea's own rhetoric: the mother alone is named because the appeal goes to tenderness, not to fraternity in general [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Three traditions the commentators bring into this passage. First, on anger: the report in Abū Dāwūd from Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ told the angry person standing to sit and, if the anger does not leave, to lie down; and the report of Abū Wāʾil that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Anger is from Satan, and Satan was created from fire, and fire is extinguished only by water; so when one of you is angry, let him perform ablution" — transmitted through ʿAtiyya, whose status is that of a weak chain *(weak)* [Qurṭubī]. Second, Mālik's picture of Moses's anger — smoke rising from his hood and the hair of his body lifting his cloak — transmitted by Ibn al-Qāsim, which belongs to the transmitted lore about the prophets rather than to sound ḥadīth [Qurṭubī]. Third, the vast report of Qatāda about what Moses found in the Tablets and his repeated plea to be made of the nation of Aḥmad, with God's repeated answer, "That is the nation of Aḥmad." **[Ṭabarī]** transmits it in two chains and makes clear that his own reading of the verse does not rest on it; **[Qurṭubī]** refuses even to consider the use made of it, calling the report a base opinion that should not be attributed to Moses, while **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the plainer reason for the throwing — anger at the people, upon which the verse itself has already spoken [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the exchanges between Moses and Aaron reported from 20:92–94 function as the verse's internal commentary: "What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, that you followed me not?" and "O son of my mother, seize me not by my beard nor by my head; I feared lest you should say, You have caused a division among the Children of Israel and have not awaited my word" [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Rulings.** Three rulings the passage carries. First, the discipline of anger: **[Qurṭubī]** records the Prophetic instructions to sit, lie down, and perform ablution, and Ibn al-ʿArabī's characterization of Moses as the angriest of men but the quickest to recover, a balance the law itself recommends [Qurṭubī]. Second, the sanctity of revealed text and the refusal to draw licenses from the prophets' states: the Qurʾān says only that Moses "cast down" the Tablets, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of Ibn al-Jawzī's refutation dismantles the claim of those who used the incident to justify tearing clothes in ecstasy — noting that the breaking is not established, the intention to break is not established, and even if both were, the states of prophets cannot be a proof-text for the conduct of the heedless, who are addressed by the law before they ever enter the place where they lose themselves [Qurṭubī]. **[Maʿārif]**'s point is the doctrinal complement: since the prophets are protected from sin, the verse's word must be read as an indication of haste in setting the Tablets down rather than irreverence, and the description carries a warning in it [Maʿārif]. Third, the legitimacy of holding a deputy to account: Moses's questioning of Aaron and Aaron's defense — that the people had deemed him weak and nearly killed him — is recorded as an episode of accountability within leadership, and both of the sūrahs that narrate it let Aaron's plea stand [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: How evil is the course you have followed after me!" (7:150, the verse itself); "And Moses had gone back to his people, angry and grieved" (cf. 20:86); "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, that you followed me not? Have you then disobeyed my order?" (20:92–93); "He said: O son of my mother, seize me not by my beard nor by my head; I feared lest you should say, You have caused a division among the Children of Israel and have not awaited my word" (20:94); "And in Moses's anger there is a lesson for those who hold authority" (cf. 20:86–94); "And when the anger of Moses subsided, he took up the Tablets" (7:154) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The sūrah's long Egyptian arc ends here with its prophet coming down the mountain to find his people dancing around a calf, and the scene is deliberately undignified: the Tablets dropped, the brother seized by the beard, the two men arguing in front of the crowd. The commentaries refuse to smooth it into a legend of composure, and their reason is theologically interesting — the anger is described as the other face of Moses's jealousy for God, so that what looks like a failure of temper is presented as the excess of a prophet's concern [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. What the passage restrains is the reader: the prophets' states are not precedents for the rest of us, as **[Qurṭubī]** insists at some length, and the verse's own last word belongs to Aaron, who does not defend himself by accusing the people but asks only not to be counted among them [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. The next verse will close the scene, and the sūrah has already prepared the reader for its tone: when the anger subsides, the Tablets are taken up again [Study Quran].
## 7:151

*"He said, 'My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the sequel of the confrontation: when Moses's excuse for his brother became clear to him, and he knew that Aaron had not fallen short in the duty God had laid upon him by what the ignorant calf-worshippers had done, he said, "My Lord, forgive me" — seeking forgiveness for what he had done to his brother — "and my brother" — for whatever had gone before between Aaron and his Lord; that is, cover our sins with a covering from You. And "admit us into Your mercy" means: have mercy on us with Your wide mercy that embraces Your believing servants, for You are more merciful to Your servants than anyone who shows mercy to anything [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the human sequence: Moses regretted what he had hastened in his treatment of his brother before he knew his innocence of the shortcoming he had suspected in him, and so he said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother" — Aaron — "and admit us into Your mercy," that is, into the midst of it, and make Your mercy surround us from every side, for it is a fortified fortress against all evils and the place of every good and every joy; "and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful," that is, more merciful to us than every merciful one — more merciful to us than our fathers and our mothers and our children and our own selves [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** frames the prayer the same way: Moses turned to Aaron, who gave him the true account of events and said it was not his fault, since he had stopped them from the wicked act and they would not listen, so obstinate that they were about to kill him; and this cooled Moses down, and at this occasion he prayed as the verse records. He asked forgiveness for his brother for any shortcoming in his duties, and for himself either for having put away the Tablets of the Torah in a hurry — which the Qurʾān described as having been "dropped," as a gesture of warning — or, as he puts it, for teaching people that they should include themselves when asking forgiveness for others, so as to preclude any sense of complacency on their part [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** notes simply that Moses includes his brother in the supplication in order to reconcile him and to fend off any gloating over his misfortune [Jalālayn]. **[Study Quran]** reports the theological reading the commentators take: Moses's request for forgiveness for himself and his brother is considered by them to be an indication of their complete dedication to God and their desire to draw near to Him rather than an acknowledgment of sin or wrongdoing on their part, since the prophets are believed to be immune from sin according to the Islamic doctrine of the ʿiṣmah, or inerrancy, of the prophets; others suggest that Moses asked God to forgive him for his anger and to forgive Aaron for not being forceful enough with the Israelites, neither of which may be understood as rising to the level of serious sin; and Moses's anger is said by some to have been not a personal anger but a holy anger for God's sake, motivated by his intense desire to preserve worship for God alone — an anger manifested outwardly in the form of holy wrath for the sake of religion, while Moses's inner state remained characterized by calm and mercy [Study Quran] [q.v. 7:150] [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** places the supplication at the moment Moses was satisfied that his brother was innocent [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Language.** The verse's two objects are worth separating: "forgive me" (*ighfir lī*) and "forgive my brother" (*wa-li-akhī*), and the commentators refuse to collapse one into the other — **[Ṭabarī]** gives each its own content, the first covering Moses's own act toward Aaron, the second covering whatever had passed between Aaron and God [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif]. *Adkhilnā fī raḥmatika* — admit us into Your mercy — uses the language of entry into a space, which is why **[Saʿdī]** glosses it as being placed in the midst of mercy with mercy surrounding from every side: the prayer is not for a portion of mercy but for a location inside it [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī]. And "the Most Merciful of those who show mercy" is a comparative that the exegetes read literally and personally: God's mercy is not merely greater in quantity than human mercy but different in kind, and **[Saʿdī]** presses it to the point of the family — more merciful than one's own parents and children and self [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

**Belief.** The verse stands in the commentaries as a proof-text for the doctrine of the prophets' protection from sin: **[Study Quran]** notes that the request is read as veneration rather than confession, since the ʿiṣmah of the prophets excludes serious sin; and **[Maʿārif]**'s account of Moses's hurried setting down of the Tablets, explained as a gesture of warning rather than disrespect, belongs to the same doctrinal concern [Study Quran] [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "And Moses said: My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy" (7:151, the verse itself); "He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me" (28:16, in the same prophet's biography); "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs" (3:147); "My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house as a believer" (cf. 71:28); "Say: My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of the merciful" (23:118) [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Reflection.** The scene's last word before the narrative moves on is a prayer in which the two brothers stand together. Moses, who had a moment before been dragging Aaron by the beard, asks mercy for himself first and then for the brother he had wronged, and the order is the point: the man who has acted in anger takes his own share of the fault before asking anything for the other [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]**'s practical note — that a person should include himself when praying for others — turns the verse into an instruction in humility; and the tradition's insistence that neither man had committed a sin preserves both the moral authority of the prophets and the honesty of the scene, in which two sincere servants still need the mercy they ask for [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

## 7:152

*"Indeed, those who took the calf will be reached by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world; and thus do We recompense the inventors."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the plain sense: those who took the calf as a god, wrath from their Lord will reach them — God hastening it for them — and humiliation, which is disgrace, as God's punishment of them for their disbelief in their Lord, in the life of this world, in the immediate present rather than in the deferred hereafter. He then records and weighs Ibn Jurayj's restriction: that this applies to those who died among the calf-worshippers before Moses returned, and to those who fled when Moses commanded them to kill one another. Ṭabarī's own judgment is that Ibn Jurayj's view, though it has a face, is contradicted by the apparent sense of God's Book and by the interpretation of most of the exegetes, because God stated the matter generally of all who took the calf. And the reports from the Companions and the Successors are concordant that when Moses returned to the Children of Israel, God accepted the repentance of the calf-worshippers through what He told of Moses's words: "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so repent to your Maker and kill yourselves" (2:54) — and they did what their prophet commanded them. So God's command to them to kill one another was out of His wrath at their calf-worship, and their killing of one another was their humiliation and the disgrace by which God abased them in this life, with their repentance to God before it. And Ṭabarī adds the legal point: no one may transfer a report that the Book gives in general to a specific instance without a proof from report or reason, and no such proof exists here. "And thus do We recompense the inventors" — as We recompensed those who took the calf as a god, by bringing wrath upon them and abasing them in this life for their disbelief and their apostasy after faith, so We recompense everyone who invents a lie against God by denying Him and affirming divinity to other than Him, or worshipping an idol besides Him after affirming His oneness — when he does not repent of his disbelief before his death. And he records Abū Qilāba's word, recited over this verse: "It is, by God, for every inventor, until the Day of Resurrection" — that God will abase him [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the wrath in the same concrete way: the wrath that struck the Children of Israel for their worship of the calf means that God did not accept their repentance until some of them who had not worshipped the calf killed others who had, as 2:54 records. And the humiliation pertains to the disgrace and humiliation that the Jews suffered in the life of this world; and "thus do we recompense those who invent lies" is for all those who invent an innovation in religion. He records al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's saying that the disgrace of innovation will weigh on their shoulders even if they were to gallop on their mules or trot on their work-horses, and Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah's, that every person who invents an innovation in the religion will taste disgrace [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** states the causation: God says this, making plain the state of the people of the calf who worshipped it — they angered their Lord and took His command lightly, so wrath and humiliation were due to them; and then the general rule: every inventor of lies against God, false against His law, attributing to Him what He did not say, has a share of wrath from God and humiliation in the life of this world [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gathers the readings: the wrath that shall seize the Israelites who worshipped the calf is thought by some to be a reference to the command that they atone for their sins by "slaying their own" in 2:54, understood either as the execution of the most guilty among them or as a form of collective punishment; some commentators take both God's anger and their abasement in this world (cf. 2:61) as references to later hardships suffered by the Israelites and their descendants, or assign the wrath to the Hereafter and the abasement to this world; others argue that the Israelites' repentance and atonement meant their punishment would be only in this world and not in the next; and "those who fabricate" refers to those who initiate false religious beliefs or practices (cf. 4:48–50; 5:103; 6:93; 10:59–60; 16:56) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** draws out the worldly dimension in a way the other sources only gesture at: the verse warns those who took to the worship of the calf and persisted in it of their sad fate in the Hereafter and of a disgraceful life in this world — and part of the punishment of some sins is also given in this life, as happened to al-Sāmirī, whom Moses commanded to live apart from the people, not touching anyone with his hand nor being touched by anyone; so for the rest of his life he lived a deserted life of seclusion, walking about with animals, and no human came near him. Al-Qurṭubī reports from Qatāda that his punishment was that whenever he touched someone or was touched by one of the people, both suffered from fever, and the author of Rūḥ al-Bayān observes that the symptoms of this disease are still inherited by his generations. And on the closing clause: al-Shaykh Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah said that those who invent new things in the Sharīʿah also commit the sin of fabrication and deserve such punishment, and Imām Mālik inferred from this verse that those who invent new practices in the Sharīʿah deserve the same punishment of Allah's wrath in the Hereafter and disgrace in this life [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives it compactly: those who chose the calf as a god — wrath and abasement shall come upon them from their Lord in the life of this world, and so they were punished for this deed by the command to slay themselves, and abasement was stamped upon them until the Day of Resurrection; and as We have requited them, so We requite those who invent lies against God by way of idolatry and otherwise [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Sayanaluhum* — "will reach them," from a verb of obtaining and catching up — makes the punishment something that comes to a people who are not looking for it rather than something they summon; and **[Ṭabarī]**'s "hastening it for them" keeps the sense of a payment arriving in this life [Ṭabarī]. *Ghaḍab* — wrath — is the term the verse pairs with *dhilla*, humiliation, and the pairing is the engine of the passage: the proud calf-makers are answered by being abased, and the ʿizzah they sought in an idol becomes the *dhilla* they carry [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And *al-muftarūn* — the inventors, the fabricators — is the verse's generalization, turning an ancient Egyptian-Israelite incident into a standing category: the one who fabricates against God's law is enrolled in the people of the calf. **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Maʿārif]** extend it to the inventors of religious innovation, which is how this verse became one of the standing proof-texts against *bidʿah* in the tradition [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Rulings.** The verse's legal afterlife in the commentaries is entirely about innovation. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿUyaynah: the disgrace of innovation rides the shoulders of its author no matter what mount he rides; **[Maʿārif]**'s Mālik: those who invent practices in the Sharīʿah deserve the same wrath and disgrace; and al-Sāmirī's own sentence — a lifetime of exclusion, feared to the touch — read as the exemplary punishment of a man who manufactured a religion out of borrowed gold and a trick of sound [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "And when Moses said to his people: O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so turn in repentance to your Maker and kill yourselves; that is better for you with your Maker" (2:54); "And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief" (2:93); "We have sent down upon them humiliation and misery, and they brought upon themselves wrath from God" (2:61); "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that by way of recompense from God? Those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry, and whom He has made into apes and swine" (5:60); "And whoever invents about God a lie — those will not succeed" (cf. 10:69; 16:105) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse does two things at once, and the second is what made it a permanent reference point: it settles the fate of the calf-worshippers, and it turns their crime into a category. The wrath and the abasement are the requital of those who took a manufactured god; the closing sentence tells every later reader that manufacturing claims about God is the same act in a new shape [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]**'s account of al-Sāmirī's isolated life is a portrait the story does not give elsewhere: the man who gave the people a visible god spends his remaining years untouchable, wandering with animals — the god he made was speechless, and his own end is a kind of silence [Maʿārif]. And **[Study Quran]**'s survey of the interpretations leaves the reader with the doctrine beneath the history: this-worldly disgrace and other-worldly wrath may be divided between the two clauses, but the fabrication is one [Study Quran].

## 7:153

*"But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed — indeed, your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful."*

**Meaning.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the verse as the general mercy that answers the general threat: God tells His servants that He accepts repentance from His servants for any sin — even shirk, disbelief, hypocrisy and disobedience: "But those who committed evil deeds and then repented afterwards and believed, verily, your Lord" — O Muhammad, the Messenger of Repentance and the Prophet of Mercy — "after that is indeed Forgiving, Most Merciful." He reports from Ibn Abī Ḥātim that ʿAbdallāh b. Masʿūd was asked about a man who commits fornication with a woman and then marries her, and Ibn Masʿūd recited this verse ten times, neither allowing nor disallowing it — a report the editor of the commentary indexes under this verse and that shows the early community using it as the ceiling of forgiveness rather than a ruling on a particular case [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** sets the verse in its local context and then lifts it out: those addressed first are the calf-worshippers, who had incurred God's wrath and been commanded to kill one another, and then God turned to them after that; and He states a general judgment in which they and others are included: "those who did evil deeds" — of association, and major and minor sins — "and then repented after them," by feeling remorse for what is past, desisting from it, and resolving not to return, "and believed" in God and in what God has made faith obligatory, and faith is not complete except with the acts of the heart and the acts of the limbs that follow from it; "indeed, your Lord, after that" — after this state of repentance from the evil deeds and return to obedience — "is Forgiving," forgiving sins and erasing them even if they were the fill of the earth, "Merciful," in accepting repentance, granting success to good deeds, and accepting them [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** places the verse in the Qurʾān's pattern: the reminder that God forgives those who are truly repentant and mend their ways is found throughout the Qurʾān (2:160; 3:89; 5:39; 16:119); in 4:17 the Qurʾān states that God only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then turn quickly in repentance; and in the present passage it is clear that the Israelites' repentance is quick and unconditional [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse as it stands: those who commit evil deeds and repent, desisting from them thereafter, and believe in God — indeed your Lord thereafter, that is after repentance, is truly Forgiving, Merciful toward them [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]**'s comment on the passage treats the forgiveness of the calf-worshippers as established by the very fact that God's general statement here follows the specific threat of the previous verse, and he argues from the same materials that the punishment described in 7:152 is this-worldly and the acceptance of their repentance is the plain sense of the sequence [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Maʿārif]** carry the verse in the flow of the passage [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif].

**Language.** The verse's structure is three verbs in sequence — *ʿamilū* (they did), *tābū* (they repented), *āmanū* (they believed) — and the commentators read the sequence as a definition: the deed, the remorse and reversal, and the faith that the reversal is made of [Saʿdī]. *Tawbah* in the Qurʾānic usage of the exegetes requires the three elements **[Saʿdī]** names, and the verse's "after them" and "after that" mark the temporal hinge on which the whole sentence turns: God's name "Forgiving and Merciful" is predicated on the state after repentance, not printed over the sins in advance [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī]. And *min baʿdihā* — after them — is repeated in the middle of the verse, so that the forgiveness is anchored explicitly to what comes later rather than earlier [Jalālayn].

**Belief.** The verse is used by the commentators for the widest possible scope of divine forgiveness: **[Ibn Kathīr]** says God accepts repentance for any sin, "even shirk, disbelief, hypocrisy and disobedience," which is the maximal claim the tradition allows; **[Saʿdī]**'s condition — even if the sins were the fill of the earth — states the same without boundary [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And **[Study Quran]**'s citation of 4:17 supplies the qualification that keeps the doctrine from becoming complacency: the acceptance belongs to those who turn quickly, and the passage's own narrative makes the Israelites' speed the mark of the sincerity [Study Quran] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And when those who disbelieve see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved" (cf. 16:85); "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God; indeed, God forgives all sins" (39:53); "God only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then turn quickly in repentance — it is they whom God will forgive" (4:17); "But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed God will turn to him in forgiveness" (5:39); "Except for those who repent and believe and do righteous work; for them God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds" (25:70) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the mirror held up to the previous one. Where 7:152 ended on the fate of fabricators, this verse opens the door on the same people: the calf-worshippers had been told they would meet wrath and humiliation, and the next sentence says that those who did the evil and then turned and believed will find their Lord Forgiving and Merciful [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī]. **['Abdallāh b. Masʿūd]**'s handling of the verse — reciting it ten times over a hard case and refusing to legislate from it — is a reminder that the verse's function is this: not to settle the law of every difficult case, but to state without ambiguity that the door stands open, and that the state named in the middle of the sentence is what determines whether one walks through it [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

## 7:154

*"And when the anger of Moses subsided, he took up the Tablets; and in their copy was guidance and mercy for those who hold their Lord in awe."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the verb: "when the anger subsided from Moses" means when it was restrained and quietened — every *kāff* is "silent" about something, and a speaker is *sākit* about speech because he has held off from it — and he cites the Arabic usage of a valley that flows three days and then "falls silent," meaning it withholds itself from flowing. Then: "he took the Tablets," that is, he took them after he had thrown them, with some of what had been in them having gone; "and in their copy was guidance and mercy" means in what was copied into them, that is, written in them — guidance that is the clarification of the truth, and mercy for those who fear their Lord and dread His punishment for their disobedience. He then gives the grammarians' disagreement over the *lām* in *li-rabbihim yarhabūn* — the construction that would ordinarily be "they dread their Lord" without the preposition — with several solutions offered: that the verb is simply connected by the *lām* as in "if you can interpret dreams" (12:43); or that it means "because of their Lord they dread"; or that the *lām* entered in place of the possessive construction, "those who are dreaders for their Lord"; or that because the noun was fronted before the verb, the preposition became good; and he cites the poet's line "he handed her a hundred dirhams" for the breadth of the construction [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same material at more length. Muʿāwiyah b. Qurrah read the verb with a *nūn* — "when the anger settled" — and the root of *sukūt* is *sukūn* and withholding: they say the valley ran three days and then "settled," that is, withheld itself from running. ʿIkrima said the phrase is inverted, "Moses was silent from anger," in the manner of "I put my finger in the ring" and "I put the ring on my finger," "I put the cap on my head" and "I put my head in the cap." "He took the Tablets which he had thrown down." "And in their copy was guidance and mercy" — guidance from misguidance, mercy from punishment; and *al-naskh* is the transferring of what is in one book to another, and both the original from which a copy is made and the copy itself are called *nuskhah*. He then records the several explanations of what the "copy" was: Ibn ʿAbbās's report that when the Tablets broke, Moses fasted forty days and they were returned and restored to him in two tablets, nothing of them being lost — and on this view, says al-Qushayrī, "in their copy" means in what was copied from the broken tablets and transferred to the new ones; ʿAṭāʾ's view: "in what remained of them," since only a seventh of them remained and six sevenths had gone, though nothing of the limits and the rulings was lost; another view: "in what was copied for him from the Preserved Tablet"; and another: "in what was written for him in them," with no need of an original to copy from, as one says, "copy down what so-and-so says," meaning put it in your book [Qurṭubī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the same range: Moses took up the Tablets after previously casting them down in anger; "in their inscription lay a guidance and a mercy" may simply indicate that the contents of the Tablets — namely the Torah — contained guidance and mercy, a description associated with both the Torah and the Qurʾān (6:154; 7:52; 16:64; 28:43; 31:2–3); "inscription" translates *nuskhah*, a word that generally denotes a written copy, but whose root meaning relates to substituting one thing for another, particularly as regards a text — so some commentators understand *nuskhah* as referring to new Tablets that Moses was given, containing a copy of what had been inscribed on the originals, and it may also refer more generally to the notion that guidance and mercy were inscribed upon, or copied onto, the Torah Tablets from the heavenly Preserved Tablet (85:22), from which all divine revelation derives [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as a portrait of the prophet's priorities: when the anger quieted from Moses — when his anger subsided and his soul came back to him and he recognized what he was in — he occupied himself with the most important thing before him: he took up the Tablets he had thrown, and they were tablets of great and mighty measure, "in their copy" — that is, containing and comprising — "guidance and mercy": in them is the guidance from misguidance, the clarification of the truth from falsehood, the works of good and the works of evil, and the guidance to the best deeds and morals and manners; and mercy and felicity for the one who acts by them and knows their rulings and meanings. But not everyone accepts God's guidance and mercy; only those accept it, submit to it and receive it with acceptance who hold their Lord in awe — who fear Him and stand in dread of Him; and as for the one who does not fear God nor the standing before Him, he only increases in insolence and aversion by it, and God's proof stands against him through it [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: when Moses's anger abated and subsided he took the Tablets which he had cast down, and in their copy — in what was inscribed upon them, that is, it was written that there was guidance from error and mercy for all those who hold their Lord in awe — the *lām* in "their Lord" having been inserted into the direct object because the object precedes the verb [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** carries the verse in the same flow [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** reads it with the apologetic note already made at 7:150: the Tablets were put down as a gesture of warning, and the verse's "took up" closes the episode by finding the prophet occupied with the revelation again once the temper passed [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Sakata* — to fall silent — applied to anger is a metaphor the exegetes explain both ways: the anger fell silent, or Moses fell silent from the anger; and **[Qurṭubī]**'s "inverted" reading (ʿIkrima) is the classical recognition that Arabic uses such reversals freely, as in putting the finger in the ring or the head in the cap [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. *Nuskhah* is the most technical word in the verse, and the exegetes note its double life: a copy, and the act of copying, so that "in their copy was guidance" can mean in the original inscription, in the surviving portion, or in the replacement Tablets — a range **[Study Quran]** sets out with the suggestion, which it favors as a possibility, that the word points to the Tablets' derivation from the Preserved Tablet itself [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī]. And the phrase "for those who hold their Lord in awe" (*li-rabbihim yarhabūn*) is the verse's condition: the guidance and mercy are *for* a class of readers, defined by awe, not merely available on a shelf [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī].

**Rulings.** Two things the commentators establish here. First, the material history of the Tablets: **[Qurṭubī]**'s reports — the tablets broken, Moses fasting another forty days, the tablets restored in two with nothing lost; or a seventh remaining with nothing of the rulings lost; or a fresh copy from the Preserved Tablet — show that the tradition's concern is to guarantee that the revelation was not diminished by the prophet's anger [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. Second, and more importantly for the reader, the verse's final clause functions as a statement about who receives revelation: **[Saʿdī]**'s insistence that only the God-fearing accept the guidance, while the one without awe increases in insolence and finds the proof standing against him, makes the Tablets a mirror of the reader's own disposition [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And We gave Moses the Scripture, complete for the one who would do good, and an elaboration of all things, and guidance and mercy, that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord" (6:154); "And this is a Book which We have revealed, blessed, so follow it and be mindful, that you may receive mercy" (6:155); "This is a clarification for the people and a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe" (45:20); "And We gave them the clear Scripture, and guided them to the straight path" (37:117–118); "And when the anger of Moses subsided, he took up the Tablets" (7:154, the verse itself) [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the quiet after the storm, and its shape is worth noticing: the Tablets come back into Moses's hands not because the anger was justified or unjustified but because the anger passed, and what he does with his recovered hands is take up the book. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading — the prophet attends to the most important thing the moment he is himself again — gives the passage its practical ethics: a servant may be thrown off course by grief or rage, and the measure is where he turns when the disturbance settles [Saʿdī]. And the closing phrase keeps the reader honest: the guidance and mercy were there for those who stand in awe of their Lord, and the tablets' power is not in the stone but in the fear of the one who lifts them [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

## 7:155

*"And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment. And when the earthquake seized them, he said, 'My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? It is only Your trial by which You cause to stray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of forgivers.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the setting from the early reports: Moses chose seventy men of his people — that is, from the Children of Israel — for the time and term God had appointed to meet him with them, to apologize for the folly of their foolish ones in the matter of the calf. Al-Suddī's account: God commanded Moses to come to Him with a group of the Children of Israel to apologize for the worship of the calf and promised them a time; Moses chose the seventy by his own selection and went with them; when they reached the place they said, "We will not believe you, O Moses, until we see God openly — you have spoken to Him, so show Him to us!" — and the thunderbolt seized them and they died; and Moses stood weeping and invoking God: "My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them and You have destroyed their best? Had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me." Ibn Isḥāq's fuller report: Moses chose seventy of the best of the Children of Israel and said to them, "Go to God and repent to Him for what you have done, and ask forgiveness for those of your people you have left behind; fast and purify yourselves and purify your garments." He took them out to Mount Sinai at the time God had set, and he did not come to it except by His permission and knowledge. When the seventy had done what he commanded and gone out with him to the meeting, they said to Moses, "Ask for us that we may hear the words of our Lord" — and he said, "I shall." When Moses drew near the mountain, a column of cloud fell over it until it covered the whole mountain; Moses drew near and entered it and said to the people, "Draw near"; and when God spoke to Moses, a brilliant light settled on his brow which no human being could look at, so a veil was placed between them. The people drew near, and when they entered the cloud they fell prostrate and heard God speaking with Moses, commanding him and forbidding him, do this and do not do that. When God had finished His command, the cloud lifted from Moses, and he came back to them, and they said, "We will not believe you until we see God openly" — and the earthquake seized them, which is the thunderbolt, and their souls were snatched away suddenly and they all died. Then Moses stood addressing his Lord and calling on Him and beseeching: "Lord, had You willed You could have destroyed them before, and me; they were foolish — will You destroy those behind me from the Children of Israel?" And Ibn ʿAbbās said, through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa, that God had commanded him to choose seventy men, and he chose them and went out with them to call on their Lord; and among what they said in their supplication was, "O God, give us what You have not given anyone before us and will not give anyone after us" — God disliked that from them, and the earthquake seized them. And a further report: some said the earthquake seized them because of their claim against Moses concerning the killing of Aaron — the report of ʿAlī that Moses and Aaron and Shubayr and Shabīr went out and came to a mountain where Aaron was sleeping on a bed and God took his soul; and when Moses returned to the Children of Israel they said, "Where is Aaron?" and he said, "God took him"; they said, "You killed him; you envied us his gentleness and good character" — whereupon Moses said, "Choose whom you wish," and they chose seventy men; and when they came to Aaron they asked, "Who killed you?" and he said, "No one killed me; God took my soul." They said to Moses, "You will not be disobeyed after this day" — and the earthquake seized them, and Moses went to the right and the left saying, "My Lord, had You willed You could have destroyed them before and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar and the reading of the event: "Moses chose his people" takes two objects, one with the preposition *min* dropped, as the poets show; the *rajfah* is the severe earthquake, and it is reported that they were shaken until they died. "Had You willed You could have destroyed them before and me" means You could have caused them to die before we went out to the appointment in the presence of the Children of Israel, so that they would not hold me suspect. Then the interrogative "will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?" — its purpose is denial, that is, You will not do that; and the usage is frequent in Arabic; and it may carry the sense of prayer and request, that is, do not destroy us. Al-Mubarrad said the interrogation is one of astonishment. And Moses knew that God does not destroy anyone for another's sin, so his question was like Jesus's words, "If You should punish them — indeed they are Your servants" (5:118). And on "it is only Your trial": this is nothing but Your testing and probation; Moses ascribed the trial to God and not to himself, as Abraham said, "and when I am ill, it is He who cures me" (26:80) — ascribing illness to himself and healing to God. And **[Qurṭubī]** notes that Moses learned this from God's words to him, "We have tried your people in your absence" (20:85); and on "You cause to stray whom You will and guide whom You will" he says pointedly: this is a refutation of the Qadarites [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** assembles the reports and the reason: Ibn ʿAbbās's account of the supplication that asked for what no one before or after them had been given, and the earthquake that followed; al-Suddī's account of the demand to see God; Ibn Isḥāq's account of the cloud and the light and the prostration and then the demand and the death; and then the scholars' consensus of explanation: they were seized, per Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Mujāhid and Ṭabarī, because they neither shunned nor forbade their people who worshipped the calf — an explanation supported by Moses's words, "would You destroy us for the deeds of the fools among us?" And "it is only Your trial" means affliction, test and trial, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliya, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas and several among the early and later scholars; and this is the only plausible meaning, in which Moses says: the decision is Yours, the judgment is Yours, whatever You will occurs; You misguide whom You will and guide whom You will, and none can guide whom You misguide or misguide whom You guide; none can give what You deprive or avert what You give; the sovereignty and the judgment and the creation and the decision are all Yours. And "You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, for You are the best of those who forgive": forgiveness pertains to God's covering the mistake and not punishing the sin, and whenever mercy is mentioned along with forgiveness, it includes the hope that God does not permit one to fall into that act again [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the passage as the sequence of repentance, intercession and revival: when the Children of Israel repented and returned to their right mind, Moses chose from them seventy men — of their best — to apologize for their people before their Lord, and God promised them an appointment at which they would attend. When they attended, they said, "O Moses, show us God openly!" — and they were audacious against God with a great audacity and behaved ill with Him, so the earthquake seized them and they fell in a swoon and perished. Moses kept beseeching God and devoting himself: "Lord, had You willed You would have destroyed them before" — before they attended and were in a state in which they could apologize to their people, so that they became the wronged ones themselves; "will You destroy us for what the fools among us have done?" — the weak in mind and foolish in understanding; and he pleaded that those who were audacious against God had no complete intellects to restrain them from what they said and did, and that a trial had befallen them by which a person would be alarmed and fear the loss of his religion. "It is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, for You are the best of forgivers" — that is, You are the best of those who forgive, the most entitled to show mercy, the most generous in giving and favoring. And God answered his prayer, revived them after their death, and forgave them their sins [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** frames the episode with its numbers and its narratives: most commentators indicate that the meeting with the elders followed the calf incident and was connected with the Israelites' attempt to atone for their sin; the seventy chosen by Moses, at God's command, were among those elders who had not directly participated in making or worshipping the calf (al-Rāzī); some reports say Moses chose six men from each of the twelve tribes for a total of seventy-two, two of whom, Joshua and Caleb, remained behind to supervise the camp (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī); the others were instructed to fast and purify themselves and their clothing (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī). "Earthquake" translates *rajfah*, the same word used for the physical event that destroyed the Thamūd (7:78) and the people of Midian (7:91); it was meant as a punishment for the seventy, who had not worshipped the calf but had not done enough to stop those who did (al-Mawdūdī, al-Rāzī); some say the elders were killed by the quake and then revived at Moses's plea (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī), others that the quake shook them violently but relented before they died (al-Rāzī). Then the common narrative that connects the verse with the Israelites' demand to see God (2:55): the cloud descended and enveloped the mountain; Moses entered the cloud alone, but the elders followed; as they entered they were cast down prostrate but could hear Moses speaking with God; eventually the cloud lifted and they approached Moses and asked to see God directly, at which the earthquake seized them for their insolence (al-Mawdūdī, Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī). "Hadst Thou willed, Thou wouldst have destroyed them and me beforehand" indicates that Moses would have preferred that, if God intended to kill them, He would have done so while they were still in the camp, for he feared that if God killed the elders on the mountain, the Israelites would blame Moses for their deaths (al-Rāzī). "Wilt Thou destroy us for what the fools among us have done" — the fools being those Israelites who directly participated in the calf-worship; according to al-Rāzī, Moses knew that God would not punish some for the sins of others, and his question was a way of indicating that he was certain God would not do it, as if to say, "I know Thou wouldst not destroy us for the wrongdoing of others" — an interpretation apparently supported by his subsequent statement, "It is naught but Thy trial." That some are guided by the trial while others are led astray is similar to other verses regarding revelation's dichotomous effect on different souls (2:26; 9:124–25); and that God may both guide and lead astray is found throughout the Qurʾān (6:39; 7:178; 13:27; 14:4; 16:93; 17:97; 18:17; 35:8), with the theologians divided between those who read such statements as showing that faith and disbelief are determined by God and those who argue that God leads people astray only as a punishment for previous wrongdoing [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the narrative in the same shape and supplies the reconciliation of the two words: after Moses brought the Torah for his people and bade them follow it, they — being a crooked and pretentious people — said they were not sure it was the word of God and that Moses might have written it himself; he prayed to God for certainty, and God told him to choose seventy men and bring them to Mount Sinai, and He would make them hear His word, which was done. But they said they were not certain the voice they heard was God's voice — "We shall believe only when we see Allah vividly" — and since this demand was based on ignorance and obstinacy it evoked God's wrath: they were caught by the earthquake from beneath and by a thunderclap from above, and instantly fell down senseless as dead. The word used in Sūrat al-Baqarah is *ṣāʿiqah*, which signifies thunder, while here *rajfah* denotes earthquake; the two can be reconciled by assuming they were punished by both. Moses was extremely aggrieved first because they were prominent personalities of the Israelites, and second because he did not know how he would face his people on his return — they would blame him for the deaths of all these people and might even kill him. So he said to God that he knew it was not God's will to kill them, since they could have been killed on earlier occasions more suited to their destruction — drowned with Pharaoh, or killed at the time of the calf-worship — and that God cannot kill all of them for the bad deeds of a few foolish people; and he acknowledged that this was a trial from God by which some are led astray and some guided. As a result of his prayer, all seventy men were raised to life [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the scene compactly: Moses chose of his people seventy men from among those who had not worshipped the calf, by God's command, for Our appointed time — that is, the time at which God promised him that they should come and apologize for their comrades' worship of the calf; and when the Trembling, a violent earthquake, seized them — Ibn ʿAbbās said the earthquake came because they did not separate themselves from their people when the latter took to worshipping the calf, and he added that these were not the same people who asked to see God and were struck by the thunderbolt — Moses said, "My Lord, had You willed You would have destroyed them long before," that is, before my departure with them, so that the Children of Israel might see this and not make false accusations against me, "and me with them. Will You destroy us for what the foolish ones among us have done?" — the interrogative meant as a plea for compassion, that is, do not punish us for the sins of others. "It is but Your trial" — Your test — "whereby You send astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector," looking after our affairs, "so forgive us and have mercy on us, for You are the best of those who show forgiveness" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Iṣṭafā* is not the verb here; the verse uses *ikhtāra* — Moses chose — and **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the verb takes two objects with one preposition dropped, exactly as in the poetry: "the one chosen of the men for generosity." *Rajfah* is the shuddering of the earth, and the exegetes treat the two words for the two disasters — *rajfah* earthquake and *ṣāʿiqah* thunderbolt — as two descriptions that can both be true of one event, with **[Maʿārif]** making the reconciliation explicit: they were caught from beneath and from above [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. *Sufahāʾ* — the foolish, the light-minded — is the word Moses uses of the offenders, and it is a moral diagnosis rather than an insult: those whose intellects did not restrain them from audacity against God [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And the interrogative *a-tuhlikunā* is read by the grammarians as a denial in the form of a question, or as a petition, or as a question of astonishment — **[Qurṭubī]** gives all three and notes that the denial form in Arabic often carries an affirmation [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The passage's reports run along three chains. The narrative of the demand to see God and the death by thunderbolt (al-Suddī, Ibn Isḥāq, and the report from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa about the supplication for what no one before them had been given) [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. The account of the death of Aaron and the accusation against Moses, with the seventy questioning Aaron's corpse and their deaths and — in ʿAlī's report — their revival and being made prophets: "he revived them and made them all prophets" *(a report transmitted from ʿAlī with a chain the exegetes note)* [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. And the report of Wahb b. Munabbih that they did not die but were seized by trembling from awe until their joints nearly came apart, with Moses fearing for their lives — against the report, also from Wahb in al-Baqarah, that they died a day and a night [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran].

**Belief.** The verse became a locus of the theological dispute over divine guidance: **[Qurṭubī]** states flatly that "You cause to stray whom You will and guide whom You will" is a refutation of the Qadarites, and **[Study Quran]** lays out the two positions — those who read such verses as showing that faith and disbelief are determined by God, and those who argue that God leads people astray only as a punishment for previous wrongdoing, with the broader verses on the theme gathered in support of both readings [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s exposition of Moses's words gives the doctrinal content of the shirk-free confession: the decision, judgment, creation and command are God's; none can give what He deprives or avert what He gives [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And when you said, O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God openly, so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on; then We revived you after your death" (2:55–56); "And the earthquake seized them, and they lay prostrate in their homes" (7:78, of the Thamūd); "So the earthquake seized them, and they lay prostrate in their homes" (7:91, of Midian); "If You should punish them — indeed they are Your servants; but if You forgive them — indeed it is You who is the Exalted in Wisdom" (5:118); "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me" (26:80); "Say: O God, Master of all dominion, You give dominion to whom You will and You take away dominion from whom You will" (3:26); "God guides whom He wills to a straight path" (cf. 2:213) [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The scene is the sūrah's coldest lesson about the cost of wanting the wrong proof. Seventy men, chosen from the best of their people, purified and fasting, hear the voice of God on the mountain and then ask for something more — and the ground moves. **[Maʿārif]**'s point that the same generation had already doubted whether the Torah was God's word gives the demand its context: the request for vision was less an intellectual difficulty than a failure of obedience, and the punishment fell on those who had stood by while their people worshipped the calf — a fact **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Study Quran]** both emphasize, making the earthquake a judgment on complicity rather than on one outburst of impatience [Maʿārif] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. What the verse leaves standing is Moses: a man who has just lost the leaders of his people to a quake, arguing with his Lord about what their deaths would mean, ceding all sovereignty to God in the middle of his plea, and asking for forgiveness and mercy on the ground that God is the best of forgivers — a pattern the next verse will complete with his prayer for good in both worlds [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].
## 7:156

*"And write for us good in this world and in the Hereafter; indeed, we have turned to You.' He said, 'My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will, but My mercy encompasses all things. So I will write it for those who fear Me and give the zakāt and those who believe in Our verses.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** takes the supplication first: Moses said, "write for us" — make us of those for whom You have written — "in this world a good," namely the righteous works; "and in the Hereafter," of those for whom You have written the forgiveness of their sins. Ibn Jurayj said "a good" means forgiveness. And "we have turned to You" means: we have repented to You. On this the early authorities are unanimous in substance: Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliya, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, Qatāda, al-Suddī and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas all gloss *hudnā ilayk* as "we have repented to You"; and ʿAlī said the people were called *hūd* — Jews — precisely because they said "we have turned to You" [Ṭabarī]. Then God's answer: the earthquake that struck your people is "My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will of My creation, as I afflicted these of your people"; "and My mercy encompasses all things" — My mercy has embraced all My creation. He then records the disagreement over this statement: some said its wording is general while its meaning is particular, and what is meant is "My mercy embraced the believers in Me from the community of Muhammad ﷺ," supporting that with the words that follow, "so I will write it for those who fear." Ibn ʿAbbās read the verse as "and My mercy encompasses all things, so I will write it for those who fear" and said: God made it for this community. Then the famous report of the competitor for the verse: Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, and Ibn Jurayj, and Qatāda each transmit that when "and My mercy encompasses all things" came down, Iblīs said, "I am one of the 'things'" — and God removed him from it by saying, "so I will write it for those who fear and give the zakāt and those who believe in Our verses"; then the Jews said, "We fear, and we give the zakāt, and we believe in the signs of our Lord" — and God removed them from it, saying, "those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet" (7:157): He removed it from Iblīs and from the Jews and made it for this community. And a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that Moses was not given what he asked for this way, and then God said, "My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will, and My mercy encompasses all things, so I will write it for those who fear" — up to "the unlettered prophet" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same verse in brief: "write for us in this world a good" means grant us success in the righteous deeds by which good deeds are written for us; "and in the Hereafter" means a reward for them; "we have turned to You" means we have repented, as Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliya and Qatāda said, and *al-hawd* is repentance. "My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will" — those who deserve it, that is: this earthquake and this thunderbolt are a punishment from Me which I bring upon whom I will; and it is said the meaning is "whom I will to lead astray." "And My mercy encompasses all things" is a generality with no end: whoever enters it is not beyond it; and it is said it encompasses every creature, so that even a beast has mercy and tenderness toward its young. Then he gives the celebrated exegetical anecdote: some of the exegetes said that everything hoped for in this verse — even Iblīs — saying, "I am a thing"; and God said, "so I will write it for those who fear"; and the Jews and the Christians said, "We are God-fearing"; and God said, "those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet" — so the verse left the general and entered the particular, and praise be to God. And he reports the ʿAṭāʾ b. al-Sāʾib chain from Saʿīd b. Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās: God wrote it for this community [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the supplication as the completion of Moses's plea and the answer as the law of mercy's distribution: Moses said in the completion of his prayer, "and write for us in this world a good" — of beneficial knowledge, ample provision and righteous work — "and in the Hereafter" — the good that God has prepared for His righteous friends of reward; "we have turned to You," that is, we have returned, acknowledging our shortcoming, turning back to You in all our affairs. God answered: "My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will" — of those who are wretched and expose themselves to its causes; "and My mercy encompasses all things" — of the higher and the lower world, the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever: there is no creature but God's mercy has reached it and His bounty and favor have covered it. But the special mercy that occasions the felicity of this world and the next is not for everyone; hence God says of it, "so I will write it for those who fear" — the sins both small and great — "and give the zakāt" — the obligatory alms to those entitled to it — "and those who believe in Our verses" [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the supplication as a model: Moses's beseeching God for good in this world and in the Hereafter is an example of the proper mode of supplication for believers (see 2:201); "good in this world" may mean physical goods such as health and well-being, but may also mean moral integrity and success in obeying God's commandments; "good in the Hereafter" means forgiveness of sins and reward in Paradise; praying for good only in this life would be a sign of worldliness, whereas praying only for the Hereafter might indicate a failure to recognize one's dependence on God in this life and His ability to intervene in worldly matters. "We have turned unto Thee" means that they turn in repentance to God (Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī); and since God is a Protector for His servants and Moses and his people have expressed sincere repentance and humility, it is appropriate for them to seek from God both protection against harm and the acquisition of benefit (al-Rāzī).
