The response begins with the warning: some see "I cause My punishment to smite whomsoever I will" as a specific reference to the earthquake that seized the Israelites in the previous verse, or to the atonement ordained in 2:54 that they should slay their own, indicating that Moses has no power to deflect the punishment God has decreed; and although the line asserts God's freedom and power to punish as He wishes, commentators often qualify it to mean that He punishes only those deserving of it, in accordance with His wisdom (al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī) [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the theology of the mercy as the commentators understood it: though all the disobedient deserve the punishment of Allah, out of His mercy, which encircles everything — even the wrath of Allah — He afflicts with His punishment only a few whom He wills; His mercy is so great that it includes everything, so that even those who rebel against Him and deny Him are shown some of His mercy, though limited to this world alone; and when His mercy is so covering that it includes even the disobedient, He will surely write it in full for those who deserve it by fearing Allah, paying the zakāt and believing in His verses. He then reports the question of whether Moses's prayer was granted: unlike other occasions, where acceptance is explicit — "O Moses, you have been granted your request" (20:36) and "your supplication has been answered" (10:89) — this verse contains no such statement; some commentators have therefore suggested that this prayer was not accepted in favor of the Israelites but in favor of the Muslim community. He then gives his own resolution: the prayer comprised two requests — first, mercy and forgiveness for those who were punished, and second, the writing of good for him and his people in both worlds; the acceptance of the first is mentioned in this verse, while the answer to the second comes in the next verse; and in response to the first he was told that Allah does not punish everyone who sins but only those whom He wills, so these people too would not be destroyed, and His mercy covers every creation — even those punished are not completely deprived of it, since they could have received something harder. Then he records the Sāṭanic claim: the Satan claimed that according to this verse he was also a subject of His mercy, since it extends to everything, and he was one of "everything"; and he reports his teacher Mawlānā Anwar Kashmīrī's observation that the verse says His mercy "encompassed" everything — it did not say His mercy "shall encompass" everything — and cites 6:147, "Your Lord is of all-encompassing mercy, but His punishment cannot be warded off from the criminal people," which makes clear that the vastness of His mercy does not preclude the punishment of sinners; and then the conditions laid down — piety, zakāt, and firm belief in His verses — exclude both Satan and the Jews and Christians who did not believe in the last Prophet ﷺ [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: "and prescribe for us, grant us, in this world good and in the Hereafter good; we have turned, repented, to You"; God says: "My chastisement — I smite with it whom I will to chastise, and My mercy embraces, subsumes, all things in this world; and so I shall prescribe it in the Hereafter for those who are God-fearing and pay the alms and those who believe in Our signs" [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the two halves of the supplication as first the warding off of what should be avoided and then the request for what is sought; "write for us in this world good and in the Hereafter" means ordain for us and grant us all that is good in both lives; and he notes that the meaning of "good" was already given in Sūrat al-Baqarah. And on the divine answer, he takes the mercy as the subject of a large section: God's mercy is for those who have taqwā and give zakāt and believe in His signs [Ibn Kathīr].

**Language.** *Ḥasanah* — "good" — is the verse's deliberately wide word: in this world it can be construed as beneficial knowledge, ample provision and righteous work, or as forgiveness itself (Ibn Jurayj); in the Hereafter as the reward God has prepared for the righteous. The commentators leave the breadth in place because the prayer asks for totality rather than an item [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. *Hudnā* — we have turned — is the root the exegetes connect to the name of the Jews: ʿAlī said they were called *hūd* because they said "we have turned to You," and the conversion of the verb into an ethnonym is a reminder of how this passage's vocabulary entered the language [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the verse's central contrast is between two verbs of reaching: the punishment *uṣību* — I hit, I cause to land on — and the mercy *wasiʿat* — it embraced, it was wide enough for. The pairing is not symmetrical: the punishment selects (*man ashāʾ*, whom I will) while the mercy covers (*kull shayʾ*, all things), which is why the commentators made this verse the great proof that mercy is prior and wider [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

**Belief.** The verse's history in the tradition is the history of a proof-text about the scope of divine mercy, and the commentators report its uses: **Iblīs**'s claim ("I am a thing") and the Jews' claim ("we are God-fearing") and their exclusion by the verse that follows; **[Maʿārif]**'s teacher's grammatical point that the mercy *encompasses* all things without the promise that it shall encompass them all; and the citation of 6:147, "Your Lord is of all-encompassing mercy, and His punishment cannot be warded off from the criminal people," as the reconciliation of universal mercy with real punishment [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]**'s distinction is the same in the language of distribution: the general mercy reaches every creature in the gifts of existence and provision, while the special mercy that carries the felicity of the two abodes is written for those described in the verse [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "But seek, through that which God has given you, the home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of the world" (28:77); "And among them are those who say: Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire" (2:201); "Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good" (7:56); "And your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing" (13:6); "Your Lord is of all-encompassing mercy, but His punishment cannot be warded off from the criminal people" (6:147); "Say: Indeed, I am God's servant; He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet" (cf. 19:30) [Study Quran] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** Moses's prayer here is the widest ask in the sūrah — good in both worlds, on the strength of repentance alone — and the answer's shape is instructive: God begins with the punishment before the mercy. The order is the answer to the plea, because the plea was made by people who had just watched seventy of their elders die [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran]. What the verse then does is define the mercy's address: not the claim of Iblīs, not the confident self-identification of communities that read their own virtue in the verse, but the fear, the almsgiving, and the belief in the signs [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the commentators' insistence that the mercy is nevertheless universal in its first meaning — that even the rebel is given his existence and his provision by it — keeps the passage from becoming a narrow ledger: the special mercy is written for the described, while the general mercy is what holds the described and the undescribed alike in being [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

## 7:157

*"Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in the Torah and the Gospel among them, who commands them to do right and forbids them from wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the vile, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. And those who believe in him and honor him and help him and follow the light which has been sent down with him — it is they who are successful."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the identification: this statement is God's clarification that those for whom Moses was promised the mercy He described — "and My mercy encompasses all things" — are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, because no messenger of God is described by this attribute — "the unlettered" — other than our Prophet ﷺ; and the reports from the exegetes bear it out: Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, al-Suddī and Qatāda all said "the community of Muhammad ﷺ," and Saʿīd added that Moses said, "Would that I had been created in the community of Muhammad!" He then transmits the report of Nūf al-Ḥimyarī: when Moses chose seventy men of his people for the appointment of his Lord, God said to Moses, "I shall make the earth a mosque and a purification for you, and I shall place the *sakīnah* with you in your houses, and I shall make you recite the Torah from the backs of your hearts — the man among you and the woman, the free and the slave, the young and the old." Moses said to his people, "God will make the earth a purification and a mosque for you"; they said, "We do not wish to pray anywhere but in the churches!" He said, "And He will place the *sakīnah* with you in your houses"; they said, "We want it only as it was, in the ark!" He said, "And He will make you recite the Torah from the backs of your hearts"; they said, "We want to read it only by sight!" So God said, "I shall write it for those who fear and give the zakāt and those who believe in Our signs" — up to "those are the successful" — that is, for those who follow the unlettered Messenger. And Moses said, "My Lord, make me their prophet!" and God said, "Their prophet is from among them." Moses said, "My Lord, make me one of them!" and God said, "You will never attain them." Moses said, "My Lord, I came to You with the delegation of the Children of Israel, and You have made our delegation for others!" — and God sent down, "And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:159), and Moses was satisfied. Nūf said: so praise God, who preserved your absence and took your share for you and made the delegation of the Children of Israel yours [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. Then on the description itself: "whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel" — the pronoun refers to the Messenger; the reports say they find his description, his command and his prophethood written. And Ṭabarī transmits the report of ʿAṭāʾ b. Yasār: he met ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ and asked him to tell him the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the Torah; and he said, "Yes, by God — he is described in the Torah just as he is described in the Qurʾān: 'O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, and a refuge for the unlettered; you are My servant and My messenger; I have named you the One who relies [on God]; not harsh or crude, nor loud in the marketplaces, not repaying evil with evil, but pardoning and forgiving; and God will not take him until through him He straightens the crooked religion, so that they say, "There is no god but God"; through him He opens blind hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes.'" ʿAṭāʾ said: then I met Kaʿb and asked him the same, and the two did not differ by a letter, except that Kaʿb said it in his own dialect [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī]. Then the verse's clauses: "he commands them the right" — faith in God and adherence to His obedience in what He commanded and forbade, that being the "right"; "and forbids them the wrong" — association with God and the things God forbade; "and makes lawful for them the good things," which is what the *jāhiliyyah* had forbidden of the *baḥīrah*, the *sāʾibah*, the *waṣīlah* and the *ḥāmī*; "and forbids them the vile," which is the flesh of swine, usury, and what they had made lawful of foods and drinks that God forbade, as Ibn ʿAbbās said; and "he relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them" — and on the *iṣr* the exegetes differed: some said it is the covenant and the pledge God had taken from the Children of Israel to act by what is in the Torah, as al-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the verse in ten questions. He transmits Nūf's report as above and draws from it the verse's central exclusion: these expressions removed the Jews and the Christians from the partnership that appeared in "I shall write it for those who fear," and the promise was settled for the community of Muhammad ﷺ, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. Jubayr and others said. "Those who follow" means in his law and religion and what he brought. And he gives the technical distinction between *rasūl* and *nabī*: the messenger is more specific than the prophet; the word "messenger" was placed first out of concern for the meaning of messengership, though prophethood is logically prior; and this is why the Messenger of God ﷺ corrected al-Barāʾ when he said in the prayer, "and by Your messenger whom You sent," telling him, "Say: I believe in Your prophet whom You sent" — a report in the Ṣaḥīḥ. And on *ummī*: Al-Naḥḥās, and before him Ibn ʿUzayz, hold that he is called *ummī* by relation to the unlettered community that remains on its original birth, not learning writing or reading; Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Your prophet was unlettered: he did not write, nor read, nor calculate," and cited 29:48, "you did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand"; and in the Ṣaḥīḥ from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said, "We are an unlettered community: we do not write and we do not calculate." And al-Naḥḥās also reports the view that he is called *ummī* by relation to Makkah, the mother of the towns [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the identification and then the stories that anchor it: this is the description of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the Books of the prophets — they delivered the good news of his advent to their nations and commanded them to follow him, and his descriptions were still apparent in their books, as the rabbis and the priests well know. He transmits the report of Abū Ṣakhr al-ʿUqaylī about the bedouin who brought a milk-camel to Madinah in the Prophet's lifetime and followed him until they passed a Jewish man reading from an open copy of the Torah beside his dying son: the Prophet ﷺ asked him, "I adjure you by the One who sent down the Torah: do you not find my description and my advent in your book?" and he shook his head in denial; but the boy said, "Rather yes, by the One who sent down the Torah! We find your description and your advent in our book, and I bear witness that there is no deity but God and that you are the Messenger of God" — and the Prophet ﷺ told his companions, "Take the Jew away from your brother," and personally took charge of the boy's funeral and prayed over him; a report he grades sound and notes is supported by a similar tradition from Anas. Then ʿAṭāʾ b. Yasār's report from ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAmr, recorded by al-Bukhārī, with the Torah description — and Kaʿb's matching testimony [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the theology of the verse: part of perfect faith in God's signs is knowing their meaning and acting on their requirements, and among that is following the Prophet ﷺ outwardly and inwardly in the fundamentals of religion and its branches. "Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet" — the qualification distinguishes him from the other prophets; the intended one is Muhammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and the context concerns the state of the Children of Israel and that faith in Muhammad ﷺ is a condition of their entering into faith; and the believers in him who follow him are the people of the absolute mercy God wrote for them. He is described as *ummī* because he is from the unlettered Arab community that neither reads nor writes and had no book before the Qurʾān. "Whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel" — by his name and his description, the greatest and most glorious of which is what he calls to and forbids. "He commands them the right" — everything whose goodness, soundness and benefit are known; "and forbids them the wrong" — everything whose ugliness is known in reason and in nature: he commands prayer, zakāt, fasting, pilgrimage, ties of kinship, kindness to parents, kindness to the neighbor and the slave, giving benefit to all creatures, truthfulness, chastity, righteousness and sincere counsel, and forbids association with God, the taking of life without right, fornication, intoxicants, injustice to creatures, lying and wickedness. And the greatest proof that he is the Messenger of God is what he called to, commanded, forbade, made lawful and made unlawful; for he makes lawful the good things — of foods, drinks and marriages — and forbids them the vile — of foods, drinks, marriages, sayings and deeds. "And he lays down their burden and the shackles that were upon them" — of his description is that his religion is easy, generous, facilitated, with no burden and no shackles and no hardship and no heavy obligations. "So those who believe in him and honor him" — magnify and revere him — "and help him, and follow the light which has been sent down with him" — the Qurʾān, by which one is given light in the darkness of doubt and ignorance and by which one is guided when the opinions conflict — "those are the successful," those who have attained the good of this world and the Hereafter and are safe from their evil, because they have brought the greatest of the causes of success; and as for those who do not believe in this unlettered prophet, honor him and help him and follow the light sent down with him — those are the losers [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** supplies the comparative scriptural material: the verse describes the Prophet with some of the same qualities attributed to him in the Torah — a giver of glad tidings and a warner, not doing evil to those who do evil, kind and forgiving, not rude or loud in the marketplace, a guardian for the unlettered, here probably referring to the Arabs; the ḥadīth goes on to say that he will cause even those who are astray to utter "there is no god but God," and hence open eyes, ears and hearts (al-Qurṭubī, Ṭabarī). Some commentators mention particular statements in the Torah and Gospel interpreted by Muslims as references to the coming of the Prophet Muhammad, including prophecies about the descendants of Ishmael in Genesis 16–17 and Jesus's reference to a spiritual "comforter," the "Paraclete" (*Fāraqlīṭ*, understood to mean Aḥmad), who would come after him and "will speak whatever he hears" (John 16:7–14). The Prophet enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong — a moral requirement and characteristic of every believer and of the believing community (3:110, 114; 9:67, 71; 22:41; 31:17); he makes good things lawful, meaning that the ritualistic restrictions the pagan Arabs had placed on themselves without divine sanction were abolished; he forbids bad things, such as the consumption of swine flesh and the practice of usury. He relieves them, in this case the Jews, of their burden and the shackles, referring to some of the difficult and onerous commands and prohibitions in the Torah, which the Jews were specifically obligated to follow as part of the covenant they made with God, but which were abrogated by the Qurʾān; in this regard the commentators mention a prohibition against taking spoils in warfare in earlier scriptures, as well as certain dietary restrictions; see also 3:50, where Jesus confirms the Torah but makes lawful part of what was forbidden; and the light sent down with him refers to the Qurʾān [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** presses the point about the epithet: "the Messenger, the unlettered prophet" mentions three qualities, and *ummī* signifies a person who does not know the art of reading and writing; the Qurʾān has referred to the Arabs as *ummiyyīn* because they generally had very little to do with reading and writing. Being incapable of reading and writing is obviously not a quality in itself — it is an indication of imperfection — yet the same sign of imperfection came to serve the Prophet ﷺ as a sign of his perfection of the highest degree, given the unparalleled erudition and exemplary wisdom he preached and demonstrated: a demonstration of perfect wisdom by a man of letters is considered the fruit of his education, but when such attributes come out of a personality who did not know how to read and write, it is as bright a miracle as daylight. He then makes the argument about the Torah and the Gospel: the verse did not say they would find his attributes or indications written in the Books; it said they would find *him* written in their revelations — an implicit indication that the descriptions were so expressive and detailed that reading them was like seeing him; and that the Jews and Christians of the Prophet's time never used this Qurʾānic claim against him is itself a witness that their books contained transparent references to him. He reports al-Bayhaqī's version in *Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah*: the Jewish boy in the Prophet's service who was sick, and the Prophet's ﷺ visit and his adjuration of the father reading the Torah at the boy's bedside, and the boy's declaration, after which the Prophet ﷺ bade the Companions perform his funeral rites [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sense of the clauses: those who follow the Messenger, the uninstructed Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, whom they will find inscribed in their Torah and Gospel in name and description, enjoining them to decency and forbidding them indecency, making lawful for them the good things which had been forbidden to them by their law, and making unlawful for them the vile things such as carrion and the like, and relieving them of their burden — their onus — and the shackles — the hardships they used to bear, such as the requirement to kill oneself as repentance and the severing of the part that had come into contact with any impurity; then those who believe in him, honor and revere him and help him and follow the light revealed with him — namely the Qurʾān — they are the ones who will prosper [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Ummī* is the verse's most discussed word, and the exegetes give its three senses: one who neither reads nor writes, from the unlettered community (*ummah*) that remains on its original birth; one related to Makkah, *Umm al-Qurā*, the mother of the towns; and, on the reading **[Maʿārif]** presses, a mark of imperfection that becomes the setting for the miracle [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. *Iṣr* is the burden — a weight that ties, from the root of binding — and the exegetes read it as the covenant itself or as the heavy obligations the Torah laid on Israel; *aghlāl* are the shackles or fetters, and the pair is used of the legal and moral constraints the new dispensation removes [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran] [Jalālayn]. The clause "he commands them the right and forbids them the wrong" uses *al-maʿrūf* and *al-munkar* — the known-good and the known-evil — terms the verse grounds in reason and nature as much as in revelation, which is why **[Saʿdī]** can itemize them with examples that any conscience recognizes [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And *al-nūr* — the light sent down with him — is identified by the commentators as the Qurʾān, the light by which the darkness of doubt is navigated [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The verse carries three principal traditions. The Torah description in the report of ʿAṭāʾ b. Yasār from ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, recorded by al-Bukhārī, with Kaʿb's matching testimony and the characteristic clauses: not harsh or crude, not loud in the markets, not repaying evil with evil, forgiving and pardoning, named *al-Mutawakkil*, sent to open blind hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. The report of the dying Jewish boy in Madinah who confirmed the Prophet's description in the Torah and became a Muslim, whose funeral the Prophet ﷺ himself attended — graded sound by **[Ibn Kathīr]**; and al-Bayhaqī's version narrated by **[Maʿārif]** [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. And the report of al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib in the Ṣaḥīḥ: the Prophet ﷺ correcting the phrase "by Your messenger whom You sent" to "by Your prophet whom You sent," which **[Qurṭubī]** uses for the distinction between the two titles [Qurṭubī].

**Rulings.** Two things the commentators establish. First, the identity of the promised mercy: by the consensus of the exegetes reported here, "those who follow the unlettered Messenger" are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, and the verse is the condition that settles who inherits the prayer of 7:156 — faith in the last Prophet being the door [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. Second, the character of the law the verse describes: **[Study Quran]** notes that the abolition of self-imposed pagan restrictions, the forbidding of swine flesh and usury, and the removal of the heavy burdens of earlier legislation are the verse's marks of the new dispensation; and **[Saʿdī]** states the principle that the greatest proof of prophethood is the content of what the Prophet ﷺ commanded and prohibited, made lawful and made unlawful [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel" (7:157, the verse itself); "And I will follow the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" (cf. 12:38); "Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves" (48:29, on his description in the Gospel); "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds" (21:107); "Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all" (7:158, the next verse); "You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand" (29:48); "And Jesus said: O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving glad tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Aḥmad" (61:6) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Reflection.** The verse is the hinge of the passage: the mercy that Moses asked for is here assigned its recipients, and they turn out to be a community not yet in existence when he prayed [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. The reports that Moses asked to be made their prophet and was told he would never attain them, and then was comforted by the promise of a community of his own people who would guide by the truth, give the scene its poignancy — the prophet who interceded for a people he would not live among [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the verse's own description is a portrait rather than a proof-text: a messenger who commands the known-good and forbids the known-evil, who makes the wholesome lawful and the foul unlawful, and who lifts burdens rather than adding them — which is why the tradition read the verse as the charter of the law's ease, and why **[Saʿdī]** could call the content of his command the strongest evidence of his mission [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

## 7:158

*"Say, 'O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all — He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no god but He; He gives life and causes death. So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him, that you may be guided.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the occasion and the scope: God says to His prophet Muhammad ﷺ, "Say, O Muhammad, to all people: I am the Messenger of God to you all" — not to some of you to the exclusion of others, as the messengers before me were sent to some people and not others; and whoever of them was sent in that way, my message is not to some of you to the exclusion of others but to all of you. And "He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth" is a description of God — the One who has the authority of the heavens and the earth and what is in them, and their governance and disposal; "there is no god but He" means that divinity and worship belong only to Him, not to any of the rivals and idols, since He alone has authority over everything and power to create whatever He wills and to give it life and annihilate it when He wills its death; "so believe in God and His messenger" — affirm the signs of God, who is of this description, and acknowledge His oneness, and affirm of His messenger Muhammad ﷺ that he is sent to His creation, calling them to His oneness and obedience. Then the clause "who believes in God and His words": the exegetes differed — some said "His words" means His signs, as Qatāda said; others said it means Jesus son of Mary, as Mujāhid and al-Suddī said. And Ṭabarī gives his own preference: God commanded His servants to affirm the prophethood of the unlettered Prophet who believes in God and His words, and did not specify some of God's words to the exclusion of others, but told them of all the words; so the right reading is the general one, for the Messenger of God ﷺ believed in all of God's words, as the apparent sense of God's book requires. And "follow him that you may be guided" — follow him and act by what he commanded of God's obedience; "that you may be guided," that is, so that you may be rightly guided and hit the truth in your following of him [Ṭabarī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws out the universal mission: "O mankind" is addressed to mankind red and black, Arab and non-Arab alike; the verse mentions the Prophet's honor and greatness, for he is the final prophet sent to all mankind and the jinn; and he cites the supporting verses: 6:19, "this Qurʾān has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whomsoever it may reach"; 11:17; 3:20, "and say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: have you submitted?" — and notes that there are many other verses and more hadiths than can be counted on the subject. He then records the Bukhārī ḥadīth of Abū al-Dardāʾ: Abū Bakr and ʿUmar had an argument in which Abū Bakr angered ʿUmar; ʿUmar went away angry and Abū Bakr followed asking forgiveness, and ʿUmar refused and shut the door in his face; Abū Bakr came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said, "This fellow of yours has angered someone"; ʿUmar became sorry and came and greeted him and sat next to him and told him what had happened, and the Messenger of God ﷺ became angry, so Abū Bakr said, "O Messenger of God, it was I who was unjust"; and the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Will you leave my companion alone? I said, 'O people, I am the Messenger of God to you all,' and you said, 'You lie,' but Abū Bakr said, 'You have spoken the truth.'" And he records the Musnad ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās on the five distinctions given to the Prophet ﷺ: sent to all mankind, black and white; made victorious by dread at a month's distance; spoils made lawful for him and not for those before him; the earth made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification; and given intercession, which he saved for his community on the Day of Resurrection — a chain he grades suitable though the two Ṣaḥīḥs did not record it; and he notes that the verse's description of God as the One who gives life and causes death corresponds to the divine names al-Muḥyī and al-Mumīt [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** explains why the verse comes here and what its universality means: when the Prophet ﷺ called the people of the Torah from the Children of Israel to follow him, someone might have supposed that the ruling was limited to them, so God brought what indicates universality — "Say, O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all," that is, Arab and non-Arab, the People of the Book among you and others; "He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth," disposing of the two by His cosmic decrees and His sovereign governance and by His legal and religious rulings, among which is that He sent to you a great messenger calling you to God and to the abode of His honor and warning you against everything that distances you from Him and from the abode of His honor; "there is no god but He" — no object of worship in truth except God alone, without partner, and His worship is known only by the way of His messengers; "He gives life and causes death" — among His dispositions are life-giving and death, in which no one shares with Him, and God has made death a bridge and a crossing by which one passes to the abode of permanence, so that whoever believes in it will certainly affirm His messenger Muhammad ﷺ. "So believe in God and His messenger, the unlettered prophet" — a faith of the heart comprising the acts of the heart and the limbs — "who believes in God and His words," that is, believe in this messenger who is upright in his beliefs and his deeds — "and follow him, that you may be guided" in your religious and worldly interests; for if you do not follow him, you will go far astray [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** notes the structure: here the Qurʾān interrupts the account of Moses and his people to issue a command to the Prophet to identify himself as the Messenger of God to all; this statement, situated at the end of a series of accounts about previous prophets, is understood by some commentators to mean that the Prophet Muhammad is distinguished from earlier prophets in that each of those was a prophet to his people or his region, while Muhammad is a prophet for all of humanity (al-Rāzī, Ṭabarī); and in a ḥadīth the Prophet states that his having been sent to all humanity is one of five distinctions given specifically to him (Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabarī). It notes the qualification: the claim of such a distinction may be based on the fact that the Prophet's mission was to both the People of the Book and the "unlettered" (3:20); and while the universality of his mission is supported by verses describing the Qurʾān or the Prophet as a reminder for the worlds (6:90; 12:104; 38:87; 68:52; 81:27), the assertion that he was completely unique in this regard does not seem entirely consistent with verses that describe the Book brought by Moses as a guidance for mankind (6:91) or describe Jesus, Mary and Noah as a sign for the worlds (21:91; 29:15), and Adam could also be described as a prophet for all human beings (al-Rāzī). On "His words": all of God's signs (Ṭabarī), or the three Abrahamic scriptures — the Torah, the Gospel and the Qurʾān (al-Qurṭubī) — and by implication all sacred scriptures; and according to some reports "His Words" refers specifically to Jesus, the prophet who most closely precedes Muhammad and who is referred to as a Word from God (3:45), though such an interpretation seems less plausible in this context [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** reads the verse as a statement of one of the fundamental tenets of Islam: the Prophet ﷺ has been sent as God's Messenger to the entire mankind and to the jinn coming into being up to the Day of Judgment; the verse commands him to make a general declaration that he has been sent to all the people of the world, and that his prophethood was not limited to a particular people and place as was the case with earlier prophets, who came to a particular people and place for a limited period. He draws the inference: the fact that the Prophet ﷺ was sent at the end of all prophets is an obvious reason behind the Islamic belief in the finality of prophethood — his being the last of all prophets and coming for the guidance of all people of all future times leaves no room for another prophet; and the same fact explains a characteristic quality of the Muslim community, that there shall always be a group among them defying the anti-Islamic forces and correcting false interpretations of the Qurʾān and the Sunnah, favored by God with special help — these being the real inheritors of the prophetic mission after the Prophet ﷺ. Then he cites Ibn Kathīr's citation of the Musnad report on the five distinctions at Tabuk, and notes that according to some authentic traditions Jesus will follow the law of the Prophet ﷺ after his descent in the last age, and 6:19's "to warn you and whomsoever it may reach" [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the verse briefly: it is mentioned that Moses and Jesus gave glad tidings of him, and then God commanded him to say it himself — "I am the Messenger of God to you all"; and "His words" are God's words, His books: the Torah, the Gospel and the Qurʾān [Qurṭubī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: say, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, "O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all," the Messenger of Him to whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and of the earth; there is no god but Him; He gives life and makes to die; believe then in God and His Messenger, the uninstructed Prophet who believes in God and His words, the Qurʾān, and follow him so that you may be guided aright [Jalālayn].

**Language.** The verse's grammar is a single long title: "Say, O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all — He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth." **[Ṭabarī]** parses it as an appositive on the name of God: "I am the Messenger of God, who has the dominion of the heavens and the earth, to you" [Ṭabarī]. *Jamīʿan* — "all" — is the word on which the verse's universality turns, and **[Maʿārif]** reads it against the pattern of the earlier prophets' regional missions [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. And "who believes in God and His words" (*yuʾminu bi-llāhi wa-kalimātihi*) is a description of the messenger rather than of the audience, which the exegetes note as a mark of his status: the one sent is himself a believer, first among the believers in the One who sent him [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Two traditions the commentators carry here. The Bukhārī report of the quarrel between Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, with the Prophet's ﷺ words — "I said, O people, I am the Messenger of God to you all, and you said, 'You lie,' but Abū Bakr said, 'You have spoken the truth'" — which shows the verse being claimed by the Prophet ﷺ as the credential of the first believer [Ibn Kathīr]. And the report of the five distinctions, in Aḥmad's *Musnad* from Ibn ʿAbbās and cited by **[Maʿārif]** through Ibn Kathīr: sent to all mankind black and white; victory by dread; lawful spoils; the earth as a mosque and a purification; and intercession reserved for the community [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

**Rulings.** The verse grounds two standing rulings. First, the universality of the mission and, from it, the finality of prophethood — the argument **[Maʿārif]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** both state: a messenger sent to all people of all times leaves no room for another prophet, and the earlier prophets' regional limitation stands as the contrast [Maʿārif] [Ibn Kathīr]. Second, the identification of "His words" — **[Ṭabarī]**'s preference for the general sense, all of God's words, over the restriction to a single referent, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s identification with the three scriptures, belong to the verse's role in defining what the messenger himself believed, and therefore what his followers are to believe about revelation [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all" (7:158, the verse itself); "And We have not sent you except to all mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner" (34:28); "Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds" (25:1); "And this Qurʾān has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whomsoever it may reach" (6:19); "Say: O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you" (22:49); "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds" (21:107) [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran].

**Reflection.** The verse's placement is its argument. It comes at the end of a long account of Moses and the Children of Israel, at the precise point where the mercy Moses asked for has been assigned to a community that did not yet exist, and it has God command the last prophet to announce himself — to the whole of mankind, with the divine names of sovereignty, oneness, life and death as his credentials [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. The commentators notice the interruption of the narrative and treat it as deliberate: the story of Moses is the setting in which the universality of the final message is declared, and the Quran is telling its reader that the mercy written for the followers of the unlettered prophet is not confined to the people who first heard the promise [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. What the verse asks of its hearer is stated in its last two verbs: believe, and follow — with the note that guidance is the outcome promised to the following rather than to the believing alone [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn].

## 7:159

*"And among the people of Moses there is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense plainly: among the people of Moses — meaning the Children of Israel — there is a *ummah*, that is, a group, who guide by the truth: they are guided by the truth, stand straight upon it and act by it; and "by it they do justice": by the truth they give and take and are fair, so that they do not swerve. He then records what was said about the identity of this community. Al-Suddī, through a chain from ʿIkrima b. ʿAyyāsh from Ṣadaqa Abū al-Hudhayl: a people between you and them is a river of honey — a report whose chain the editor of the printed text examines and finds weak, noting that such reports are not to be taken without decisive proof. And Ibn Jurayj: when the Children of Israel killed their prophets they disbelieved, and they were twelve tribes; one tribe absolved itself of what the others had done, apologized, and asked God to separate them from them; so God opened a tunnel for them in the earth and they traveled in it until they came out beyond China, and they are there, *ḥanīfs*, Muslims, facing our qiblah; and Ibn Jurayj said ʿIkrima said Ibn ʿAbbās cited as their verse, "And We said after him to the Children of Israel: dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you as a mixed crowd" (17:104) — and the promise of the Hereafter is Jesus son of Mary, with whom they will come out — and Ibn ʿAbbās said they traveled in the tunnel a year and a half [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the verse as the description: they call people to guidance, and "they do justice" has to do with judgment. And in the tafsīr tradition: these are a people beyond China, beyond the river of sand, who worship God with truth and justice, who believed in Muhammad ﷺ and abandoned the Sabbath, facing our qiblah; no one of them reaches us and no one of us reaches them. He reports the tradition that when disagreement fell after Moses there was among them a community who guided by the truth, but they could not remain amid the Children of Israel, so God brought them out to a side of His earth in isolation from creation, and there was a tunnel in the earth for them, and they walked in it a year and a half until they came out beyond China, and they are upon the truth until now, with a sea between them and the rest so that none can reach them; and that Gabriel took the Prophet ﷺ to them on the night of the Ascension and they believed in him and he taught them sūrahs of the Qurʾān, and asked them: do you have a measure and a balance? They said no. So how do you live? They said: we go out to the wilderness and sow, and when we harvest we put the produce there, and whoever of us needs something takes what he needs. He asked: where are your women? They said: in a quarter apart from us, and whoever needs his wife goes to her when the need arises. He asked: does any of you lie in his speech? They said: if anyone of us did that, a flame would seize him — the fire comes down and burns him. He asked: why are your houses all equal? They said: so that none of us should exalt himself over another. He asked: why are your graves at your doors? They said: so that we should not forget death. Then when the Messenger of God ﷺ returned to this world on the night of the Ascension, there was revealed to him, "And among those We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:181) — meaning the community of Muhammad ﷺ, informing him that what He gave Moses among his people He had given him among his own. And other views: they are those who believed in our prophet Muhammad ﷺ from the People of the Book; or a people of the Children of Israel who held to the law of Moses before its abrogation, did not alter and did not kill the prophets [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the verse as the statement of exception within Israel: of the Children of Israel there are some who follow the truth and judge by it, and he cites 3:113, "A party of the people of the Scripture stand for the right, they recite the verses of God during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves"; 3:199, on those among the People of the Scripture who believe in God and in what was revealed to you and to them, humbling themselves before God, not selling the verses of God for a small price; 28:52–54, on those who were given the Scripture before and believe in it, saying, "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord; indeed we were, even before it, of those who submit," who will be given their reward twice over; and 17:107–109, on those given knowledge before it falling on their faces in prostration and weeping, and it increasing them in humility [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the verse's function and its meaning: they guide people by the truth in their teaching of them and in their fatwas, and they do justice by it among them in judging their cases — as God says elsewhere, "And We made them leaders, guiding by Our command, when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs" (32:24). And he notes why the verse comes where it does: in this there is a virtue for the community of Moses, that God made among them guides who guide by His command; and the coming of this noble verse contains a kind of exception to what preceded, since God had mentioned a set of the faults of the Children of Israel that contradict perfection and nullify guidance — and someone might think this covered all of them — so God mentions that among them is a group upright, guiding and guided [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** lays out the disagreement fully: commentators differed regarding the identity of the community among the followers of Moses that guides by the truth and does justice, that is, renders judgment according to the principles of truth; see also 7:181, where the same description is given to a community among those We have created. Despite the clear statement that among the people of Moses — the Jews — are those who are just and rightly guided, commentators have often sought to limit the application: according to legendary accounts, the community refers to a group or tribe of Israelites who separated themselves from the rest when the latter began to go astray and traveled eastward beyond China; some say they continue to live according to the law brought by Moses, others that they became Muslims; and still others assert this refers to those Jews in Madinah in the Prophet's time who became Muslims, although this seems inconsistent with the verse's description of this group as a community (*ummah*), which often connotes an independent religious community or at least a sizable group, and Jews who became Muslim were thereafter considered part of the Muslim community rather than a separate one. **[Study Quran]** then gives its own judgment: these various attempts to qualify the reference to this righteous community among the people of Moses contradict the plain sense of the verse, which indicates that a group among the people of Moses, in the sense of being followers of Jewish law and ritual, continue to live and worship righteously according to the teachings of the Torah; other verses support the literal reading, including 7:168, which indicates that there were communities of righteous Jews still existing at the time of the revelation of the Qurʾān (see also 3:113–15, 199); and the commentators do not usually support the most literal and obvious meaning, perhaps because it seems inconsistent with the common interpretation of 7:157 as meaning that all human beings should recognize and follow Muhammad as their prophet [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the plain meaning and then asks who is referred to: this refers to the people who faithfully followed the commandments of the Torah and the Gospel at the time they were revealed, and those who readily accepted Islam after the appearance of the Prophet ﷺ according to the predictions contained in them; and the Qurʾān has referred to this group in commendable terms in a number of verses, which he cites (3:113; 28:52). He then reports the narrative found in the commentaries of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Kathīr about the group of Israelites who despised the corrupt practices of their tribesmen and prayed for a separate land, and whom God carried to a land in the Far East to practice the original faith; and the further report that in the Prophet's time they were given the opportunity to embrace Islam on his hands, when Gabriel took him to them on the night of the Ascension, and they accepted the faith and he taught them sūrahs. He gives the dialogue about measures, cultivation, lies punished by heavenly fire, equal houses and graves at the doors, and then notes: al-Qurṭubī has narrated this event along with other suggestions and has remarked that this narrative was not authentic; Ibn Kathīr, however, has termed it an unusual event but did not reject it. And he concludes: in short, this verse makes clear that there has always been a group among the Israelites who followed the truth — be they the people described, or the ones who embraced Islam after the appearance of the Prophet ﷺ [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse in a line: and among the people of Moses there is a community, a group, who guide people by the truth and act justly according to it when passing judgments [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Ummah* here carries its sense of a distinct body of people — a community within a community — which is why **[Study Quran]** uses the term to criticize the reading that reduces the verse to a handful of converts: an *ummah* implies a body with its own religious life [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī]. *Yahdūna bi-l-ḥaqq* — they guide by the truth — is transitive, which the exegetes note: they are not merely guided but guides, teaching and giving fatwas and judgments [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. And *yaʿdilūn* — they do justice — is the root of equity, and the verse places it in the context of giving and taking and of judging, so that the community described is defined by its administration of justice among itself as much as by its doctrine [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The tunnel-and-China tradition comes through Ibn Jurayj from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās (Ṭabarī) and is given at length by **[Qurṭubī]**, including the night of the Ascension visit and the dialogue; **[Maʿārif]** records that al-Qurṭubī himself noted the narrative is not authentic and that Ibn Kathīr called it unusual without rejecting it — a judgment the reader should carry when using it *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif].

**Rulings.** The verse's exegetical significance is its function as the exception clause of the sūrah: **[Saʿdī]** states it explicitly — God had enumerated the faults of the Children of Israel, and one might have supposed the condemnation covered all of them, so the verse names a group who are upright, guiding and guided [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. And **[Study Quran]**'s methodological point is worth recording as a ruling of interpretation: the commentators' effort to explain the verse away, in the interest of making 7:157 universal, is precisely what the verse's plain sense resists; the two verses stand together — a community among the people of Moses who guide by the truth, and the command to all mankind to follow the unlettered prophet [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And among those We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:181); "Among the People of the Book is a community standing for the right, reciting the verses of God during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves" (3:113); "And among the People of the Book is he who, if you entrust him with a great amount, will return it to you" (cf. 3:75); "And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture those who believe in God and in that which has been revealed to you and in that which has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before God" (3:199); "Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it — they believe in it" (28:52); "And We made them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs" (32:24) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The verse does for the Children of Israel what 7:181 will do for humanity in general, and its placement is the moral of the sūrah's long account: after the calf, the demand for sight, the earthquake and the exceptions and the revivals, the text refuses to let the condemnation swallow the people. There is a community among them that guides by the truth and does justice — and the tradition's inability to leave the plain sense alone, the tunnels and the far countries and the emigration, is itself testimony to how uncomfortable that plain sense has been [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. The most defensible reading, and the one **[Maʿārif]** ends with, is the simplest: at every stage of Israel's history there were those who held to the truth of their own revelation and judged by it, and the verse names them so that the verdict on the many is not the verdict on the whole [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī].

## 7:160

*"And We divided them into twelve tribes, communities. And We inspired Moses, when his people asked him for water: 'Strike the rock with your staff.' Then there gushed forth from it twelve springs; each people knew its drinking place. And We shaded them with the clouds and sent down upon them the manna and the quails: 'Eat of the good things We have provided you.' And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the division as the arrangement of the people: "We divided them" — We separated the people of Moses of the Children of Israel and made them distinct tribes, twelve tribes — and he gives the grammarians' dispute over the feminine "twelve" with the masculine "tribes": the Baṣran grammarians said the intended word was "twelve bands" (*firaq*), and the word "tribes" was the predicate, the number not being made to agree with it; others held the number must follow the word it governs; the Kūfans said the feminine came because the speech turned to "communities" (*umam*), the feminine being preferred, as in the poet's line "and indeed Kilāb are ten stomachs, and you are free of their ten tribes," where "stomach" was taken in the sense of tribe and clan; and Ṭabarī's own preference is that "twelve" is feminine because of the implied feminine "pieces" — the meaning being "We cut them into pieces, twelve," and then he interpreted the "pieces" as "tribes," and it is not permissible for "tribes" to be the explicative noun of "twelve," since with numbers from eleven to nineteen the explicative is singular, not plural, as one says "I have twelve women" and not "twelve wives." And "communities" means groups, and the *sibṭ* among the Children of Israel is like the *qarn* elsewhere; and it was said they were divided into tribes because of their differences in religion. Then the water: God says that when He had divided the Children of Israel into twelve companies and had made them wander in the wilderness, they asked Moses for water out of thirst and the sinking of the wells; and God revealed to him, "Strike the rock with your staff" — and it poured and burst out from the rock with twelve springs of water; "each people knew their drinking place," no tribe entering upon another's; "and We shaded them with the clouds," covering them from the heat of the sun and its harm; and "We sent down upon them the manna and the quails" as food for them; and "eat of the good things We have provided you," that is, We said to them: eat of the lawful that We have provided you and made good for you. And "they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves": there is an omitted clause in the speech, left out because the apparent sense dispenses with it — namely, that they found it distasteful and said, "We will not patiently endure one food," and asked to exchange the better for the worse; "they did not wrong Us" means they brought no deficiency into God's dominion and authority by their request and their deed; "but they were wronging themselves," that is, diminishing their own shares by exchanging the lower for the better and the worse for the more excellent [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the division as a favor and a convenience: God numbered His blessings to the Children of Israel; and He made them tribes so that each tribe's affair should be known through its leader, and the matter should be light upon Moses; and he cites 5:12, "and We raised among them twelve chieftains." On the grammar, the feminine "twelve" with the masculine "tribe" — al-Farrāʾ said it is permissible to say "twelve" with the masculine, and the feminine was carried to "communities"; and al-Zajjāj said the meaning is "We cut them into twelve companies," "tribes" being an apposition and "communities" a description of the tribes. He notes the reading of al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim with the verb lightened, and the lexical note that the *asbāṭ* in the children of Isaac are like the tribes in the children of Ishmael, and that *sabaṭ* is a plant that camels feed on. And he closes the passage with the report of Maʿmar from Hammām b. Munabbih from Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the substitution "a grain in a hair" and the entry of the gate dragging on their buttocks — a report that belongs to the following verses [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the verse with a note on the differences of placement: these verses were discussed in Sūrat al-Baqarah, which was revealed in Madinah, while these were revealed in Makkah, and the difference between the two narrations has been mentioned there, so there is no need to repeat it [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the whole verse as a catalogue of completed favors: "We divided them into twelve tribes, communities" — twelve familiar tribes, mutually allied, each of the sons of Jacob a tribe; "and We inspired Moses, when his people asked him for water" — they asked him to pray to God to give them water to drink and for their livestock, since they were, as God knows best, in a place with little water; so God revealed to Moses, in answer to their request, "Strike the rock with your staff" — and it may be a specific rock and it may be a generic noun covering any rock — and he struck it, and there gushed out of it twelve springs flowing; "each people knew their drinking place" — the twelve springs were divided among the twelve tribes, one for each, and they knew it, and so they were secure and at ease and relieved of hardship and crowding: this too was of the completeness of God's favor to them. "And We shaded them with the clouds," which covered them from the heat of the sun; "and We sent down upon them the manna," which is the sweet, "and the quails," which is the flesh of a bird of the finest and most delicious kinds; so God combined for them shade, drink and wholesome food of sweets and meats in comfort and tranquility; and it was said to them: "Eat of the good things We have provided you." And "they did not wrong Us" — when they did not thank God and did not fulfill what God had made obligatory upon them; "but they were wronging themselves," in that they deprived themselves of every good and exposed themselves to evil and punishment. And this was during the period of their stay in the wilderness [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the parallels: cf. 2:57–60 for a similar account of these events; regarding the division into twelve tribes, see also 5:12, where God had made a covenant with the Children of Israel and raised among them twelve chieftains; for Moses's striking of the rock and the gushing forth of twelve streams, see 2:60; the Bible, in Exodus 15:27, mentions the Israelites coming upon a place in the desert called Elim where there were twelve wells, and Exodus 17:1–6 recounts Moses being instructed by God to strike a rock with his staff to produce water, although no mention is made of twelve springs specifically; and regarding God's shading the Israelites and providing them with manna and quails and the command to eat of the good things provided, see the nearly identical passage in 2:57, and also 20:80–81 — and the Qurʾān repeatedly exhorts people to eat the wholesome and lawful food provided by God, for other examples not exclusively addressed to the Israelites, see 2:168, 172; 6:141–42; 16:69, 114; 23:51; 67:15 [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** notes that the verses enumerate various favors Allah bestowed upon the Israelites and speak of their deviation from His commands resulting in a heavenly punishment for their transgression, and that the relevant details have already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sequence: "and We divided them, We separated, the Children of Israel into twelve tribes" — with the grammatical notes — "communities"; "and We revealed to Moses when his people asked him for water in the wilderness, saying, 'Strike the rock with your staff,' and he struck it, and there gushed forth from it twelve fountains equal to the number of the tribes, each people, each tribe among them, now knew their drinking place; and We made the cloud overshadow them in the wilderness from the heat of the sun; and We sent down to them manna and quails — which are respectively a type of citrus and the quail — and We said to them, 'Eat of the good things We have provided for you.' And they did not wrong Us but they wronged themselves" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** *Qaṭṭaʿnāhum* — We cut them into pieces — carries the verse's image of social architecture: the people are cut into twelve coherent bodies, and **[Study Quran]**'s note that the same root underlies the covenant's "twelve chieftains" (5:12) shows the political dimension of the favor [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī]. *Asbāṭ* is the plural of *sibṭ*, Israelite tribal unit, comparable to the Arab *qabīlah*; **[Qurṭubī]** adds the etymology from *sabaṭ*, a plant camels graze on [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Inbajasat* — gushed forth — is the verb of the springs bursting from the stone, distinct from the word used in al-Baqarah (2:60, *infajarat*), and both are read by the exegetes as the sudden opening of water where there was none [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]. *Mann* the exegetes identify as a sweet and *salwā* as the quail, and the pair stands in the tradition as the emblem of provision given freely and received with complaint [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn].

**Rulings.** The verse's closing clause became a standing principle of the tradition's anthropology: "they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves." **[Ṭabarī]** spells out the accounting — no deficiency entered God's dominion by their disobedience, but their own shares were diminished and exchanged, the lower taken for the better, the worse for the more excellent — and **[Saʿdī]** gives the general application: the one who disobeys deprives only himself [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And the provision material carries its own instruction: **[Study Quran]** notes that the Qurʾān's repeated command to eat the wholesome and lawful is not addressed to the Israelites alone, so that the passage's mercies are read as a pattern of the divine economy rather than as a tribal privilege [Study Quran] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And We shaded you with clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails: eat of the good things We have provided you; and they wronged Us not, but they were wronging themselves" (2:57); "And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff; then twelve springs gushed forth from it" (2:60); "And We made the clouds a shade over them, and sent down manna and quails upon them: eat of the good things We have provided you" (cf. 20:80–81); "Indeed, God made a covenant with the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains" (5:12); "O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy and made a covenant with you on the right side of the Mount, and sent down upon you the manna and the quails" (20:80) [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** The verse is the last of the great mercies recounted in this section, and it is told in the key of order: twelve tribes, twelve springs, each people at its own drinking place — the wilderness provided for with the precision of a household. The commentators note that the division was itself a mercy, since it made each group's affairs knowable through its leader and eased the burden on Moses [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. And then the turn the sūrah never omits: shade, sweet and meat, and a people who took them and complained — "they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves" [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī]. The bookkeeping of the sentence is the doctrine the reader is meant to carry out of the wilderness: God's dominion is not diminished by human disobedience, and the loss is entirely the wrongdoer's own [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].
## 7:161

*"And when it was said to them, 'Dwell in this city and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, "Ḥiṭṭah," and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins — We will increase the doers of good.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the recollection of a second failure of the people, placed alongside the first: God says to His prophet Muhammad ﷺ, "and remember also, O Muhammad, the error of these people's deed, and their opposition to their Lord, and their disobedience to their prophet Moses, and their substitution of the word they were commanded to say, when God said to them: 'Dwell in this city'" — and the city, he says, is the city of Bayt al-Maqdis. "And eat from it wherever you wish" — that is, from its fruits, grains and plants, from any place in it you wish; "and say, 'ḥiṭṭah'" — say: this act of ours is a *ḥiṭṭah* that removes our sins; "We will forgive you," your Lord will cover over the sins that have passed from you and pardon you, so that He will not take you to account for them; "We will increase the doers of good" among you — those who obey God — beyond what I have promised you of the forgiveness of sins [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the same in fuller detail: the city is Iliyā (Jerusalem), a city of many trees, abundant fruits and ample living, which is why God commanded them to eat from it wherever they wished; and when they entered the gate they were to say "ḥiṭṭah" — that is, "remove from us our sins and pardon us" — and to enter prostrating, that is, submissive to their Lord, humbled before His might, thankful for His favor. He notes that God combined the two things the servant needs: humility of body and the asking of forgiveness — "so He commanded them with submission and the requesting of pardon, and promised them in return for that the forgiveness of their sins and reward both immediate and deferred," as He said: "We will forgive you your sins — We will increase the doers of good," of the good of this world and of the Hereafter [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** renders the clauses with its usual brevity: "And mention when it was said to them 'Dwell in this city,' the Holy House of Jerusalem, 'and eat therein wherever you will, and say: our concern is for an exoneration, and enter the gate,' that is the gate of the city, 'prostrating' — a prostration that is actually a bow. 'We shall forgive' — read *naghfir*, or the passive *tughfar* — 'you your transgressions; We shall give more to those who are virtuous' through obedience, in terms of reward" [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Maʿārif]** both handle the verse by referral: this passage and its parallel in Sūrat al-Baqarah are the same event, and the detail — the city, the word, the gate, the manner of entering — was set out there; **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the note that the verses of al-Baqarah were revealed in Madinah while these were revealed in Makkah, and that the difference between the two narrations has been mentioned in its place, so there is no need to repeat it here [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]**, closing his treatment of the preceding verses, gives the same instruction for this passage: what belongs to this verse of meanings and rulings has already been set out in the commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah, and praise belongs to God [Qurṭubī].

**Language.** *Ḥiṭṭah* is a word the exegetes treat as a sentence compressed into a noun: it is from *ḥaṭṭa*, to put down or unload, and the early authorities glossed it as the prayer "remove from us our sins," or as the declaration that this act of ours is a putting-down of our burden [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn]. The verse's verbs of movement are also noted: they are to *enter* the gate *sujjadan* — prostrating or bowing in humility — so that the request for forgiveness is framed by bodily submission, the inward act carried by the outward one [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn]. And the promise carries a comparative: forgiveness for what has passed, and *ziyādah* — increase — for the doers of good, a pairing the commentators read as the two stages of the divine response, remission and then surplus [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī].

**Readings.** **[Jalālayn]** records the variant in the verb of forgiveness: *naghfir* as read in the first person, "We shall forgive," or the passive *tughfar*, "your transgressions shall be forgiven"; **[Qurṭubī]**'s discussion of the same verb pair in al-Baqarah is the place where its several readings are collected, and he refers the reader there [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "And when We said, 'Enter this city and eat from it wherever you wish in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say, "Ḥiṭṭah," and We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good'" (2:58); "But those who wronged among them changed the word for another, so We sent down upon them a punishment from the sky because they were wronging" (2:59); "And it was said to the Children of Israel after him: dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you as a mixed crowd" (17:104) [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse is one of the sūrah's recurring openings: a favor given with a condition attached, and a condition easy to meet. Enter a city of fruit and water, bow, and ask. The commentators note the economy of the command — humility and petition, the two things a people needs after wrongdoing — and the generosity of the promise — forgiveness and then increase [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī]. Its placement here, beside the manna and the springs and the shade, is what makes the following verse's substitution so heavy: what was demanded was a word the tongue could carry [Jalālayn] [Ṭabarī].

## 7:162

*"But those who wronged among them changed the word for other than what was said to them; so We sent upon them a punishment from the heaven because they were wronging."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the substitution plainly: "those who disbelieved in God among them altered what God had commanded them to say, and said — when they had been told, 'Say: this is a ḥiṭṭah' — *ḥinṭah fī shaʿīrah*, 'a grain of wheat in a barley' (or: a grain in a hair)." He notes that in saying this they were saying something other than the word they were told to say. Then "so We sent upon them a *rijz* from the heaven" — We dispatched upon them a punishment, and destroyed them for their changing of what they were commanded, doing the contrary of what God had ordered them to do and saying other than what He had ordered them to say; and he notes that the meaning of *rijz* has been explained before, in the commentary on al-Baqarah [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the report of Maʿmar from Hammām b. Munabbih from Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the verse: they said, "a grain in a hair," and where they had been told to enter the gate prostrating, they entered dragging themselves on their hindquarters — and he notes the grammatical point that "because they were wronging" (*bimā kānū yaẓlimūn*) is marfūʿ because it is a future-tense verb in naṣb position, and that "what" (*mā*) here carries the sense of a verbal noun, meaning "because of their wrongdoing" [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** draws the transition that the syntax leaves implicit: "they did not comply with this divine command; rather those of them who did wrong substituted — that is, they disobeyed God and treated His command lightly — a saying other than that which was said to them." He then makes the argument the substitution invites: when they substituted the saying although it was easy and light, their substitution of the deed is more likely and more certain; and for this reason they entered dragging on their buttocks. Then "so We sent upon them" — when they opposed God's command and disobeyed Him — "*rijzan min al-samāʾ*," a severe punishment, whether the plague or another of the heavenly chastisements; and God did not wrong them by His punishment, it was only "because they were wronging" [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** gives it in two sentences: "But the evildoers among them substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them — they said instead 'a grain inside a hair' — and entered the gate dragging themselves on their rears; so We sent down upon them terror, a chastisement from the heaven, for their evildoing" [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Maʿārif]** both treat the verse with the parallel passage of al-Baqarah, where the substitution and its punishment are detailed; **[Maʿārif]** phrases the whole sequence as the enumeration of divine favors followed by deviation from the commands and the resulting heavenly punishment for the transgression [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Tabdīl* — substitution — is the verse's operative word, and the exegetes keep it in the realm of speech before the realm of action: a commanded sentence is replaced by a pun on its sound (the similar-sounding "grain" for "putting-down"), which **[Ṭabarī]** simply calls saying other than what one was told to say [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Rijz* is glossed as punishment, the word the whole tradition reads together with *rijs*, defilement, and the two are cross-referenced to the treatment of the plague and the heavenly scourges in al-Baqarah [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. And the closing clause's grammar — *bimā kānū yaẓlimūn*, with the imperfect verb — is noticed by **[Qurṭubī]** as the mark of an ongoing habit of wrongdoing rather than a single lapse [Qurṭubī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** carries the Prophetic report of Abū Hurayrah through Maʿmar and Hammām: the substitution of the word by "a grain in a hair," and the entrance crawling on the hindquarters — the tradition's picture of how contempt for a command shows itself in stance as well as speech [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "But those who wronged among them changed the word for another than what was said to them, so We sent upon them a plague from the heaven for their wrongdoing" (2:59); "Do you covet that they will believe in your religion when a party of them used to hear the words of God and then distort it after they had understood it, knowingly?" (2:75); "O you who have been given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down confirming what is with you" (cf. 4:47) [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse's small word is the whole diagnosis: the people were commanded a formula of humility and substituted for it a joke about grain. The exegetes notice that the substitution cost them nothing to avoid and gained them nothing to make, which is precisely why **[Saʿdī]** calls it a light matter that proves a heavier one: contempt for the command, showing itself first on the tongue and then in the body's posture [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. The punishment named "from the heaven" closes the circle opened by the manna sent down from heaven — the same direction that brought provision brought the scourge, and the people who would not bow when it was easy crawled instead [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn].

## 7:163

*"And ask them about the city that was by the sea, when they transgressed the Sabbath — their fish came to them on the day of their Sabbath, surfacing; but the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come. Thus did We try them because they were defiantly disobedient."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the address: "ask, O Muhammad, these Jews, who are your neighbors, about the affair of the city that was present by the sea" — that is, it was in the presence of the sea, at its shore and beside it; and he notes the disagreement over which city it was. Ibn ʿAbbās said, through the chain of Muhammad b. Isḥāq from Dāwūd b. al-Ḥuṣayn from ʿIkrima: "it is a city called Aylah, between Midian and al-Ṭūr." ʿIkrima's own report is the famous one: he entered upon Ibn ʿAbbās while the muṣḥaf was in his lap and he was weeping, and asked him what made him weep; and Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Woe to you — do you know the city that was present by the sea?" and he said, "That is Aylah." And Ibn ʿAbbās through another chain simply said "Aylah"; and through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa: a city on the shore of the sea between Egypt and Madinah called Aylah; al-Suddī said the people of Aylah; Mujāhid said Aylah; Qatāda said it was a city on the shore of the sea called Aylah; and Ibn Zayd said it was a city called Maqnā between Midian and ʿAynūnā; and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās has it as Midian, between Aylah and al-Ṭūr. Ṭabarī then gives his own judgment: the sound position is that it was a city present by the sea, and it may have been Aylah, or Midian, or Maqnā, because each of these is present by the sea, and there is no report from the Messenger of God ﷺ that would cut off the excuse by settling which of them it was; and knowledge of what has passed and gone out of sight is reached only by a report that necessitates knowledge, and there is no such report here [Ṭabarī]. Then the transgression: "when they transgressed the Sabbath" — its people transgressed the command of God regarding the Sabbath by overstepping to what God had forbidden them; and the transgression in the Sabbath was that God had forbidden them the Sabbath and they used to fish in it. "When their fish came to them on the day of their Sabbath, surfacing" — emerging on the water from every path and direction, like the openings of roads; Ibn ʿAbbās said, "visible upon the water," and in another report, "from every place." "And the day they did not observe the Sabbath" — the day they did not honor it as they honored the Sabbath, that is, the rest of the days — "they did not come": the fish did not come.
