"Thus did We try them" — as We have described to you of the testing and trial — by showing the fish on the surface of the water on the day on which fishing was forbidden, and hiding them on the day on which it was permitted — "because they were defiantly disobedient," because of their going out of God's obedience [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the frame of the address: "ask them" means ask the Jews, your neighbors, about the reports of their forebears and what God transformed of them into apes and pigs; this is a question of confirmation and rebuke, and it was a sign of the Prophet's ﷺ truthfulness, since God informed him of those matters without his having learned them — the point being that they used to say, "We are the children of God and His beloved, for we are of the line of His friend Abraham, and of the line of Israel who is God's firstborn, and of the line of Moses the one God spoke to, and of the line of his son ʿUzayr, so we are of their descendants"; and God said to His prophet: ask them about the city — did I not punish them for their sins, and that for the change of a single branch of the law? He notes that the Jews used to conceal this story because of the disgrace in it. On the identity of the city, he gives the full range: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and al-Suddī say Aylah; another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Midian between Aylah and al-Ṭūr; al-Zuhrī says Tabariyyah; Qatāda and Zayd b. Aslam say it was a shore of the Syrian shores between Midian and ʿAynūn, called Maqnāth. On the lexicon of the Sabbath he gives the root's meanings — the Jews "sabata" when they left work on their Sabbath; "sabata al-rajul" in the passive means slumber seized him; "asbata" means he was still and did not move; and the day is called the Sabbath from rest and cutting — and he reports the ḥadīth of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever has himself cupped on the Sabbath and is struck with leprosy, let him blame none but himself," the scholars explaining that blood congeals on the Sabbath, so that when it is drawn out it does not flow and turns to leprosy. He records the readings: the majority read *yaʿdūna*; Abū Nahīk read *yuʿiddūna*, "they prepare," meaning they prepare the instrument to take it; Ibn al-Samayqaʿ read *fī al-asbāt* and *asbātihim*, the plural of Sabbath. "Surfacing" (*shurraʿan*) means spread out and visible on the water in abundance; al-Layth said it means raising their heads; and it was said that the fish of the sea used to come on the Sabbath day in herds, crowding Aylah, God having inspired them that they are not caught on the Sabbath because of His prohibition to the Jews; and it was said they used to spread out at their doors like white rams, raising their heads. Then the devices: the story is told that Iblīs whispered to them, "You are only forbidden to take them on the Sabbath, so make pools," and they used to drive the fish into them on Friday, where the fish would stay, unable to leave for the scant water, and they would take them on Sunday. And Mālik's report through Ashhab, from Ibn Rūmān: a man among them took a rope and a piece of cloth, tied it to the tail of a fish and left it in the water until the sun set on Sunday, then dragged it out by the rope and roasted it; a neighbor smelled the fish in his house and confronted him, and the man denied it, but when the neighbor looked into his oven, there it was; the neighbor said, "I think God will punish you" — but when no punishment came quickly, the practice spread, until a man took two fish the next Sabbath, and the neighbor saw him and still no punishment came quickly, and they went on fishing until it became open, carried in the markets, and the sinners announced it; so a group of the Children of Israel stood and forbade it and separated themselves; and it was said the forbidder said, "We will not live with you," and they divided the city with a wall. Then one morning the forbidder found no one emerging from among the transgressors; they climbed over the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes; they opened the door and went in among them, and the apes recognized their blood-relations among the human beings though the human beings did not recognize theirs among the apes; the apes would come to their kinsman, sniff his clothes and weep, and he would say, "Did we not forbid you?" and the ape would nod its head, "Yes." And Qatāda said: the young men became apes and the elders became pigs, and none was saved but those who forbade, and the rest perished. On that view the Children of Israel split into only two groups, and the sense of "and when a community among them said, why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy" would be that the doers said it to the warners when the warners admonished them: "If you know that God is going to destroy us, why do you admonish us?" — and God transformed them into apes [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the verse as the explanation of the earlier statement, "and indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath" (2:65), and notes two purposes in "ask them": to ask the Jews then present about the story of their fellows who defied God's command so that His punishment overtook them suddenly for their evil actions, transgression and defiance by deceit; and to warn those same Jews against hiding the Prophet's description that they find in their books, lest there befall them what befell their forefathers. He gives the city as Aylah on the shore of the Qulzum Sea, with the identification of Ibn ʿAbbās and the agreement of ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Suddī; he notes that the fish were visible on the surface on the Sabbath and hidden on the permitted days, citing his teacher's explanation (i.e., Ṭabarī's); and he draws the verse's general lesson with the report of Ibn Baṭṭah from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Do not commit what the Jews committed, so that you make lawful the prohibitions of God by the meanest of tricks" — a report whose chain he grades reasonable [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the account of a test built into nature: God had commanded them to honor and respect the Sabbath and not to hunt in it; so God tried them and tested them, and the fish used to come to them on the day of their Sabbath, *shurraʿan* — many, floating on the face of the water; and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, when the Sabbath had passed, they did not come, disappearing into the sea so that they saw nothing of them; "thus We tried them because they were defiantly disobedient" — their defiance is what made God try them and bring this ordeal upon them; had they not rebelled, He would have spared them and not exposed them to trial and evil [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** sets out the comparative and interpretive material: the commentators speculate about the town, some identifying it as Aylah between Midian and Sinai, others taking it as Tiberias or Midian itself; the Israelites transgressed the Sabbath by performing acts God had forbidden on the day reserved for worship alone; and although in Islam there is no "Sabbath" in the same sense as in Judaism with its extensive ritual proscriptions, the Qurʾān nonetheless understands the observance of the Sabbath to be a requirement established in the Torah for the Children of Israel and the Jews in particular, with the relevant verses cited elsewhere. It notes that on the day of their Sabbath the fish would appear all around them on the surface of the water while on other days they remained hidden below, so that fishing was especially easy and fruitful on the forbidden day, making it tempting — and in this sense it was a way for God to try them for their iniquity. And it reports that the question of fishing divided the Israelites of that town into three: a third who wanted to fish, a third who admonished against it, and a third who neither fished nor admonished [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** keeps the treatment brief and points to the detailed discussion in Sūrat al-Baqarah, adding the purpose of the address: the Holy Prophet ﷺ has been asked to warn the Israelites present in his time by reminding them of the events of these verses, whose events are clear and require no explanation [Maʿārif].

**Language.** The city is named by the sea rather than by its own name — *al-qaryah allatī kānat ḥāḍirata al-baḥr* — and the exegetes treat the participle as a place-name manqué: the town "present to the sea," on its shore, whether that be Aylah, Midian, Maqnā or Tabariyyah [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. *Shurraʿan* is the verse's telling detail, and the glosses circle the same image: the fish "coming out" onto the water as streets open onto a road, spread out and visible, raising their heads, coming in herds, so that the sea itself seemed to arrange the temptation [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. The root *s-b-t* supplies a cluster the commentators work through: leaving work, being still, resting, cutting — from which the day and its observance take their name, with *yasbitūn* read as "honoring the Sabbath" and, in al-Ḥasan's reading, *yusbitūn*, "entering into the Sabbath," formed like "we entered the month" [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. And the closing *yafsuqūn* — they were defiantly disobedient, going out of obedience — is the verse's explanation of why the trial came at all [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Two reports the commentators attach to this verse. The ḥadīth of **[Qurṭubī]**: "Whoever has himself cupped on the Sabbath and is struck with leprosy, let him blame none but himself," with the scholars' physiological explanation of congealed blood [Qurṭubī]. And the Prophetic prohibition carried by **[Ibn Kathīr]** from Ibn Baṭṭah through Abū Hurayrah: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, so that you make lawful the prohibitions of God by the meanest of tricks" — the verse read as a standing warning against legal stratagem, which **[Ibn Kathīr]** presents as the moral of the whole passage: a people who took an action legal on its surface but intended to transgress the prohibition [Ibn Kathīr]. To these the commentaries add the famous scene of Ibn ʿAbbās weeping over the passage with the muṣḥaf in his lap, and ʿIkrima's remonstrance with him — a scene whose two versions are given below, in the discussion of the following verses, since their subject is the fate of the onlookers [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

**Rulings.** Two rulings emerge. First, the Sabbath as a revealed institution for Israel: **[Study Quran]** notes that the Qurʾān treats its observance as a requirement established in the Torah for the Children of Israel and the Jews in particular, even though Islam has no parallel institution [Study Quran] [Ṭabarī]. Second, the sin of the stratagem: the commentaries on this verse are the classic locus for the prohibition of *ḥiyal* — devices that make a forbidden thing lawful in form while violating it in intent — with **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth as the proof text, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s account of the pools and the tethered fish as the case study [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Cross-references.** "And indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them: be apes, despised" (2:65); "Ask the Children of Israel how many a clear sign We gave them" (2:211); "And We had made the Sabbath a burden upon those who differed concerning it" (cf. 16:124); "And the Sabbath was ordained only for those who differed about it" (16:124); "Do not transgress the Sabbath" — from the covenant of the Children of Israel (4:154); "So taste the punishment because of what you used to do" (cf. 16:94) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse turns a natural detail into a moral instrument: the fish surface on the forbidden day and vanish on the permitted one, and the commentators call the arrangement exactly what it is — a test, and a test calibrated to a people whose disobedience had already been registered [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. What the tradition carries forward from the passage is not the geography — Ṭabarī refuses to fix the city without a decisive report, and says so with unusual firmness — but the anatomy of a violation: the command, the stratagem, the minority who forbid, the majority who follow the spread of the practice into the markets, and the wall that finally divides the community [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:164

*"And when a community among them said, 'Why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?' They said, 'As an excuse before your Lord, and that haply they may be reverent.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** frames the exchange: remember, O Muhammad, when a community — a group — among them said to a group that had been admonishing the transgressors of the Sabbath and forbidding them God's disobedience: "Why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy in this world for their disobedience of Him and their opposition to His command and their making lawful what He had forbidden, or to punish with a severe punishment in the Hereafter?" And those who were forbidding them from God's disobedience answered: "Our admonishing them is an excuse to your Lord, as we discharge the duty He laid upon us of enjoining the right and forbidding the wrong; and haply they may be reverent" — that is, haply they may fear God and so turn back to His obedience and repent of their disobedience and of their overstepping what He had forbidden them in the matter of the Sabbath [Ṭabarī]. He then reports the exegetical reports: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrima, glosses "they said: an excuse to your Lord" as "out of our wrath at their deeds" — the admonition as the expression of anger for God's sake; and Ibn Zayd glosses "and haply they may be reverent" as "they may abandon the practice they were engaged in." He gives the reading dispute: the majority of the readers of the Ḥijāz, Kūfah and Baṣrah read *maʿdhiratun* with the nominative, in the sense described; and some of the people of Kūfah read *maʿdhiratan* in the accusative, meaning "as an excusing of ourselves, and we admonished them and did that." And then the substantive disagreement: whether the faction that said "why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy" belonged to the saved or to the destroyed. Some said it belonged to the saved, because it was the group that was forbidding the doomed group from transgressing the Sabbath. He then transmits the long Ibn ʿAbbās report of the city on the shore between Makkah and Madinah called Aylah: the fish came to them on the Sabbath at the water's edge, and when the Sabbath passed they could not get at them; the people stayed thus as long as God willed; then a party of them took the fish on the Sabbath day, and a party forbade them, saying, "You take them when God has forbidden them to you on your Sabbath!" — but they only increased in error and arrogance, and another party began to forbid them. When that grew long upon them, a party of the forbidder said, "Know that these are a people against whom punishment has become due; why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy?" — and they were angrier for God's sake than the other party, and they said, "An excuse to your Lord, and haply they may be reverent." All of them had been forbidding; and when God's wrath fell upon them, both of the parties that had spoken were saved, and God destroyed the people of disobedience who had taken the fish, making them apes and pigs [Ṭabarī]. And he gives the report of Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿIkrima on the doubt itself: Ibn ʿAbbās read the verse and said, "I do not know whether the group that said 'why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy' was saved or not!" — and ʿIkrima said, "I kept at him until I made him know that they had been saved, and he clothed me in a garment." And the report of ʿIkrima's own encounter: he entered upon Ibn ʿAbbās while the muṣḥaf was in his lap and he was weeping, and asked why; Ibn ʿAbbās read "ask them about the city that was present by the sea" down to "because they were defiantly disobedient," and said, "I do not hear the third group mentioned — I fear that we may be like them!" and ʿIkrima said, "Do you not hear God saying, 'and when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden'?" — and he was relieved, and clothed him in a garment. And in the long version related by Ibn Jurayj from ʿIkrima: Ibn ʿAbbās read the passage in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf and asked, "Do you know Aylah?" — and told the story: there was a Jewish tribe to whom the fish were driven on the Sabbath, white and fat as if about to calve, spreading their bellies on the ground in their courtyards, until Satan whispered to them that they were only forbidden to eat them on the Sabbath, so they should take them on that day and eat them on others; a party of them said exactly that, and another party said, "No, you were forbidden to eat them, take them and hunt them on the Sabbath day." They remained so until the next Friday came; one party transgressed with its own people, wives and children; one party withdrew to the right; and one party withdrew to the left and stayed silent. The people of the right said, "Woe to you, God, God — we forbid you to expose yourselves to God's punishment!" and the people of the left said, "Why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" The people of the right said, "An excuse to your Lord, and haply they may be reverent" — that is, they may desist; it is dearer to us that they not be afflicted and destroyed; and if they do not desist, there is at least an excuse before your Lord. The people went on in their sin, and the people of the right said, "You have done it, O enemies of God! By God, we will not spend the night with you in your city; we do not see you reaching the morning before God strikes you with a sinking, a pelting, or some of what He has of punishment." When morning came they knocked on their door and called, and no one answered; they put up a ladder and a man climbed the wall and looked; he turned to them and said, "O servants of God — apes, by God, with tails, howling!" They opened the door and went in, and the apes recognized their lineages from the humans though the humans did not recognize theirs from the apes; the apes would come to their kinsman among the humans and sniff his clothes and weep, and he would say, "Did we not forbid you such and such?" and the ape would nod its head: yes. Then Ibn ʿAbbās recited, "And when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who did wrong with a grievous punishment because they were defiantly disobedient," and said, "So I see that the Jews who forbade were saved; and I do not see the others mentioned; and we see things we disapprove of and do not speak about them!" ʿIkrima said, "May God make me your ransom — do you not see that they hated what those people were upon and opposed them, saying, 'why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish with a severe punishment'?" — and Ibn ʿAbbās ordered that he be given two coarse cloaks. And Qatāda's summary: the people became three factions — one that held back from violating God's sanctity and forbade God's disobedience; one that held back from violating God's sanctity out of awe of God; and one that tore the sanctity and fell into sin [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the same material and adds his readings of the exchange: the majority of the exegetes hold that the Children of Israel split into three groups — the offending group that fished, some seventy thousand of them; a group that stood apart, neither forbidding nor offending; and the forbidding group; and that the standing-apart group said to the forbidding group, "Why do you admonish a people — meaning the disobedient — whom God is about to destroy or punish," on the strength of their supposition and of what they knew of God's way with disobedient nations; and the forbidding group answered, "Our admonition is an excuse before God, that they may be reverent." He notes an argument for the three-group reading: had there been only two groups, the forbidding group would have said to the offending group, "and haply you may be reverent," with the second-person pronoun. He then reports the further disagreement about the fate of the group that neither forbade nor offended: one report from Ibn ʿAbbās says they perished with the offenders as a penalty for abandoning the forbidding of wrong; another report from him says, "I do not know what was done with them" — which is the apparent sense of the verse — and al-Ḥasan held that view; and ʿIkrima's account of convincing Ibn ʿAbbās that they were saved, for which he was given a garment. He gives the evidence that only the transgressing group perished: God says "and We seized those who did wrong," not "those who were silent"; and the earlier verse, "and indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath." He records that ʿĪsā and Ṭalḥa read *maʿdhiratan* in the accusative, that al-Kisāʾī explained the accusative in two ways — as an absolute object, or as "we did that as an excuse" — that it is the reading of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and that the others read the nominative, which he prefers, since they did not intend a fresh apology for something they were blamed for, but answered the question "why do you admonish?" with "our admonition is an excuse"; and he cites Sībawayh's rule that a man saying "an excuse to God and to you concerning such a thing," intending an apology, would use the accusative. And he draws out the legal principle the verse establishes: the obligation of blocking the means to what is forbidden — the admonition itself being the prevention — and he refers the reader to the discussions of enjoining right in the places where they are set out [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the three groups: one that committed the prohibition, catching fish on the Sabbath; one that forbade them and kept away from them; and a third that neither prohibited nor participated, which said to the preachers, "Why do you preach to a people whom God is about to destroy or punish with a severe torment?" — that is, "why do you forbid these people from evil when you know they are destroyed and have earned God's punishment?" — for, they said, there is no benefit in forbidding them. The preachers answered, "In order to be free from guilt before your Lord," for we were commanded to enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, "and perhaps they may fear God" — for on account of our advice they might stop this evil and repent, and if they repent God will accept their repentance and grant them mercy [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** supplies the mechanics of the stratagem as context for the exchange: they contrived for the hunt by digging pits for the fish and setting nets, so that when the fish came on the Sabbath day and fell into the pits and nets, they would not take them that day, and when Sunday came they took them; the practice grew among them and they split into three groups — most of them transgressing and daring and announcing it openly; a group announcing its prohibition and objection; and a group content with the objection of those others and their prohibition, saying, "Why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" — as if to say: there is no benefit in admonishing one who has plunged into God's sacred limits and does not listen to counsel but continues in his transgression and arrogance, for God will certainly punish him, either by destruction or by severe torment. The preachers said: "We admonish them and forbid them as an excuse to your Lord" — so that we may be excused regarding them — "and haply they may be reverent," that is, leave the disobedience they are in; so let us not despair of their guidance, for perhaps the admonition will take effect in them and the reproach will leave a mark, and this is the greatest purpose of forbidding wrong: that it be an excuse and the establishment of a proof against the one commanded and forbidden, and that God may guide him, so that he acts according to what was commanded and forbidden [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** notes that the community among them refers to those Israelites in the town who did not participate in fishing on the Sabbath but also did not admonish those who did, and that this group addresses those who tried actively to forbid or discourage the fishermen, asking why they make the effort to admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish; their response is that it serves as an excuse before God, meaning that they consider themselves obligated to forbid wrong and, having done so, have fulfilled their moral duty; and "that haply they may be reverent" indicates that the admonishers also hoped their warnings might succeed in bringing the violators back to reverence for God and for Mosaic law [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the exchange with the grammatical note that "and when" here is a supplement to the preceding "when": a community among them who neither fished nor prohibited said to those who prohibited, "Why do you preach admonition to a folk whom God is about to destroy or chastise with a severe chastisement?" They said, "Our admonishing them is an exculpation by which we excuse ourselves before your Lord, lest we are reproached for failing to prohibit them in any way; and so that they might be wary of fishing" [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** includes the passage among the events whose detail is set out in Sūrat al-Baqarah [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Maʿdhiratun* — an excuse, an exculpation — is the verse's key term, and the readings attach different faces to it: the nominative reading makes the admonition itself the excuse ("our admonishing is an excuse"); the accusative makes it the motive or purpose ("we admonished as an excuse"), read by ʿĪsā and Ṭalḥa and, on **[Qurṭubī]**'s report, also by Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim; and Sībawayh's distinction between a fresh apology and an answer to a question is brought in to prefer the nominative [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]. The question itself — *lima taʿiẓūna* — turns on *waʿẓ*, admonition, and **[Ṭabarī]**'s gloss of the answer, "we discharge the duty laid on us," identifies the practice as the communal obligation of enjoining right [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And "and haply they may be reverent" (*laʿallahum yattaqūn*) is read as the survival of hope inside a settled verdict: the commentators keep *laʿalla*, "perhaps," as an expression of the human possibility of change, not of divine uncertainty [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The verse's material is dominated by the Ibn ʿAbbās\-ʿIkrima cycle: the three groups and their fates; the doubt Ibn ʿAbbās expressed about the silent group ("I do not know what was done with them," and in a second version, "I fear we may be like them") and ʿIkrima's argument that moved him, drawing from him a garment on more than one occasion; and the city-wall scene in which the apes recognize their human kin. **[Qurṭubī]** gives both the reports of the saved and the report of those who said the silent group perished for abandoning the forbidding of wrong, and notes that the apparent sense of the verse supports the saved reading since the punishment is assigned to "those who did wrong" [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. Jalālayn records as well the report that ʿIkrima's opinion was referred through a ḥadīth report to Ibn ʿAbbās, who was delighted by it [Jalālayn].

**Rulings.** Two. First, the obligation and the purpose of enjoining right and forbidding wrong: **[Saʿdī]** states its primary purpose — that the warner be excused and the proof be established against the one warned, and that God may guide him; **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives it as the preachers' own answer — "we were commanded to enjoin righteousness and forbid evil" — with the added hope of repentance; and **[Qurṭubī]** cites the verse as evidence for blocking the means to the forbidden [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī]. Second, the fate of the silent third: **[Saʿdī]** argues that the apparent sense is that they were saved, since God confined destruction to the wrongdoers and did not describe the silent as wrongdoers, and since enjoining good is a communal obligation (*farḍ kifāyah*) discharged for the rest when some perform it — and the words the silent group spoke showed their anger at the deed; **[Qurṭubī]** reports both views, with Ibn ʿAbbās on each side and al-Ḥasan supporting the verse's apparent sense; and **[Study Quran]** records the same division, with some considering the abstainers among the saved [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And let there be from among you a community inviting to good and enjoining right and forbidding wrong; it is they who are successful" (3:104); "The believers, men and women, are allies of one another: they enjoin right and forbid wrong" (9:71); "Then they were succeeded by a generation who neglected the prayer and followed desires; they will meet with error" (19:59); "You are the best community brought forth for mankind: you enjoin right and forbid wrong and believe in God" (3:110) [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī].

**Reflection.** The exchange is the sūrah's picture of a moral minority inside a decaying people: they know the outcome is likely settled, they say so, and they admonish anyway. The commentaries notice that the men who asked the question were not the offenders but the onlookers, and that the answer given them — "an excuse before your Lord" — is the charter of every subsequent community that must speak when it cannot save [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. The tradition's own unease about the third group, the silence that neither fishes nor forbids, is instructive: **[Qurṭubī]** reports Ibn ʿAbbās saying "I fear we may be like them," and the consolation found in the verse; the reader of the passage is meant to identify, and the passage is arranged so that the identification is uncomfortable [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran].

## 7:165

*"And when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment because they were defiantly disobedient."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads "when they forgot" as deliberate abandonment: when the party that had transgressed in the Sabbath left what God had commanded them of refraining from transgression, and wasted the admonition with which the admonishing party had admonished and reminded them, warning them of God's punishment for their disobedience, and pressed on into making lawful what God had forbidden them — then God saved those among them who forbade evil, meaning God's disobedience and the making lawful of His sanctities; and God seized those who did wrong, meaning the ones who transgressed in the Sabbath by making lawful the fishing and eating of fish on it, and brought His severity down upon them and destroyed them with a severe punishment for their opposing God's command, for going out of His obedience into His disobedience, and that is the *fisq* [Ṭabarī]. He then gives the reports: Ibn Jurayj said that "when they forgot what they had been reminded of" refers to their forgetting the admonition of the believers who had said, "why do you admonish a people"; and Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrima, is reported with the exclamation, "Would that I knew what the evil was that they forbade!" — a report that leaves the content of the warning undefined and puts the emphasis on the act of forbidding itself [Ṭabarī]. Then the difficult word: "with a *baʾīs* punishment." Ṭabarī records the readings: the majority of the readers of Madinah read *bīs* with the bāʾ kasrah and a lightened yāʾ, without hamzah, on the pattern *fiʿl*; some of the readers of Kūfah and Baṣrah read *baʾīs* on the pattern *faʿīl*, from *buʾs*, with the bāʾ opened and the hamzah kasrah and a medial vowel; some of the Meccans read it that way but with the bāʾ kasrah, *biʾīs*, on the pattern *fiʿīl*; some of the Kūfans read *bayʾis*, on the pattern *fayʿil* — which he calls anomalous with the grammarians, since with a sound root *fayʿil* takes a fatḥah in its middle letter in the eloquent speech of the Arabs, like *ṣayqal* and *nayrab*, while the kasrah occurs in roots with wāw or yāʾ, like *sayyid* and *mayyit*, and he cites the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays b. ʿĀbis al-Kindī with *bayʾis* and the kasrah of the middle letter; and another Kūfan read *bayʾas*, on the pattern *fayʿal*, like *ṣayqal*; and one of the Baṣrans read *baʾis*, on the pattern *faʿil*; and another read *biʾsa*, with the bāʾ kasrah and the sīn fatḥah, in the sense "evil is the punishment." Ṭabarī's own choice is the reading *baʾīs* on the pattern *faʿīl*, with the bāʾ opened and the hammed vowel lengthened, because the exegetes agree that its meaning is "severe," and he cites the verse of Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī with *baʾīsan*; and he reports the glosses: Ibn ʿAbbās said "painful and sore," Mujāhid said "severe," and in another report "painful and severe," Qatāda said "painful," and Ibn Zayd said "a severe punishment" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the lexical point about forgetting: *nisyān* is used of the heedless, but the deliberate one is "the abandoner," as in "when they forgot what they had been reminded of" — they abandoned it deliberately — and his proof is the other verse, "they forgot God, so He forgot them." He notes that "with a *baʾīs* punishment" means a severe one, and that there are eleven readings of the word, which al-Naḥḥās collected: the reading of Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī as *baʾīs* on the pattern *faʿīl*; the reading of the people of Makkah as *biʾīs* with the bāʾ kasrah and the same pattern; the reading of the people of Madinah as *bīs* with the bāʾ kasrah followed by a static yāʾ, then a sīn with kasrah and tanwīn — with two explanations, al-Kisāʾī holding that the original was *baʾīs* with a light hamzah, that the two yāʾ-like letters met and one was dropped and the first letter given kasrah, like *raghīf* and *shahīd*, or that it was *baʾisa* on the pattern *faʿila*, with the first given kasrah and the hamzah lightened; the reading of al-Ḥasan with the bāʾ kasrah, then a static hamzah, then a sīn with fatḥah; the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muqriʾ as *baʾis* with the bāʾ fatḥah and the hamzah and sīn kasrah and tanwīn; the reading reported by Yaʿqūb the reciter from some readers as *baʾisa* with the bāʾ fatḥah, the hamzah kasrah and the sīn fatḥah; the reading of al-Aʿmash as *bayʾal* and, on another report, *bayʾas*, and, on another, *baʾʾis* with a doubled hamzah; the reading of Naṣr b. ʿĀṣim as *bayyis* with the bāʾ fatḥah and a doubled yāʾ without hamzah; and a reading reported by Yaʿqūb as *biʾyas* with the bāʾ kasrah, a static hamzah and a yāʾ with fatḥah. He notes ʿAlī b. Sulaymān's explanation that the Arabs say "he came with the daughters of *bīs*," meaning with something bad, so that "with a *bīs* punishment" means with a bad punishment; and he reports that Abū Ḥātim said al-Ḥasan's reading has no justification, since one does not say "I passed by a man *biʾsa*" unless one says "biʾsa al-rajul" or "biʾsa rajulan" — and al-Naḥḥās's reply that Abū Ḥātim's objection is rejected, since the grammarians report "if you do such and such, then it is with it, and how good" meaning "in it, and how good the trait is," so that al-Ḥasan's reading is construed as "with a punishment — evil is the punishment" [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the sequence as the pattern of God's way with His servants: "when they forgot what they had been reminded of" — that is, they left what they had been reminded of and continued in their error and transgression — "We saved those who forbade evil": and this is God's way among His servants, that when the punishment descends, those who command the right and forbid the wrong are saved from it; "and We took those who did wrong" — the ones who transgressed on the Sabbath — "with a *baʾīs* punishment," that is, a severe one, "because they were defiantly disobedient." He then steps into the disagreement about the silent group: the exegetes differed about their salvation and destruction, and the apparent sense is that they were among the saved, for God confined destruction to the wrongdoers and did not mention that the silent were wrongdoers — which indicates that the punishment was particular to the Sabbath transgressors; and because commanding right and forbidding wrong is a communal obligation that drops from the rest when some perform it, and these were content with the objection of those others; and because they showed, in their own words, the anger at the deed that implies they detested it with the strongest detestation and knew God would punish it most severely [Saʿdī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same sequence and draws the same inference from the verse's silence about the third group: God stated that those who enjoined good were saved while those who committed the transgression were destroyed, and He did not mention the end of those who were passive, "for the recompense is comparable to the deed": that type neither did what would warrant praise nor committed wrong so as to be admonished. And he records the Ibn ʿAbbās report through ʿIkrima — the repeated doubt and the garment — and his own verdict on the verse: that the ones who remained were saved, which the specific naming of "those who did wrong" indicates; and he glosses *baʾīs* as severe, according to Mujāhid, or painful, according to Qatāda, the meanings being synonymous and God knowing best; and "despised" (*khāsiʾīn*) as humiliated, disgraced and rejected [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** reads the verse as the completion: when the violators forgot what they had been reminded of by those who admonished them, God punished the violators and saved those who forbade evil — that is, by exhorting their fellow Israelites to observe the Sabbath; and the commentators are divided on the fate of those who abstained both from fishing on the Sabbath and from forbidding others to do so, some considering them to be among the saved [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: "And when they forgot — overlooked — that whereof they had been reminded, and did not desist, We delivered those who forbade evil and seized those who did wrong through transgression with a grievous, terrible chastisement for their defiance" [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** keeps to the referral to Sūrat al-Baqarah [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *Baʾīs* is the verse's philological monument: eleven readings are counted by **[Qurṭubī]**, and **[Ṭabarī]** works through seven of them with metrical analogies (*fiʿl*, *faʿīl*, *fiʿīl*, *fayʿil*, *fayʿal*, *faʿil*, *biʾsa*) and a verse of Imruʾ al-Qays b. ʿĀbis as evidence for the form with the doubled middle; both settle on the reading that means "severe," because, as Ṭabarī says, the exegetes agree on the meaning while differing on the form [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Nisyān* is given its two senses: heedlessness and deliberate abandonment, with the context requiring the second [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. And the verse's two verbs — *anjaynā*, We saved, and *akhadhnā*, We seized — carry the whole moral structure: the plural object of the first is the forbidders, and of the second "those who did wrong," the pairing on which every position about the silent group depends [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Rulings.** The verse furnishes the tradition's standing doctrine about the fate of the community when punishment falls: the reformers are saved and the wrongdoers are taken, and the fate of the merely silent is left unstated by the text. **[Saʿdī]** argues from this silence and from the communal-obligation principle that the silent were saved; **[Ibn Kathīr]** argues from the same silence that their recompense matches their deed, neither praised nor punished; **[Qurṭubī]** reports both views and notes that some held the silent perished for abandoning the forbidding of wrong; and **[Study Quran]** records the division [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. The legal corollary drawn from the passage as a whole is the obligation's communal structure: when some discharge it, the rest are absolved — the basis of the *farḍ kifāyah* reading of enjoining right and forbidding wrong [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Cross-references.** "And when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden, We said to them: be apes, despised" (7:166, the following verse); "And indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: be apes, despised; and We made it a punishment exemplary for those before them and for those after, and an admonition for the God-fearing" (2:65–66); "Then We saved Our messengers and those who believed; thus it is incumbent upon Us to save the believers" (10:103); "So We saved him and those with him by mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs" (7:72) [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Reflection.** The verse's shape is the whole answer to the question that opened the passage: the admonishers asked whether they were excusing themselves to no purpose, and the text answers by naming them in the first person of deliverance — "We saved those who forbade evil" [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. What the commentators then do with the third group is the tradition thinking aloud about responsibility: the silence of the Qurʾān here is a space each of them fills according to his reading of the obligation's weight, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s Ibn ʿAbbās, weeping over the verse, fearing he might be one of those the text does not mention, is the passage's truest reflection of its own difficulty [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn].
## 7:166

*"And when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden, We said to them, 'Be apes, despised.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the completion of the sequence: when they persisted in rebellion (*tamarradū*) regarding what they had been forbidden — their transgression in the Sabbath and their making lawful what God had forbidden them of fishing and eating fish — and continued in it, "We said to them: be apes, despised," that is, driven far from good. He reports the glosses: Qatāda said, "when the people became hardened in disobedience, 'We said to them: be apes, despised' — so they became apes with tails, howling, after having been men and women"; and Ibn ʿAbbās, through the chain of his father from his grandfather, said that God made of them the apes and the pigs, and he maintained that the young men of the people became apes and the elders became pigs; and al-Suddī, or Saʿīd b. Jubayr with him, reported that Moses ﷺ saw a man carrying firewood on the Sabbath day, and struck off his neck — the account of the law's severity before the transformation [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the two words in brief: "when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden" means when they went beyond bounds in disobedience to God; and "be apes, despised" — from *khasāʾtu* which means I drove him away and banished him, with the fuller treatment of the root already given in the commentary on al-Baqarah. He draws the theological point: the verse indicates that acts of disobedience are a cause of vengeance, and this is not hidden; and he records the disagreement over the mode of the address — some said God said it to them with a speech which they heard, and they became as He said; others said the meaning is "We made them apes," the imperative standing for the creative command [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** gives the shape of the sentence: "when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden" — when they hardened and did not soften and took no admonition — "We said to them" with a decree of the divine measure (*qawlan qadariyyan*), "'be apes, despised' — so they were turned into apes by God's leave, and God drove them far from His mercy" [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** adds the tradition's note about the third group: "when they disdained to desist from what was prohibited to them, We said to them, 'Be apes, despised' — abased; and they became so. This is an explication of what preceded with regard to the details of their grievous chastisement. Ibn ʿAbbās said, 'I do not know what befell the group that abstained.' ʿIkrima said, 'That group was not destroyed because they had been averse to what the others did and had said, "Why do you preach admonition…"' — and al-Ḥākim reported in a ḥadīth that ʿIkrima referred this opinion to Ibn ʿAbbās, who was delighted by it" [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** glosses the final word in the same key as the tradition before it: "despised" means humiliated, disgraced and rejected; and he sets the verse in its section heading — that those who breached the Sabbath were turned into monkeys while those who prohibited their actions were saved [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Study Quran]** collects the interpretive options on the transformation: "be apes, outcast" is understood by many commentators to mean that they were physically transformed into apes, since the divine imperative here may be taken as a command that brings the named thing into being; but some reject this literal reading and suggest rather that the hearts of the Sabbath violators were transformed to be like those of apes, though not their physical form, with the fuller discussion to be found at 2:65; and the imperative may also indicate that God is leaving them to indulge their baser instincts, which can lead only to their humiliation and their being outcast in their community — the last being consistent with the Biblical statement that one who works on the Sabbath shall be "cut off from among the people" [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** includes the verse with the rest of the passage whose details have been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah [Maʿārif].

**Language.** *ʿataw* is glossed as rebellion and hardening — going past the limit and staying past it — and the commentators keep the progression: transgression, persistence, insolence [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. *Khāsiʾīn* is the participle of banishment: driven away, abased, rejected, from the same root as driving off a dog — a word whose force the tradition does not soften [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the sentence's grammar became a question in tafsīr: "We said" is read either as a spoken command that was heard and effected, or as the creative *kun* whose imperative names what God made — with **[Qurṭubī]** reporting both and no resolution beyond the fact of the transformation itself [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Three strands of tradition attach here. The reports on the composition of the punishment: Qatāda's apes with tails and howls; Ibn ʿAbbās's division between the young men made apes and the elders made pigs; and al-Suddī's or Saʿīd b. Jubayr's report that Moses ﷺ executed a man found carrying firewood on the Sabbath [Ṭabarī]. The Ibn ʿAbbās\-ʿIkrima cycle on the fate of the third group, with the words "I do not know what befell the group that abstained," ʿIkrima's counter-argument, and al-Ḥākim's report that Ibn ʿAbbās was delighted when the opinion was attributed to him [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī]. And the material about the nature of the transformation, which **[Study Quran]** presents as a live disagreement, literal metamorphosis against a transformation of hearts or a handing over to bestial impulse — the discussions cross-referenced to the parallel at al-Baqarah [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī]. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

**Rulings.** The verse's legal weight in the tradition is as a warning about the consequences of persistence and of the stratagem: the crime punished here was not the deed alone but the refusal to desist after the prohibition was made clear, which is why the sūrah keeps the offenders and their forbidden act in view across four verses [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the commentators draw from the final word the permanence of the disgrace: the punishment was not merely the change of form but the casting out — the community is made monstrous and then excluded from itself [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: be apes, despised" (2:65); "So We made them a punishment exemplary for those before them and those after them, and an admonition for the God-fearing" (2:66); "Say: shall I inform you of something worse than that in recompense with God? Those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry, and of whom He has made apes and pigs and servants of false deities" (5:60); "And when a community among them said, why do you admonish a people…" (7:164) [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrah's hardest image, and the tradition handles it with the two moves available: it takes the transformation seriously as a divine act, and it reads the banishment as the deeper punishment — the offenders kept their kinship with the apes who mourned them and lost their standing among the humans who had warned them [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]**'s phrase for the divine word — a decree of the measure, not a sentence debated in the court of the command — keeps the event in the register of God's sovereign disposal, and **[Study Quran]**'s note about hearts like those of apes offers the reader who cannot accept the metamorphosis a reading that preserves both the offence and its consequence [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. What no source attempts is to soften the trade the passage records: a decree, a warning, a reminder, and then a people who would not desist until the day their children were apes [Jalālayn] [Ṭabarī].

## 7:167

*"And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them a terrible punishment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in retribution, and indeed He is forgiving, merciful."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the construction first: "and when your Lord proclaimed" means, "and remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord announced and informed" — for the form is *tafaʿʿala* from *īdhān*, "to inform," as al-Aʿshā said, "My neighbors today announced their departure with the relics of a parting they had made"; and Mujāhid said in both his chains: "your Lord commanded." Then the content of the proclamation: "that He would surely send against them" — against the Jews — "until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them a terrible punishment." Ṭabarī notes the report that those sent were the Arabs, whom God sent against the Jews, fighting those who did not become Muslim or pay the jizyah, while whoever paid the jizyah did so in humiliation and subjection. He then gives the chains: Ibn ʿAbbās said, "It is the jizyah, and those who impose it are Muhammad ﷺ and his community until the Day of Resurrection"; Ibn ʿAbbās in another report said it is the misery and the taking of the jizyah from them; Ibn Juraysh's chain from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Jews, and what was struck upon them of humiliation and misery"; Qatāda said, "God sent against them this tribe of the Arabs, so they are in punishment from them until the Day of Resurrection"; and Saʿīd b. Jubayr said the Arabs were sent, and that "sūʾ al-ʿadhāb" is the land tax (*kharāj*), and that the first to institute the kharāj was Moses, who collected it for seven years — and in another report, thirteen years — then stopped, and that no prophet collected the kharāj except Moses and the Prophet ﷺ; al-Suddī said God sends against the Children of Israel the Arabs, who inflict on them a terrible punishment, taking the jizyah from them and killing them; and Ibn Zayd said the sending is against the Jews [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the proclamation as directed to the ancestors: God informed their forebears that if they changed and did not believe in the unlettered prophet, God would send against them those who would punish them. He gives the lexical pair: Abū ʿAlī said *ādhana* with the medial vowel means "informed" and *adhdhana* with the doubled letter means "called out"; and some said both carry the sense of informing, as one says "he was certain" and "he grew certain," and he cites Zuhayr's line, "So I said: know that for the game there is a snare" — with *taʿallam*, "know," standing for "know!" He glosses "those who would inflict upon them" as "who would make them taste," with the fuller discussion of the verb given in al-Baqarah; and he sets out the dispute about the agents: some said Nebuchadnezzar; some said the Arabs; some said the community of Muhammad ﷺ — and he notes that this last is the most apparent, "for they are the ones remaining until the Day of Resurrection, and God knows best." Ibn ʿAbbās said that the "terrible punishment" here is the taking of the jizyah; and when it is objected that they were transformed into apes, so how could the jizyah be taken from them, he answers that it is taken from their children and descendants, who are the most abased of peoples — and they are the Jews; Saʿīd b. Jubayr said it means the kharāj, and that no prophet ever collected the kharāj except Moses, who was the first to institute it, collecting it thirteen years and then stopping, and our Prophet ﷺ [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads *taʾadhdhana* as "declared," according to Mujāhid, or "ordained," according to others, and notes that the construction indicates a vow: "that He will keep on sending against them" — against the Jews, until the Day of Resurrection — on account of their disobedience, their defying of God's orders and law, and their use of tricks to transgress the prohibitions. He gives the historical sketch: Moses required the Jews to pay the production tax for seven or thirteen years, and was the first to do so; the Jews then fell under the humiliating rule of the Greeks, the Chaldeans and later the Christians, who subjugated and disgraced them and required the jizyah of them; and when Islam came and Muhammad ﷺ was sent, they came under his power and had to pay it too; so the humiliating torment includes the disgrace and the jizyah, as al-ʿAwfī related from Ibn ʿAbbās. He adds the report concerning the last times: the Jews will support the Dajjāl, and the Muslims together with ʿĪsā son of Mary will kill the Jews, shortly before the end of the world. Then the two closing divine descriptions: "indeed, your Lord is swift in retribution" with those who disobey Him and defy His law, "and indeed He is forgiving, merciful" for those who repent and return to Him; and he makes the pastoral point the pairing invites: the verse mentions both the mercy and the punishment so that no despair is felt — God often mentions encouragement and warning together, so that hearts always have hope and fear [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the two verses together as the two punishments of the Israelites: the first is the continuing subjection, and he reads it in the frame of favor and justice — God's informing them of what He would do because of their changing His Book and disbelieving in His prophet, and His sending against them to the Day of Resurrection those who would exact the jizyah and the kharāj from them, "and God did with them what He promised them: they remain in humiliation and abasement, under the rule of others; no banner of theirs is raised and no standard of theirs is given victory" [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** gives the passage's contemporary reading: the first two verses refer to the two punishments given to the Israelites; as for the first, God will keep sending, up to the Day of Doom, some individuals or groups who will punish and disgrace them — and this is what has been happening to them to this day, dominated and disdainfully treated by others as history records; and it addresses the reader's moment with the observation that the state of Israel in part of Palestine should cause no doubt, for it is in fact a creature of the world powers, made for their political objectives against the Muslim nation, and remains ruled and dominated by them — a military base, whose existence would not outlast the aid it receives; and he cites the prophecies that the Jews must come together in that land in the last age, that ʿĪsā will descend in Syria and fight them, so that God has saved the trouble of hunting them in the ends of the earth by gathering them in Palestine; and he notes the history of their persecution from the time of Solomon to the present, including Nebuchadnezzar and their defeat at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ and ʿUmar, with the translator's note citing the persecution under Hitler as a further instance of the Qurʾānic declaration [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** lays out the interpretive range: "thy Lord proclaimed" indicates that He decreed, commanded or swore; that He will send against them those who would inflict punishment may mean that He will give other people authority over them; and it notes that before the coming of Islam the Zoroastrian Persians, as well as the Greeks, Romans and Christians, had gained authority over the Jewish community, while those sent "against them" could also refer to the Arabs or Muslims, who assumed political authority over much of the Jewish population after the early Islamic conquests. It cross-refers to 2:61 and 3:112 on abasement, and to 17:5–8 on the destruction of Jewish homes and land and the Temple by others possessed of great might, and draws the theological observation: the punishment Jews received for their transgressions occurred in this world and was inherited by later generations of their descendants, similar to the perspective of the Hebrew scriptures, though from the Islamic perspective this does not exclude punishment in the Hereafter; and unlike the peoples of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot and Shuʿayb, the Israelites were not destroyed as a people, so that their transgenerational punishment extends the point that divine punishment can be meted out in this life as well as in the next. God is swift in retribution against those who invite His punishment through disobedience and lack of faith, but forgiving and merciful toward the repentant [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse with the narrative identifications: "And when your Lord proclaimed — made it known — that He would send against them, that is the Jews, to the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict on them grievous torment through humiliation and the exacting of the jizyah-tax; thus God sent Solomon against them, and after him Nebuchadnezzar, who slaughtered some of them and took others captive and imposed the jizyah on them; they continued to pay this tax to the Magians up until the sending of our Prophet ﷺ, who also imposed it on them. Lo! your Lord is swift in requital of those who disobey Him; and lo! He is forgiving to those who obey Him, merciful in dealing with them" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** The verse's opening verb is a study in itself: *taʾadhdhana* is read by **[Ṭabarī]** from the root of informing, on the authority of Mujāhid reading it as "your Lord commanded," while **[Qurṭubī]** distinguishes *ādhana*, informed, from *adhdhana*, called out, and reports the view that the two forms are interchangeable like "he was certain" and "he grew certain"; **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives "declared" and "ordained" and notes that the construction has the force of an oath, its answer introduced by the emphatic *li-yabʿathanna* [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. *Yasūmuhum* — the word rendered "inflict" — is glossed as "make them taste," the verb of feeding someone a thing by force, which is why the exegetes read the jizyah and the kharāj into it [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the verse's closing pair sets the two attributes that the tradition reads as the balance of hope and fear: swift in retribution for the defiant, forgiving and merciful for the returning [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn].

**Rulings.** The verse is the locus for the ruling of the jizyah as the instrument of the humiliation described here. **[Ṭabarī]** transmits the reports from Ibn ʿAbbās identifying "the terrible punishment" with the jizyah and its collectors with the community of Muhammad ﷺ to the Day of Resurrection; **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same identification, adds Saʿīd b. Jubayr's gloss of it as the kharāj, and answers the objection about the metamorphosis — the tax falls on descendants, "the most abased of peoples," the Jews; **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Maʿārif]** extend the same reading to the historical subjection of the Jews under successive powers, in which light they read the contemporary state of Israel as a continuation of dependence rather than its end [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. The remaining ruling is theological: the pairing of the swift retribution with the forgiving mercy, which **[Ibn Kathīr]** states as a deliberate pattern — encouragement and warning together, so that hearts keep both hope and fear [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And they were struck with humiliation and misery, and they brought upon themselves wrath from God" (2:61); "Abasement shall be pitched upon them wherever they are found, except through a covenant with God and a covenant with the people" (3:112); "And We sent against them Our servants possessed of great might, and they went through the dwellings, and it was a promise fulfilled" (17:5); "Then We gave you a return of victory over them, and We aided you with wealth and children" (17:6); "Say: shall I inform you of something worse than that in recompense with God?" (5:60) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif].

**Reflection.** The verse turns the story's moral into history: what begins as a punishment for the Sabbath and the calf is extended by proclamation to the Day of Resurrection, and the commentators read three thousand years of subjection into it — under Nebuchadnezzar, under the Greeks and Romans, under the jizyah of the Muslim conquests [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī]. What remains striking in the exegesis is how carefully the sources avoid letting the verdict become a licence: **[Ibn Kathīr]***'s* note that the verse closes with the forgiving, the merciful, "so that no despair is felt," and **[Study Quran]**'s* point that unlike the peoples who were destroyed root and branch, Israel was scattered rather than erased, keep the passage's punishment within the framework of correction rather than annihilation [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran] [Saʿdī].

## 7:168

*"And We divided them on the earth into nations; among them are the righteous, and among them are those below that. And We tried them with good things and evil things, that haply they might return."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the recounting of the dispersal: "and We scattered the Children of Israel in the earth" — and "nations" means various groups, scattered; Ibn ʿAbbās said, "In every land some Jews enter it"; Mujāhid said simply, "Jews." "Among them are the righteous" — among these people whom God describes, the righteous are those who believe in God and His messengers; "and among them are those below that" — below the righteous. Ṭabarī notes the qualification: God described them as they were before their apostasy from their religion and before their disbelief in their Lord, that is, before Jesus son of Mary was sent among them. And "We tried them with good things and evil things, that haply they might return" — We tested them with ease of living, comfort in the world, comfort and ample provision, which are the "good things," and by "evil things" the hardship of living, straitness in it, and calamities and losses in wealth — "that haply they might return," that is, return to the obedience of their Lord and turn to it, and repent of their disobedience [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the division as the shattering of a polity: "and We divided them in the earth into nations" means We scattered them in the lands; the intent is the dispersal of their affair, so that no unity was gathered for them — "among them the righteous," in the nominative as the subject, and the meaning is those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, and those among them who did not alter and died before the abrogation of the law of Moses, or they are the ones beyond China, as has preceded; "and among them those below that," in the accusative as an adverb, and al-Naḥḥās said, "We do not know of anyone who read it with the nominative," the reference being to the disbelievers among them; "and We tried them" means We tested them "with good things," that is, prosperity and health, "and evil things," that is, drought and hardships, "that haply they might return" from their disbelief [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the scattering as the emblem of their condition: God divided the Jews into various nations, sects and groups, and he sets beneath the verse the words of 17:104 — "and We said to the Children of Israel after him: dwell in the land, and when the final promise comes, We shall bring you altogether as a mixed crowd" — and the parallel from the jinn: "and among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that; we are groups of different ways" (72:11). He glosses the trial's terms as the times of ease and difficulty, eagerness and fear, well-being and affliction, "in order that they might turn to God" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads it as the catalogue of a scattered people's composition: "and We divided them in the earth into nations" — We scattered and tore them apart after they had been gathered; "among them the righteous," those who fulfill the rights of God and the rights of His servants; "and among them those below that" — below righteousness, either the middling or those who wrong themselves; "and We tried them," according to our custom and way, "with good things and evil things," that is, with ease and hardship, "that haply they might return" from the ruin they were standing in and come back to the guidance for which they were created; and so they remained between righteous, corrupt, and middling [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads the dispersal concretely: that the Israelites are divided into communities on the earth is taken as a reference to the Diaspora, the existence of smaller communities of Jews in various locations throughout the world; "some of them are righteous," since a life of righteousness continues to be possible for those who follow Jewish law and ritual as prescribed in the Torah, as indicated by the importance the Qurʾān places on observance of the Sabbath; and "those who are otherwise" refers to those who do not follow the law, although they continue to be members of this community. It notes the tendency of many commentators to see the Qurʾānic affirmation of righteousness among some Jews, here and in 7:159 and 3:113, 199, as pertaining to the Jewish community of the past — before the coming of the Prophet Muhammad or even before the coming of Jesus — or else to the Jews of Madinah who became Muslim; and it questions those readings, since the verse is clearly in the present tense and seemingly refers to those who have remained Jews rather than those who joined the Islamic community. The good things with which God tries them include worldly provision and ease, the evil things various forms of worldly adversity; and the trial by good and bad fortune is not particular to the Jewish population but is meant in a more general sense, as in 21:35, "We try you with evil and with good as a test, and unto Us shall you be returned" [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** renders: "and We divided them — We separated them — into communities, sects, in the earth; some of them are righteous and some of them are people who are otherwise, disbelievers and wicked; and We tried them with good things, graces, and evil things, misfortunes, so that they might revert from their wickedness" [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** draws the verse's political theology: the phrase "and We divided them on the earth as separate communities" refers to the fact that the Jewish populace has been cut into fragments scattered in all parts of the world, unable to integrate into a solid nation; the word *qaṭṭaʿnā* signifies breaking into pieces, and *umam* is the plural of *ummah*, a group or party. He then states the inference: this indicates that being integrated into a whole, or having an entity as a nation, is a blessing of God, while being disorganized into parts separated from each other is a punishment from Him; the Muslims have always enjoyed the blessing of their own entity and being recognized as an organized people in the world, from Madinah in the time of the Prophet ﷺ to the present day, with Islamic countries from the Far East to the West as obvious proof; and their present state in Palestine should cause no doubt, since they must come together in that place in the last age according to the prophecies, so that ʿĪsā, descending in Syria, will find them gathered rather than scattered. As for the two descriptions within the verse: the righteous among them are those who followed the commandments of the Torah faithfully and did not try to distort them as others did, while those termed "otherwise" include the infidels and those who obstinately disobeyed and even killed their prophets; and the two terms may also refer to those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ and followed the Qurʾānic guidance after its revelation, as opposed to those who believed in the Torah as God's word yet disobeyed or distorted it and sold their eternal salvation for petty gains [Maʿārif].

**Language.** The verse uses two verbs of division: *qaṭṭaʿnā* here and *farraqnā* in the commentaries' paraphrase — cutting into pieces and scattering — and the tradition reads the physical dispersal as the outward sign of a broken unity [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. *Umam* — nations, communities — is the plural of *ummah*, and **[Study Quran]** uses the term's weight to argue against confining the verse's righteous to converts, since the verse speaks of communities that continue [Study Quran] [Saʿdī]. The pair *ḥasanāt* and *sayyiʾāt* is consistently unpacked as prosperity and drought, ease and hardship, health and affliction — the two hands with which provision is administered [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī]. And *laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — that haply they might return — keeps the purpose of the trial in the register of hope rather than vengeance [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn].

**Rulings.** The verse's principal legacy in the commentaries is the judgement about national cohesion: **[Maʿārif]** states it as a general principle drawn from the verse — integration into a people and an entity is a divine blessing, fragmentation a punishment — and reads the condition of the Jews in his own time through it, while **[Study Quran]** reads the same verse as the Diaspora and locates its righteous in the continuing communities of Jewish observance, present tense [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. The second ruling is interpretive: the identity of "the righteous" among them, whether the believers of the past, the Madinan converts, or those who remained faithful to the Torah — a disagreement in which **[Study Quran]** explicitly doubts the restriction to the past [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran].

**Cross-references.** "And We said to the Children of Israel after him: dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you as a mixed crowd" (17:104); "And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that; we are groups of different ways" (72:11); "We try you with evil and with good as a test, and unto Us shall you be returned" (21:35); "And every nation has its messenger" (cf. 10:47); "And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:159) [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the geography of a punishment that is also a mercy: a people cut apart "into nations" is a people whose affairs cannot be gathered, and **[Maʿārif]** reads the dispersal itself as the sentence — while noting that the verse also distributes the community's grades, righteous and less than righteous, so that the verdict is not uniform [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī]. The trial's alternation of ease and hardship is the mechanism the sūrah has been describing throughout: gifts and calamities, both of them reminders, and the purpose stated as return [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. What remains of the verse's subject after its dispersal is the Diaspora — a community maintained in fragments, some of whose members the text still calls righteous [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:169

*"Then there succeeded after them a generation who inherited the Book: they take the goods of this lower world and say, 'It will be forgiven us.' And if a like offering comes to them, they take it. Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them that they should not say of God anything but the truth? And they have studied what is in it. And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear. Do you not then understand?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the verse's opening as a succession of badness: "then there succeeded after these people whom God has described a *khalaf*" — a bad successor: there arose after them, and differed from them, a replacement of evil. He works through the lexicon: the Arabs say "he is a *khalaf* of truthfulness" and "a *khalaf* of evil"; most often praise comes with the medial vowel opened and blame with it static, though both occur in either; and for the static letter in praise he cites Ḥassān's line about the men who follow, and for the opened in blame the verse of Labīd, "Those in whose shade one used to live are gone, and I remain among a *khalaf* like the hide of a mangy camel" — and he suggests the derivation of the corrupt successor from the milk that turns sour from long standing in the skin, until it spoils, or from "the mouth of the fasting person changed," and he cites Labīd's verse in the static form, "and I remained in a *khalaf*." He notes that some said the *khalaf* mentioned here, who succeeded those before them, were the Christians, as Mujāhid said; but his own position is that God described a bad successor to the people whose story He had told in the preceding verses, and that He did not tell us they were Christians in His book, and that their story resembles the story of the Jews more than the story of the Christians; and moreover, what precedes the verse is news of the Children of Israel and what follows it is the same, so that the passage between them being news of the Children of Israel is the more fitting, there being no indication in the verse to divert the report from them to others, nor any evidence making that position sound. So the sense of the speech is: there took the place of those before them an evil replacement, who inherited the Book of God and taught it, and wasted acting by it, opposing its rulings, being bribed in the judgment of God, taking the bribe from the goods of this present, nearer world — and "the nearer" he glosses as the nearer as against the deferred and far — and saying when they do that, "God will forgive us our sins," wishing upon God false hopes, as God said of them elsewhere, "Woe to those who write the Book with their own hands and then say, this is from God, that they may buy with it a small price" (2:79). And "and if a like offering comes to them, they take it": if a prohibited thing of the same sort, from bribery, is laid out for them afterward, they take it and treat it as lawful, and do not restrain themselves from it — God informing us that they are a people of insistence upon their sins, not a people of turning or repentance. He then gives the reports: Saʿīd b. Jubayr, through Manṣūr: "They commit the sin, then ask forgiveness of God; and if the like of that sin comes again, they take it"; and in his other chains, "the like of it" is "sins"; Mujāhid said: "Whatever is offered them in the day of this world, lawful or unlawful, if they desire it they take it, and they seek forgiveness; and if they find the like tomorrow they take it" — with Ibn Jurayj's variant, "they wish for forgiveness"; Qatāda said, "By God, an evil successor, who inherited the Book after their prophets and messengers, God having made them its inheritors and charged them" — and he cites 19:59, "then there succeeded them a posterity who neglected the prayer and followed desires" — and "they wish on God vain wishes, by which they are deluded; neither does anything distract them from anything nor forbid them from that: whenever anything of the world is offered them they devour it, careless whether it is lawful or unlawful"; and al-Suddī said the Children of Israel never appointed a judge without his taking bribes in judgment, and their best gathered and took covenants from one another that they would not do it, but when one of them was made a judge he took bribes, and when it was said to him, "What is the matter with you, taking bribes in judgment?" he said, "I will be forgiven"; the others would attack him for what he had done — and then, when he died or was removed and a man from among those who had attacked him was appointed in his place, he too took bribes; "so if the latter are offered the goods of the world, they take it"; and Ibn ʿAbbās said: "They take what they get and leave what they wish, lawful or unlawful, and say, 'We shall be forgiven'": and Ibn Zayd said, "the book which they wrote themselves; they say, we do not associate anything with God" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** carries the *khalaf* lexicon as well, with Abū Ḥātim's distinction — *khalaf* with the static letter for children and descendants, singular and plural alike, and *khalaf* with the opened letter for a substitute, whether a child or a stranger; Ibn al-Aʿrābī's rule that the opened form belongs to the righteous and the static to the corrupt; the line of Labīd, the derivation of "the worthless *khalaf* of speech," and the proverb "he was silent for a thousand and spoke a *khalaf*"; and the report that these successors are the Jews, who inherited the Book of God and read it and knew it, and opposed its rulings and committed its prohibitions despite studying it — which was rebuke and reproach for them. Then the taking of the goods of this lower world out of greed and appetite; and "they say, 'it will be forgiven us'" — while they do not repent; and the proof that they do not repent is God's next words, "and if a like offering comes to them, they take it." He gives the lexical note that *ʿaraḍ* with the medial vowel is the goods of this world, and with the static letter property other than dirhams and dinars; and that the reference in this verse is to bribes and base earnings; then God censures them for their delusion in saying "we shall be forgiven," since they are in a state in which, if the opportunity were to come to them a second time, they would commit it again — they have decided on the strength of their delusion about forgiveness while persisting; and only the one who desists and regrets says "we shall be forgiven." Then **[Qurṭubī]** adds his own note to the reader: "This description with which God censured these people exists among us," and he transmits the report of al-Dārimī from Muʿādh b. Jabal: "The Qurʾān will wear out in the breasts of a people as a garment wears out and falls apart; they recite it and find in it no desire or pleasure; they wear the skins of sheep over the hearts of wolves; their deeds are greed unmixed with fear: if they fall short they say, 'We shall reach'; and if they do wrong they say, 'We shall be forgiven; we do not associate anything with God.'" And it was said that the pronoun in "if a like comes to them" refers to the Jews of Madinah — that if there comes to the Jews of Yathrib, who were in the Prophet's ﷺ time, an offering like it, they take it as their ancestors took it.
