Then "was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say of God anything but the truth?": the Book is the Torah; and this is a tightening of the obligation to speak the truth in law and in judgments, and that judges should not incline with bribes toward falsehood. And **[Qurṭubī]** adds his own reflection: this that was imposed on them and covenanted with them concerning speaking the truth is imposed on us through the tongue of our Prophet and the Book of our Lord, with no disagreement in any of the revealed laws among the scholars. Then "and they have studied what is in it" — that is, they have read it, being recently acquainted with it; Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read "and they have caused it to be studied," with the consonant assimilated; Ibn Zayd said, "A man with a just claim used to come to them with a bribe, and they would bring out the Book of God and judge for him by it; and when a man with a false claim came, they would take the bribe from him and bring out their own book, which they had written with their own hands, and judge for him by it"; and Ibn ʿAbbās said, "that they should not say of God anything but the truth" — and they had said falsehood in the forgiveness of their sins, which they declared obligatory and asserted decisively; and Ibn Zayd said it refers to the judgments they pass. And some scholars said the meaning of "and they have studied what is in it" is "they have effaced it," by abandoning action by it and understanding of it, from the phrase "the wind effaced the traces," when it wipes them out, and "a worn inscription" and "an effaced dwelling" when the trace is wiped and effaced — a meaning consistent with "a party of those who were given the Book threw away the Book of God behind their backs" and "so they threw it behind their backs." Then "and the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear" — the fear being of what is forbidden — "do you not then understand?" [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the generation's character: after the generation made up of righteous and unrighteous people, another generation came that did not have goodness in them, and they inherited the Tawrah and studied it; Mujāhid's gloss that they will consume anything they can consume in this life, whether legal or illegal, and yet wish for forgiveness; Qatāda's "this, by God, is an evil generation which inherited the Book after their prophets and messengers, for they were entrusted with this job by God's command to them," with 19:59 beneath it; and the observation that they wish and hope from God while deceiving themselves, nothing stopping them, "for whenever they are given an opportunity in this life, they will consume regardless of whether it is allowed or not"; and al-Suddī's account of the corrupt judges and the covenant they took among themselves; then the verse's rebuke: "was not the covenant of the Book taken from them that they would not say about God anything but the truth?" — an admonition, God having taken a pledge from them that they would declare the truth to people and not hide it, as in 3:187, "and when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: you shall make it clear to mankind and not conceal it, but they threw it behind their backs and bought with it a miserable price"; and Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbās: their claim that God will forgive the sins they keep committing without repenting of them. Then "and the home of the Hereafter is better for those who have taqwā; do you not then understand?" — encouraging them to seek God's tremendous reward and warning them against His severe torment: "My reward and what is with Me are better for those who avoid prohibitions, abandon lusts and become active in the obedience of their Lord"; and "do you not then understand?" — do not these people, who preferred this life to what is with Me, have any sense to prohibit them from their foolish and extravagant ways? [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the portrait of the inheritors: until there succeeded, after them, a *khalaf* whose evil increased, who inherited the Book — the reference to it passed to them, and they began to dispose of it according to their whims, and money was spread out to them to give rulings and judgments by other than the truth, and bribery spread among them; "they take the goods of this lower world and say, 'it will be forgiven us'" — while acknowledging that it is a sin and that they are wrongdoers — and this is a saying empty of reality, for it is not truly a seeking of forgiveness and a request for pardon: had it been so, they would have regretted what they did and resolved not to return to it; but when another offering and another bribe comes to them, they take it, having sold the verses of God for a small price and exchanged what is lower for what is better. Then God's censure and the exposure of their boldness: "was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say of God anything but the truth?" — so what is their case, that they say of Him other than the truth, following their whims and inclining with their appetites? — "and they have studied what is in it": there is no obscurity left for them in it, but they come to their affair deliberately and act with insight, which makes the sin greater, the blame severer and the punishment more shameful; and this is from the deficiency of their minds and the folly of their judgement, in preferring the life of this world to the Hereafter: "and the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear" — better than what God has forbidden them of food taken or bribes for judging by other than what God sent down and other kinds of the forbidden. "Do you not then understand?" — will you not have minds to weigh between what should be preferred and what should be preferred over, and what is worthier to be striven for and put first? The property of the intellect is looking to consequences; and one who looks at a petty, fleeting present thing and forfeits a great, enduring bliss — how should he have intellect or judgement? [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** gives the passage its context: the generation who succeeded the followers of Moses is understood by commentators to refer to some later Jews, and Jewish religious leaders in particular, who brought about a certain corruption in the teachings and law of Moses by allowing some commands and prohibitions to be neglected; and some suggest that certain Jewish leaders took bribes in exchange for easing the requirements of the law, with 19:59 cited again for the pattern of a generation who neglected prayer and followed base desires. The corrupt among this later generation grasp the ephemeralities of this lower world, taking whatever they desire of fleeting worldly things, whether lawful or unlawful or even sinful, and assume they will be forgiven for it; and other passages show that certain Jews were overly confident about God's leniency, as in 2:80 and 3:24, where they claim "the Fire will not touch us save for days numbered." That they would grasp a like offering again indicates that they are not truly repentant and that their intention is to persist in disobedience; the covenant of the Book refers to the covenantal obligations imposed on the Jews by the Torah, one of which was to speak only truthfully about God in accordance with what is taught in the scripture, including that God's forgiveness is only for those who are truly repentant and mend their ways, not for those who persist — for which 16:119 is cited: "then truly your Lord — for those who commit evil in ignorance, then later repent and make amends — truly your Lord thereafter is forgiving, merciful." And that the Hereafter is better for the reverent is also stated in 4:77 and 6:32 [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** supplies the verse's lexical and moral analysis: the word *khalaf* signifies a deputy or one trusted with work in one's absence, and the form used here with the merged letter generally denotes a deputy marked with wickedness, as opposed to the good practices of his elders; *warithū* is from inheritance; *ʿaraḍ* means something bought with money and sometimes simply something possessed, and its use for money indicates that anything owned in this world is temporary, since the word, as the antonym of "substance," is used of an object that requires something else to show its existence, like color which needs another thing to appear; and *adnā* is from *dunū*, nearness, so that *dunyā* is its feminine, and it may also be from *danāʾah*, disgrace, in which case it refers to something disgraced. The verse implies that there were two groups among the early Jews, the righteous and the wrongdoers; the people of later generations who inherited the Torah acted opposite to their elders and made the Book an object of trading or a means of earning, manipulating and distorting the text of the Torah for money offered to them; and more than this, they claimed forgiveness despite committing as great a sin as distorting the Book of God. They are warned of the error in the very next sentence: if there comes to them similar stuff they would take to it again — that is, they are in such a state of perversion that if they are offered money for changing another text, they shall readily accept it. The verse has implied that God's forgiveness is always there for those who are mindful of their error and turn to their Lord in repentance, showing remorse and making a firm promise not to repeat the mistake; to persist in sin and claim forgiveness is sheer self-deception. The next part of the verse puts the question to them: were they not made to enter a covenant with God that they would never say anything but truth about God? Yes — they read this pledge in their Book. It is nothing but their impudence and obstinacy that stops them from realizing the truth of the Hereafter, which is exclusively the fate of those who fear God [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** renders the verse: "And there succeeded after them a generation who inherited the Scripture, the Torah, from their forefathers, choosing the transient things of this inferior life — that is, the ephemeral aspects of this lowly thing that the world is — in the way of what is lawful and what is unlawful, and saying, 'It will be forgiven us' for what we have done; and yet if similar transient things were to come to them they would take them. This sentence is a circumstantial qualifier: in other words, they hope for forgiveness whilst committing the same offence again and persisting in it, and in the Torah there is no such promise about forgiveness for persistence in sin. Has not the covenant of the Scripture been taken — the annexation functioning in place of 'in', that is, the covenant in the Scripture — an interrogative meant as an affirmative: that they should not say about God anything but the truth? And they have studied what is in it — this being a supplement to 'has it not been taken?' — they have read what is in it, so why do they impute lies to the Scripture by ascribing to it the idea of forgiveness for persistence in sin? And the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are wary of what is unlawful. Do they not understand — *yaʿqilūn*, which may also be read *taʿqilūn*, 'do you not understand?' that it is better, and so prefer it to the abode of this world?" [Jalālayn].

**Language.** The verse's opening word carries the whole judgement: *khalaf*, a successor, and the philologists' distinction between the opened and static middle letter — the opened form mostly for the good successor, the static for the bad, though **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** both note the usage crosses over, with verses of Ḥassān and Labīd on each side and the proverb about silence and speech; **[Maʿārif]** gives the same in the key of succession, the deputy who betrays the trust of his elders [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. *ʿAraḍ* — the verse's word for what they take — is glossed as the goods of this world, with **[Maʿārif]** drawing the etymology that makes the point: it is the accident that needs another to be seen, unlike substance, and so names what cannot last [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. *Al-adnā* — the nearer, lower — is read as the nearer against the deferred far, and the same root supplies *dunyā* [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif]. And *darasū* — "they have studied" — is given its double edge by **[Qurṭubī]**: either they read it and knew it, which aggravates the offence, or (on the other reported reading of the sense) they effaced it by abandoning its practice, the traces worn away like an inscription in the wind [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī].

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Three strands attach to the verse. The report of al-Dārimī from Muʿādh b. Jabal, carried by **[Qurṭubī]** and applied to his own community: the Qurʾān wearing out in the breasts of a people like a garment, recited without desire, sheep's skins over wolves' hearts, deeds of greed without fear, and the three sayings — "we shall reach," "we shall be forgiven," "we do not associate anything with God" [Qurṭubī]. The judges-and-bribes accounts of al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd: the covenant their best took among themselves against bribery, broken by each in turn, and the two books brought out, God's Book for the paying litigant and the book written by their own hands for the bribing one [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the Prophetic report of the covenant's content, invoked by **[Ibn Kathīr]** through 3:187: that they would make the Scripture clear to mankind and not conceal it [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Rulings.** The verse is the tradition's locus for two standing rulings: the prohibition of taking payment or bribes in judgment, with the covenant to speak only the truth about God and to judge by what He sent down as the obligation the inheritors of scripture broke — and **[Qurṭubī]** extends the obligation to this community expressly, saying that what was imposed on them is imposed on us through the tongue of our Prophet and the Book of our Lord, with no disagreement in any revealed law [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. And the doctrine of repentance that the verse states negatively: forgiveness belongs to the one who desists and regrets, not to the one who persists and presumes; the saying "it will be forgiven us" that accompanies a repeat offence is the verse's own definition of self-deception, and **[Study Quran]** notes the covenant included precisely this — that God's forgiveness is for the truly repentant who mend their ways [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].

**Cross-references.** "Then they were succeeded by a generation who neglected the prayer and followed desires; they will meet with error" (19:59); "And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: you shall make it clear to mankind and not conceal it — but they threw it behind their backs and bought with it a miserable price" (3:187); "Woe to those who write the Book with their own hands and then say, this is from God, that they may buy with it a small price" (2:79); "And they say, the Fire will not touch us except for days numbered" (2:80); "That is because they say, the Fire will not touch us except for days numbered" (3:24); "Then truly your Lord — for those who commit evil in ignorance, then later repent and make amends — truly your Lord thereafter is forgiving, merciful" (16:119); "And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear" (cf. 4:77; 6:32) [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse's indictment is precise, and it is aimed at a class rather than a race: the inheritors of a Book who learned it, judged by it when it suited them, and priced it when it did not, comforting themselves with a forgiveness they never asked for properly [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. The most telling clause is the one the interpreters gloss as a dilemma: "and if a like offering comes to them, they take it" — the evidence that the request for pardon was never a change of direction [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Qurṭubī]**'s decision to turn the mirror is the tradition's own use of the passage: the description, he says, exists among us, and he sets beside it Muʿādh's words about a later people who recite the Book without desire and say "we shall be forgiven" [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr].

## 7:170

*"And those who hold fast to the Book and establish the prayer — indeed, We do not waste the reward of the doers of good."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the reading: the reciters differed over the verb, some reading *yumsikūn* with the mīm lightened and static, from *amsaka yumsiku*, and others reading *yumas-* with the mīm opened and the sīn doubled, from *massaka yumassiku*. The meaning in either case, he says: those who act by what is in the Book of God, and who establish the prayer, within its limits and without wasting its times; "indeed, We do not waste the reward of the doers of good" — whoever of My creation does that, I do not waste the reward of his righteous deed. He transmits Ibn Zayd's gloss that the Book is the Book of God which Moses brought, and Mujāhid's that those who hold fast to the Book are "of the Jews or the Christians" [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the phrase with the Book as the Torah and the holding fast as acting by it, noting that one says "he held fast to it" and "he clung to it," meaning he took hold of it firmly; and he reports that Abū al-ʿĀliya and ʿĀṣim, in the report of Abū Bakr, read the verb lightened, from *amsaka yumsiku* — while the first reading, with the doubled letter, is the preferable one, because it conveys the sense of repetition and intensity in holding fast to the Book of God and to His religion, and by that they are praised; holding fast to God's Book and religion requires perseverance and the repetition of the act. And he cites the line of Kaʿb b. Zuhayr about the man who never truly held to the covenant he claimed but as sieves hold water — the verse's word for clinging set against the image of what cannot be held [Qurṭubī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the verse as praise of the other sort of inheritor: God praises those who adhere to His Book, which directs them to follow His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, adhering to it, implementing its commands and refraining from its prohibitions, and who perform the prayer — and the promise: "certainly We shall never waste the reward of those who do righteous deeds" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** frames the verse as the answer to the previous one: the truly wise are those whom God described in His saying, "and those who hold fast to the Book" — that is, they cling to it in knowledge and in action: they know what is in it of rulings and reports, which are the noblest of the sciences, and they act by what is in it of commands, which are the delight of the eyes, the joy of the hearts, the gladness of the spirits, and the welfare of this world and the next. And among the greatest of the commanded things that must be held fast is the establishment of the prayer, outwardly and inwardly — which is why God singled it out for mention, because of its excellence and honor, its being the balance of faith, and because establishing it is a summons to establishing the rest of the acts of worship. And since all their work was reform, God said, "indeed, We do not waste the reward of the doers of good" — in their sayings, their deeds and their intentions, reforming themselves and others. He then draws the verse's general lesson: this verse and its like show that God sent His messengers, blessings and peace be upon them, with reform and not with corruption, with benefits and not with harms, and that they were sent for the welfare of the two abodes; so that whoever is more righteous is closer to following them [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** reads "those who cling to the Book" as those who continue to adhere to the teachings, commands and prohibitions established in the Torah; the promise that God does not neglect the reward of the righteous means He will not fail to reward them for their deeds, and the verse indicates that those who are Jews and continue to follow the Torah and Mosaic law will be rewarded for their good deeds — with 2:62 cited, that Jews, Sabeans and Christians who believe and work righteousness shall have their reward with their Lord, and 5:69 alongside it [Study Quran]. **[Maʿārif]** reads the verse as the extension of the previous theme: the preceding verse mentioned the covenant made with the religious leaders of the Israelites in particular, that they would make no changes in the Torah and would ascribe to God nothing but the truth; they violated that pledge and distorted the contents of the Torah for petty amounts of money; and this verse says that there are some among their religious leaders who truthfully follow the commands of the Torah and firmly adhere to its guidance, and who established the prayer as required — and to such people the assurance is given that they shall not be deprived of their reward: those who have been true to their faith and fulfilled its demands are the righteous among them. He then makes three points. The Book most probably refers to the Torah, though it may refer to all the heavenly books — the Torah, the Gospel and the Qurʾān. Merely keeping the book of God and showing respect to it without following its commandments does not fulfill the very object of its revelation, which is why the verse used "hold fast" rather than "take" or "read": holding fast to the Book requires following all its injunctions and commands. And out of the many doctrines of the Torah, the verse mentions only the establishing of the prayer, because the prayer is the most significant and purposeful act among the precepts enjoined by God, the most basic and quintessential way of expressing faith in and obedience to Him; offering it regularly makes one capable of regularity in other acts of worship, more willingly and with more ease; the Holy Prophet ﷺ has termed the prayer the pillar of Islam, on which the whole edifice rests — whoever has erected it properly has built the whole structure of his faith on a stronghold, and anyone not regular in the prayer is of no worth to God, even if he is seen reciting His name at all times and has unusual visions and does extraordinary acts [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the verse in a line: "And those who adhere — read *yumassikūn* or *yumsikūn* — to the Scripture from among them and have established the prayer, the likes of ʿAbdallāh b. Salām and his companions: verily We shall not let the wages of the reformers go to waste" — with the note that the sentence is the predicate of "those who," and that the verse replaces the pronoun with the explicit noun "the reformers," that is, their wage [Jalālayn].

**Language.** The verse's verb is its argument: *yumassikūna* with the doubled sīn, against the lighter *yumsikūna*, and **[Qurṭubī]** explains the preference for the doubled form precisely as a semantic matter — it conveys repetition and intensity, the perseverance that holding fast to revelation requires; his citation of Kaʿb b. Zuhayr's line, where the man who never held the covenant is like sieves holding water, shows what the lighter holding amounts to [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. *Aqāmū al-ṣalāh* — they established the prayer — is distinguished from merely praying: **[Saʿdī]** and **[Maʿārif]** both read establishment as outward and inward performance, with **[Ṭabarī]** glossing it as performing it within its limits and not wasting its times [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. And the verse's closing word, *al-muṣliḥīn*, the reformers or doers of good, is the noun the exegetes hear as the summary of everything the Book asks: **[Saʿdī]** takes it as the reform of sayings, deeds and intentions, of oneself and of others, and **[Jalālayn]** reads the substitution of "the reformers" for the pronoun as the naming of the wage itself [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr].

**Rulings.** The verse states the standing principle that God does not waste the reward of the righteous, applied here to those who hold fast to the Book they have inherited. **[Study Quran]** draws from it the ruling that Jews who continue to follow the Torah and Mosaic law will be rewarded for their good deeds, placing the verse with 2:62 and 5:69 and against the readings that confine "the righteous" of this passage to converts; and it notes the continuity with the preceding verse's criticism, so that the passage does not condemn a people wholesale [Study Quran] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** draws the practical ruling from the verse's word choice: respect for the book without compliance does not fulfill the purpose of revelation, and the singling out of the prayer marks it as the pillar on which the rest of the religion's structure stands [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. And **[Qurṭubī]**'s preference for the intensive reading establishes the requirement of perseverance in holding fast, not a single act of adhesion [Qurṭubī].

**Cross-references.** "Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews and the Christians and the Sabeans — whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteousness — shall have their reward with their Lord" (2:62); "And if only the People of the Book had believed and been righteous, We would have removed from them their misdeeds" (cf. 5:65); "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will surely give them a good reward" (cf. 3:171); "And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it" (3:115); "And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice" (7:159) [Study Quran] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī].

**Reflection.** The verse is the passage's counterweight, placed exactly where the sūrah needed it: after the inheritors who sell the Book and the judges who take bribes, the text names those who hold it fast — with the tense of persistence, the doubled letter the reciters argued over — and who establish the prayer [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the sequence as the answer to the question "do you not then understand?" — the intelligent are the ones described here — and draws out of it the largest claim in the passage's exegesis: that the messengers were sent with reform and not with corruption, so that whoever is more of a reformer is nearer to them [Saʿdī]. And **[Study Quran]**'s insistence that the verse speaks in the present tense about Jews who continue in the Torah keeps this consolation in place rather than assigning it wholly to the past [Study Quran] [Maʿārif].
